en: Exhortation to Uphold the Śūraṃgama-sūtra, composed by the śramaṇa of Siṃhalavana, Weishi (Vijñaptimātra).
The King of Śūraṃgamas is fully endowed with the myriad practices and encompasses all dhāraṇīs and samādhis. It perfumes and cultivates the path of śamatha and opens...
To show sentient beings that the wondrous lies in transcending through a single gate:
because Ānanda regretted his excessive learning yet had not fully perfected the power of the Way, Kāśyapa (Kagun) used the pretext of false views to point directly to the human mind.

Through the inquiry of the seven locations, the dust was polished from the precious mirror and its original luminosity manifested spontaneously; through the analysis of the eight returns, the cataracts were scraped away with a golden lancet and illusory shadows dissolved accordingly.
To reject攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective clinging) is to show that the mind is not [the true] mind; to reveal true awakening is to show that even seeing is already free from seeing.

Thus, while manifesting the truth to shatter delusion, one still speaks of the truth by means of delusion. One exhaustively investigates the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), arranging them into these four categories.
Causes and conditions arise spontaneously; both are cast aside. The earth, water, fire, and wind elements are unified and collectively termed the "Seven Great Elements.
The Middle Way of the True and the Conventional is the perfect fusion of the Three Truths. Originating from the Tathāgatagarbha, it encompasses and gives forth the ten voids;
according to the minds of sentient beings, it manifests all phenomena. Thus, even the one and the many are mutually identical, the small and the large contain one another, and precious lands appear.
Turning the wheel of Dharma upon the tip of a hair, and attaining non-obstruction within a speck of dust:

for those who have dissolved inverted perceptions over billions of kalpas, and do not follow discursive thought, the wild mind ceasing is itself bodhi. Those with the faculties of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching have already deciphered the secret cause.
For those of middling and inferior capacities, one must set forth sublime practices. Thus, the path for returning home from afar is opened;
the gate to the dwelling bestowed by the Heavenly King is pointed out; and the fundamental cause of the various sages is interrogated through discourse based on realization.

Taking the initial expedient means as the primary principle of the teaching of this land, the faculty of hearing is selected as the foremost perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). Next, for the purpose of gathering the mind, it is further emphasized.
Generosity and precepts rely on what precedes them. The World-Honored One raised his finger as a pure and luminous instruction, manifesting a transformation-body Buddha who proclaimed secret verses.
When the three trainings are fully perfected, that which is realized is not partial; all delusions vanish, so what need is there for "non-falsity"?

How much more so when one meticulously studies the seven destinies and how beings take birth according to their karma—how painful it is to be likened to the six modes of interaction, where habits invite retribution!
The response reveals fifty kinds of *dhyāna* realms to deeply guard against the demons of craving and false views;
it provides eighty thousand kinds of expedient means for liberation to counteract the defilements of worldly toil and affliction.

It maintains and protects, and exhorts and entrusts the propagation [of the teaching], from beginning to end, such that everything is nothing other than the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization. Whether refuting or establishing, nothing departs from the eternally abiding true mind.
Once the lutes, zithers, and harps encounter skillful fingers, the forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sounds of the Dharma.

This causes those of the icchantika nature to abandon their Mleccha ways and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from within samādhi. Some, by realizing their own true nature, settle securely in the ranks of the sages;
others, through mutual interpenetration, transcend to the final stage of mind. Seated at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimanda*), they ascend to the Unsurpassed.

Awakened! All matters are ultimately firm and solid. He extensively opens the many gates of skillful means for bodhisattvas, traversing the worlds of the ten directions with effortless spontaneity, so that all may together enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments. His teaching is supreme; his merit is magnificent.
I feel ashamed that my errors have led me to venture this attempt at harmonization, yet out of a profound love for the Dharma, I offer these words of praise and exhortation once more.
I invite scholars from all quarters to examine and peruse this work. The preface concludes.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Crown and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle One.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra during the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Mīghaśikṣā of the kingdom of Ujjayinī;
orally interpreted by the Bodhisattva-śīla disciple Fáng Róng of Qīnghé, formerly Grand Master for Regular Counsel,
concurrently Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Director of the Secretariat.
Composed by the Buddhist disciple from Huaihai, Layman Yunkong Lu Xixing;
the Imperial Decree confirmed by Li Dai, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel;
and approved by Liu Dawen, Minister of the Second Grade, Prefect of Huaian Prefecture, Zhili.
Proofread by Yang Xun, Minister of the Second Grade of Merit, Prefect of Yangzhou Prefecture, Zhili Province;
collated by Chen Nanjin, a junior scholar of Huainan.
△ General Explanation of the Scripture Title.
The essence of the Tathāgata’s fruition is inherently such; why should it depend on secret causes? The function of the Bodhisattva’s path is non-active;

what need is there for the support of myriad practices? Being without cause and without action, without cultivation and without realization, and without either understanding or lack thereof, all names and marks—whether great or small—are not established.
This is the true Śūraṅgama, the ultimate and adamantine state. It is especially so.
Because the Tathāgata is hidden within the *tathāgatagarbha* of sentient beings, it cannot be revealed without the secret cause.
Because sentient beings and bodhisattvas have sunk into the seven realms of existence, they cannot escape without cultivating the ten thousand practices.

Thus, the Buddha-king manifested the Great Dharma for them, so that they would not be deluded by minor paths and might silently attain the essence that is beyond all bounds. He illustrated this through the metaphor of the Buddha’s crown, so that they would not...
It causes one to transcend attachment to appearances and reach the ultimate pinnacle of the unsurpassed principle;
it reveals the secret cause of the Tathāgata so that one may clarify the fundamentally wondrous mind, and makes known that all Buddhas of the three periods of time take this as their primary cause.

It clarifies the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization, enabling one to awaken to the ultimate Dharma, and makes known that all sages realize the fruit of enlightenment by relying upon this. Thus...
Reaching the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva’s ten thousand pure practices, there is nothing among all phenomena that is not brought to ultimate completion.

Arriving at the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is firm and indestructible, it is therefore named *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.
It begins with the investigation of the mind and the discernment of vision, and concludes with the destruction of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
To strip away demons is nothing other than the discernment of the marks of vigor.
Tianru said: "The Sanskrit term *śūraṃgama* is the general name for the Great Samādhi. This is translated as 'the ultimate firmness of all phenomena.
An ancient master said: 'Before one has cultivated this samādhi, all phenomena appear as distinct and differentiated.'"

[This is] extraordinary. Bound by the Dharma, once one attains this samādhi, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—all these are quiescent and extinguished in their very place;
this is precisely the eternally abiding mind-nature. Therefore, it is called "ultimately firm and solid."
△ Judging the Sequence of the Sutras (Revising the Old Text):
Now, when the Dharma King preaches the Dharma, there is order and no confusion. First, he teaches the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle to establish the foundation; this is the *Avataṃsaka*.
Next, he teaches the Gradual Teaching of the Three Vehicles to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings; these are the *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras.
Furthermore, the later teaching of the One Vehicle Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna-pūrṇa-śāsana) is used to reveal the ultimate reality; this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* is situated within the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, serving as the ultimate teaching of the true Mahāyāna.

Therefore, the secret causes of the Tathāgata and the methods for the cultivation and realization of the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas are all brought to their final conclusion herein. From this point onward, there is no further progress or cultivation to be made; one directly penetrates [to the source].
This is the perfectly wondrous path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is no further discourse on stages (*bhūmi*);
it speaks solely of the wondrous Dharma, confirming beings according to their faculties and bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) that they shall become Buddhas.

Following the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was then preached, concluding with the constant exposition of supporting the Vinaya. "Supporting the Vinaya" refers to entrusting matters to future generations; "discoursing on the eternal" refers to...
This is why he demonstrates true quiescence. This matter of his final entrustment at the moment of death is not something added to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Yet, commentators who do not base themselves on the intent of "upholding the Vinaya" (*fulü*) have arbitrarily ranked the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* as following after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, also calling it "upholding the Vinaya while discussing the Eternal.
If this were the case, it would mean upholding the Vinaya again after having already upheld it; how could one advance in cultivation?
Thereafter, they continued their cultivation; first they added the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and later they appended the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
This inversion and redundancy have thrown the Dharma of the Dharma King into disorder. To prove this by means of the sūtras:
once a destitute child has received the precious treasury, what more would he seek? Once those at the illusory city have reached the place of jewels, why would they advance further?
After Dīpaṃkara preached the Lotus Sūtra, he entered nirvāṇa at midnight. After Śākyamuni preached the Lotus Sūtra, he immediately proclaimed his extinction before the fourfold assembly.
Why, then, would you further entangle yourself with the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*? If you must insist that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* be placed later, [you contradict these facts].
Thus, although Ānanda had already exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he had not yet exhausted all outflows regarding the *Śūraṅgama*.
Although he was worthy of receiving the Buddha’s prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, his power of the Path (*mārgabala*) was not yet complete regarding the *Śūraṅgama*.

Although he had previously attained realization of the wondrous Dharma, he did not yet know the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Although he had already established himself securely in the Buddha-way, and yet again...
To be immersed in the brothels of sensual desire is entirely inverted; such a principle is inherently impossible.

Therefore, the reason the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is placed after the *Prajñāpāramitā* is that following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the study of wisdom (*prajñā*) flourishes while the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not yet complete.

People may then become submerged in mere erudition and lose the correct state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). It is for this reason that the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama is revealed to support the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

O Mahāmati, one must ensure that concentration and wisdom are balanced so that both study and practice are perfected, ultimately leading toward the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

This is what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* teaches. Regarding the general purport of these three sūtras, they are all for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*mahāntam artham*), yet they necessarily begin with the *Prajñāpāramitā* to bring about illumination, proceed next with the *Śūraṅgama* for cultivation and realization, and conclude with the *Dharma*... [text ends]... 法.
He adorned [the teaching] and granted his seal of approval; thereafter, he brought all the Buddha’s tasks to completion. Such is indeed the natural sequence of these events.
Nevertheless, for guiding one toward the vehicle of dhyāna and for discerning right view, nothing surpasses the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
△ The Main Body in Five Sections:
The main body of this sutra consists of five sections. First is the Section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

Initially, by means of seven inquiries, it reveals the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity (i.e., the first fascicle). Next, by means of the eight returns, it distinguishes the wondrously pure seeing-essence, thereby manifesting the Tathāgata-nature.

The *Ālayavijñāna* (i.e., the second and third fascicles). Furthermore, regarding the mountains, rivers, and myriad phenomena, within the proclamation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it reveals the nature of the true ultimate (*tattva-paramārtha*) (from the beginning to the middle of the fourth fascicle).

All of this serves to enable the practitioner to clarify the mind and perceive its nature (*citta-darśana*), acting as the secret cause for cultivation and realization; therefore, it is called the "Section on Seeing the Path" (*darśanamārga-bhāga*).

Second, the "Section on Cultivating the Path" (*bhāvanāmārga-bhāga*): at its outset, it presents the two definitive meanings for the beginner, causing them to examine the causal mind and the resultant [mind].
He awakens. Furthermore, he examines the root of afflictions as the true foundation for cultivation (from the fourth section to the end).

He definitively reveals the six sense faculties and the sequence for unraveling their knots, enabling the mind that seeks liberation to attain wondrous, perfect penetration—this is the essential requirement for cultivation (from the fifth to the middle of the sixth).
This marks the conclusion of the progressive practice for those of sharp faculties; thus, Āṭavika reached this point and clearly understood the locus of Bodhi.

On the road back, he claimed to have already realized the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood and vowed to deliver beings in the final age. He further requested instructions on how to establish a *bodhimaṇḍa* and the rules for concentrating the mind.

Thereupon, he heard the three trainings in the absence of outflows (*trīṇi śikṣāny anāsravāṇi*), the four types of discipline (*caturvidha-saṃvara*), and the great divine mantras (from the sixth section to the end).

These collectively serve as skillful means for cultivation; therefore, they are called the "Section on Cultivating the Path" (*bhāvanā-aṅga*). Third is the "Section on Realizing the Fruit" (*phala-sākṣāt-kriyā-aṅga*).

Beginning from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and ending with Great *Nirvāṇa*, it sequentially demonstrates the progress through the fifty-five stages until the ultimate attainment of the wondrous enlightenment (*miàojué*) and the realization of the Unsurpassed Way;
therefore, this is called the "Section on Realizing the Fruit. Fourth is the "Section on Concluding the Sūtra," which enumerates five gates to summarize and clarify the great purport.
(8b) Fifth is the "Section on Aids to the Path": first, it clarifies that the heavens, hells, and the seven destinies are all created solely by the mind. Next...

This clarifies the subtle demonic activities within *śamatha*. Fearing that practitioners might purify their minds incorrectly, commit errors, and fall [into lower realms], it is therefore called "Aids to the Path" (*aṣṭama-madhyama-daśama-anta*).
Now, one realizes the Path (*darśana-mārga*) before practicing the Path (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and one realizes the fruit (*phala*) after practicing the Path.
Once the tasks of practice and realization are completed, the sutra concludes here. Thus ends the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. And so says the World-Honored One.

With great compassion, [the Buddha] further desired that sentient beings who uphold the precepts remain scrupulously pure and free from transgressions, and that true practitioners not encounter divergent paths;
thus, he taught the dharmas that assist the Way as his final instructions. Consequently, these teachings entered into circulation and reached their ultimate fulfillment.
This constitutes a single, continuous thread, linked together without interruption; its general outline is as follows.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, [The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa].
△ Main Text: Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling [at Śrāvastī]... with Mañjuśrī as the chief.
This generally describes the assembly for the compilation at the Jeta Grove. Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana [was foremost in supernatural powers].
Śāriputra was foremost in penetrating the truths; Kauṣṭhila was foremost in extensive learning; Pūrṇa was foremost in preaching the Dharma;
Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness; and Upāli was foremost in realizing the emptiness of form.
At that time, King Prasenajit, for the sake of his father the king (and so forth), along with Mādrī and Gaṅgā, returned to the Buddha’s dwelling.
He related in detail the circumstances by which Ānanda had mistakenly fallen into a brothel. King Prasenajit was the ruler of Śrāvastī;
he belonged to the Kṣatriya caste. Caṇḍālas are those who slaughter and butcher, as well as families who engage in prostitution and the sale of alcohol.

Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief. He lamented that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning, yet had not fully perfected his power of the Way.
With earnest sincerity, he entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the attainment of Bodhi through the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.

This was the initial expedient means. At that time, there were also bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as great arhats and pratyekabuddhas from the ten directions, who all wished to hear [the teaching] with joy; they withdrew to sit silently, awaiting the holy instruction. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"You and I share the same life-force; our feelings are equal to those of natural kin. When you first resolved your mind within my Dharma, what superior signs did you see that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy affection for the world?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "I saw that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks were supremely wonderful and peerless.
His physical form was translucent, like lapis lazuli. I constantly reflected that these marks could not have arisen..."
It is produced by the craving of desire. Why is this? The vapor of desire is coarse and turbid; it is a foul-smelling, carnal union where pus and blood are in chaotic confusion.
It cannot give rise to the supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous mass of purple-gold light. Therefore, out of thirsty longing, he followed the Buddha to shave his head.
The Buddha said, "Excellent! Ānanda, you should know that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been in a state of birth and death."
[Continued: It is all because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure brightness, and instead employ various false thoughts.

Because these thoughts are not real, there is cyclic existence. If you now wish to investigate the nature of the true illumination of unsurpassed Bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.
This is because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow the same path; in leaving birth and death, they all rely on straightforwardness.
The mind. Because the words for the mind are straightforward, from the beginning stages to the final level, there is never any sign of crookedness in between.
Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved your mind upon the thirty-two marks of the Tathāgata, what did you see, and who was it that felt this love and delight?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, such love and delight arose through my..."
With his mind and eyes, he beheld the sublime marks of the Tathāgata and gave rise to a heart of love and joy; therefore, I resolved my mind, vowing to abandon birth and death.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "That which you have realized is truly what is loved and cherished, yet it is due to the mind and eyes.
If you do not recognize the location of the mind and eyes, you will be unable to subdue worldly afflictions. It is like a king who has been invaded by bandits."
I shall dispatch troops to suppress and eliminate them. These soldiers must first know the location of the enemy; yet you have been made to wander in saṃsāra because your mind and eyes are at fault.
I now ask you: where, precisely, are this mind and these eyes located?
△ Chapter One: Examining the Mind.
Ānanda was, by means of a celestial Brahma-mantra, drawn into a brothel by the woman Mātangī. His precept-body was about to be destroyed.
"About to" (*jiāng*) is a term indicating that while it was imminent, it was not yet necessarily so. Thus, Ānanda’s spiritual power was seen to be slight in this instance.
However, it was not yet complete. The Buddha proclaimed for him the *dhāraṇī* and he returned home.
Deeply repenting that his power of the Way was not yet perfected, he requested from the Tathāgata the initial expedient means of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
*Śamatha* is cessation; *samādhi* is contemplation; *dhyāna* is meditative concentration. Thereupon, the World-Honored One resolved this for him.
Distinguishing between the real and the false as the secret cause, [the Buddha] first asked Ānanda: "What did you see that led you to sever your attachments and leave the household life?
Ānanda replied: "I saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, which were supremely wonderful and peerless;
because of this, I yearned for him with longing and shaved my head under the Buddha. Thus we know that Ānanda’s seeing of the marks was merely the discrimination of sensory objects.
I see that the mind which has thus been aroused is precisely the mind of deluded conceptualization and攀缘 (*pán-yuán*, object-dependent clinging).
All sentient beings have, since beginningless time, continued in the cycle of birth and death solely because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity.
By means of various deluded thoughts—since these thoughts are not true—there is cyclic existence.
If you wish to investigate unsurpassed Bodhi, you must precisely distinguish between the true and the false. The source from which delusion arises lies within the mind and the eyes.
Thus, the Tathāgata first questioned Ānanda to discover the source of his perception, its characteristics, and his attachment to them. He asked: "Where do your mind and eyes reside now?"
In the following, the seven inquiries and eight refutations all reveal that the deluded mind and deluded views have no fixed substance of their own;

they arise from grasping at conditions. This is called the root of beginningless birth and death, which must be shattered and severed before one can enter the correct samādhi of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
△ 1. The Interrogation (Answering that the consciousness-mind resides within):
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One... [up to] ...it is impossible for it to reside within the body."
Ānanda said, "The conscious mind is within, while the visual faculty resides without.

The Buddha said, "As you sit in this lecture hall, you first see me, the Tathāgata, and only afterwards do you gaze at the gardens and groves. If the mind were situated within your body, it would naturally perceive the internal organs first."
Now, this is not possible. This is called not seeing the Tathāgata, but seeing what is outside the hall.
To claim that the mind which is fully awakened and capable of cognition dwells within the body—such a thing is impossible.
△ 2. The Interrogation (further doubting that the conscious mind is outside):
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and said to the Buddha: [up to] "it is impossible for it to dwell outside the body."
Ānanda spoke again: "I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body; it is like a lamp placed outside a room, which cannot illuminate the interior.
The Buddha said: "If the mind resided outside, then the body and the mind would naturally be unaware of one another."
Just as that food cannot provide this satiety, so too, when one sees my hand with the eyes, the mind immediately discriminates;
it seems to recognize the object through the eye-faculty and consciousness. How could it be that [the mind] exists outside?
Therefore, the notion that the discerning, cognizing mind dwells outside the body is impossible.
△ Third Interrogation (Furthermore, it is suspected that the consciousness-mind lies latent within the sense organs).
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...it would be impossible for them to be like a union of lapis lazuli."
Ānanda was further enlightened: "As the Buddha has said, since the mind does not see within, it is clear that the mind is not inside.
Since the body and mind know each other, it is clear that the mind is not outside. As I reflect upon this, I have come to fully understand this mind."
It lies latent within the sense organ, like a crystal covering the eye; although objects may come into contact with it, they do not obstruct it, and that eye perceives accordingly.
This knowing mind, which is capable of cognition and awareness, cannot see inwardly because it resides within the sense organ.
It is clearly perceived externally because it is hidden within the sense organ. The Buddha said: "You claim that the mind is hidden inside the organ like a crystal vessel.
When that vessel covers the eye, do you see the crystal? Ānanda replied: "I certainly see the crystal. The Buddha said:
"If the mind is hidden inside the organ and can yet see the crystal outside, why can it not see the eye itself?"
If the eye were able to see, then the eye and its object would be co-located, and it could not be established as following [the object].
If it cannot see, then your claim that it is hidden within the sense organ is untenable.
△ Fourth Interrogation (Furthermore, calculating that the vision of darkness is named as being within the body):
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One... [up to] ...there is no such principle as naming the vision as being internal.”
Ānanda further reflected: "The viscera of sentient beings reside within, while the orifices reside without.
Because there are viscera, there is darkness; because there are orifices, there is light. Furthermore, I reckon that my mind resides within;
therefore, when I open my eyes, I see light, and when I close my eyes, I see darkness. The Buddha said: "When you close your eyes and see darkness, as for this realm of darkness, does it..."
Regarding "the eye facing [objects]" and "not facing with the eye": that which is called "facing with the eye" refers to darkness being before one's eyes; how can this be established as internal?

If it does not face [the object], how can there be seeing? If you see darkness when closing your eyes and call that "within the body," then when opening your eyes and seeing light, why do you not see your own face?
If you could see your own face, then this mind of discernment would reside in empty space.
If it is empty space, how can it exist within? If it were in empty space, then it would be as if you were seeing my face.

But when you see my face, is that not your own body? If you insist that both the body and the eye are distinct perceptions, then one person would possess two cognitions, and your single body would become two Buddhas. Therefore, your claim that "seeing darkness is called being within" is untenable.
Such a thing is impossible. △ Five:
The Interrogation (Furthermore, it is reckoned that wherever the mind conjoins, there the mind follows and exists).
Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly... [up to] ...that the mind follows and exists—such a thing is impossible."

Ānanda further reflected to himself: "If my present mode of reflection—this very act of thinking in accordance with objects—is indeed the essence of my mind, then wherever it encounters an object, the mind exists there; it is neither within nor without, nor does it abide in between.
For that which takes reflection as its essence is merely a floating thought; it is not the substantial reality. The Buddha said:
Because they arise from phenomena (*dharma*), various minds are produced; wherever they encounter conditions, the mind accordingly comes to exist.
This is what you mean by saying that the mind has no essence (*asvabhāva*). If the mind has no essence, how can it encounter conditions? If it possesses an essence, how can it follow conditions?
If it were to encounter conditions while lacking an essence, then it would be as Pāpīyān has said: "The nineteen elements (*dhātu*) are caused by the seven."

"The combination of *dharmas* (dusts). This interpretation is not correct; it is clear. The 'nineteen realms, seven *dharmas*, five truths, and six aggregates' were taught by Māra to delude the elder Śūra.
[He asked: 'Where are the realms located? Where are the *dharmas* located? How can that which lacks intrinsic substance combine? Therefore, it is said: 'This interpretation is not [correct]...'"
Nevertheless, if it possesses a physical substance, you should try this for yourself: touch your own body. Does the mind that perceives do so by emerging from within, or does it enter from without?
If it emerges from within, you should see what is inside your body; if it enters from without, why do you not see your own face?
Since you neither see what is within your body nor can you see your own face, where does the substance of the mind reside? Ānanda!
This is difficult to explain. You claim that seeing the body is seeing the face, and thus it is "seeing with the eyes.
To take what is known by the mind as "seeing" is not correct in principle. The Buddha said: "If the eye were able to see, then dead people—who still possess eyes—should be able to see objects.
If they can see objects, how can they be called dead? Your assertion that 'seeing is seeing with the eyes' is not right."
Furthermore, regarding this mind of yours that is capable of awareness and cognition, which you consider to have a substantial body:
let us inquire whether this body is a single entity or multiple entities; does it pervade your entire body or does it not pervade it?
If it were a single entity, when one limb is touched by the hand, the other four limbs should likewise feel it. If it were multiple entities, then it would be called many people. Why?
The substance [of sensation] belongs to you; it resides within your body. If it pervades the entire body, then when one part is pricked, as before, there should be sensation in every place.
If it does not pervade the entire body, then even if you were to touch both your head and feet simultaneously, only the head would have sensation.

The feet ought to be devoid of cognition; yet this is not the case for you. Furthermore, it is not that they are not pervasive. Therefore, your claim that "cognition arises wherever there is conjunction" is untenable.
What would be the consequence if there were no conjunction? Then there would be no establishment of annihilation. A permanently abiding true mind must not be like this.
For by means of the wondrous enlightenment of the true mind, which is eternally quiescent yet eternally responsive, all points of contact are transparently clear.
It is neither internal nor external; neither one nor many; neither pervasive nor non-pervasive. To attempt to recognize it through discursive thought is to distance oneself from it ever further.
Ānanda, you simply do not understand this.
△ 6. Investigation (Furthermore, calculating that the mind resides between the sense organ and the object):
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I have also heard from the Buddha... [up to] ...that it should reside in between—that is not possible."
Ānanda further reflected to himself: "This mind has no object of knowledge within; thus it cannot be established as being inside. The body and mind know one another;

thus it cannot be established as being outside. Now, since they know each other, yet there is no seeing [of the mind itself], it is known that this mind is neither inside nor outside, nor is it in the sense organs.
It must be in between. The Buddha said: "That which is called 'in between'—does it reside within the body?"

If it were located within the objective field, or if it were within the body, it would likewise be "inside. If it were within the objective field, one would necessarily have to establish a physical marker (*pratiśedha*).

Once a marker is established, looking east would result in seeing west, and looking south would result in seeing north; since the substance of the marker is not fixed, the mind would become confused and disordered.
Ānanda said: "What I call the 'middle' does not refer to the center of the body, but rather to the [center] between the sense faculties and their objects."
It is in the middle. As the World-Honored One said: "With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
The eye has discrimination; the dust of form is without cognition. When consciousness arises within the dust, that is where the mind resides. The Buddha said:
"If this mind resides between the faculty and the object, then does the essence of this mind partake of both, or does it not partake of both? If it partakes of both, then it cannot [be one]."

Regarding the term "middle": what is it? It is because objects and substance are in a state of confusion. Objects are not known by substance. "Objects" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*);

"substance" refers to the essence of the mind (*cittatattva*). The sense organs and their objects lack cognition; the essence of the mind possesses cognition. Since objects and the essence of the mind stand as two opposing entities, how can there be a middle?
If they are not combined, one cannot call it the middle. Why? Because if they do not combine, then the sense organs exist in isolation.

When [the mind] resides in the sense faculties, it is not conscious. If it does not simultaneously engage with objects, there is only the mind alone. When the mind resides within, it is not that it lacks consciousness;

yet, if it were neither conscious nor unconscious, it would have no essential nature. What, then, would its characteristic be in the interim? Therefore, one should understand that this refers to the state of being "in the middle."
"It is impossible. △ Seven:
Investigation (Furthermore, calculating that non-attachment is called the mind).
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I previously saw the Buddha... [up to] ...calling it the 'awakened-knowing mind'—it is impossible."
Ānanda again cited what the Buddha had often said: "The nature of the mind that perceives and discriminates does not reside within, nor without, nor in between;
it has no location whatsoever. It is entirely free from attachment. Ānanda asked, "Is this state of non-attachment what you call the 'mind'?
The Buddha said, "Whatever possesses characteristics is called 'all things. Regarding your state of non-attachment, do you consider these objects to be existent or non-existent?"
If it were non-existent, it would be the same as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; how could it be something to which one could be attached, such that one could be called "unattached"?
If this [state] is not non-existent, then "non-existence" is itself a characteristic (lakṣaṇa). Where there is a characteristic, there is a locus; how then could one be unattached?
Therefore, to claim that one who knows and perceives the mind is "unattached to all things" is impossible. Indeed, the mind is empty, false, and floating.
They exist through conditioned perception; fundamentally, they have no fixed essence, nor do they have a fixed location.
With these seven preceding points, he refutes their false locus, intending thereby to reveal the truth. Since Ānanda had not yet attained awakening, he subsequently requested further instruction.
Gushan said: "Taken together, these seven turns seem to refute the four natures. When [the visual faculty] is latent within, seeing within seems to be the nature of self;
when it is outside, it seems to be the nature of other; in between, it seems to be the nature of both; and when it follows conditions without attachment, it seems to be the nature of no cause."
Nāgārjuna said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. Therefore, they are said to be unarisen.
Thus, through seven successive refutations, the Tathāgata leaves the slightest deluded mind with no place of escape.
Once the thieves of delusion are eliminated, the True King is revealed, and the principle of non-arising is seen therein. This...
This refers to the meaning beyond the words.
△ In the second chapter, "Discerning Views," the *Yin Fu Jing* states: "The mind is born from objects and dies because of objects; the mechanism lies in the eyes. From this, one knows that the mind—

Therefore, that which gives rise to birth is designated as the "window" of the eyes. Among those who are lost, there are those who double their confusion by turning their vision toward external objects, thereby becoming utterly deluded regarding the Truth.
For this reason, the World-Honored One urgently provided a point of instruction, so that we might know our own nature of seeing is fundamentally never deluded;
it is the eternally abiding master who does not return, whereas those external objects—
Discriminating reflections: when they depart, they do not remain, for they cannot be recognized as real. This has been illustrated by analogy:

the seeing is like the substance of a mirror, while objects are like reflected images. When the objects depart, the substance of the mirror remains ever-luminous; it has never been seen to undergo change or extinction.
At that time, Ānanda was among the great assembly... [until] "...because you have lost your original constancy, you undergo cyclic existence.

Due to the preceding inquiry, Ānanda came to realize his own delusion and confusion; thereupon, he piteously entreated to reach the limit of reality, wishing for the Buddha to show him the correct path of *śamatha*.
The Buddha said: "All sentient beings, since beginningless time, have been subject to various kinds of inversions."

The seeds of karma arise spontaneously; that practitioners fail to achieve the perfect fruit is entirely due to their ignorance of the two kinds of fundamental roots and their consequent confused cultivation.

What are these two? First is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is this very攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pān-yuán-xīn*—the攀緣心, or "clinging and discriminating mind") that you now take to be your own self-nature. Second is the root of beginningless Bodhi and Nirvana.
The primordial, pure essence is precisely that which you now possess as the fundamental clarity of the cognitive faculty (*vijñāna-sāra-prakāśa*), capable of giving rise to all conditions;

it is that which has been lost. What is meant by "lost to conditions"? It is when, through the arising of conditions, one produces empty, false imaginings and inverted reflections of phenomena—just as a person merely sees the reflection in a mirror and forgets the substance of the mirror itself. Thus, the true nature is lost. Now, I shall [explain] this for you.
“Discern this for me. Raising his arm and bending his fingers into a radiant fist, the Buddha asked Ānanda, “Do you see it?
Ānanda replied, “I see the World-Honored One raising his radiant fist, which dazzles my eyes and mind. The Buddha said, “By means of what do you see it?”
Ānanda replied, "I see with my eyes. The Buddha said, "If you see with your eyes, what do you take to be the mind?
When I was shining my fist [at you], Ānanda said, 'The Tathāgata is now investigating the location of the mind, and I am using my mind to investigate and pursue it;
that which is capable of this investigation, I take to be the mind. The Buddha said, 'Alas, Ānanda! This is not [the mind]...'"
Ānanda’s mind was startled and he lost his composure. He addressed the Buddha, saying, "This is not my mind. What should it be called?
The Buddha said, "This is a false conceptualization arising from the illusory nature of external objects; it deludes your true nature.

Reaching this present life, you have mistaken a thief for your son and lost your original constancy; therefore, you undergo the cycle of rebirth. After this single reminder, [the teaching] proceeded point by point.
[The text is] compact; it should be studied with great care.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One" [up to] "...with palms joined and a pure mind, he waited for the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
The World-Honored One desired to cause Ānanda and all sentient beings to obtain the wondrously luminous mind and attain the pure eye.
Therefore, having previously granted [the existence of] the mind that perceives, this section further clarifies the nature of seeing.
Building upon the preceding light, which brilliantly illuminates the eyes and the mind, the Buddha establishes a metaphor and asks Ānanda: "If there were no hand of mine, my fist would not be formed;
if there were no eye of yours, your seeing would not be formed. Is this principle not the same? This principle is fundamentally not the same, yet Ānanda says it is. The Buddha said:
This argument is not correct. Why? Because while the fist of one without hands is ultimately extinguished, the vision of one without eyes has never been extinguished.
Now, if we take a blind person as our example and ask them, they will surely say: "Right now, before my eyes, by nature I see darkness.
Judging from this principle, it is the external object that is dark; what deficiency could there be in the seeing itself to cause the sudden absence of sight for one who lacks eyes?
When one obtains the light of the eyes and perceives external objects, manifesting them as various forms and colors, this is called "seeing with the eyes.
How does this differ from a person in darkness who suddenly obtains the light of a lamp and sees various forms and colors—is this still "seeing with the eyes," or is it "seeing with the lamp"?
One should know that while the lamp can reveal color, the one who actually sees the color is the eye, not the lamp. By this analogy, one should understand that it is the eye that is able to see form.
Thus, for one who sees in this manner, it is the mind that sees and not the eye; knowing and seeing do not depend on the eye but reside directly within the mind.
This constitutes the true awakening to the nature of seeing, whereby one directly transcends the burdens of form and may attain the pure Dharma-eye.
Yet Ānanda had still not attained awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his cotton-soft (tūla-piṇḍa-like) [hand]... [to whom does it move? The Buddha said, "It is so.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "In the past, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, for the sake of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the five bhikṣus, and the fourfold assembly, I spoke:
'That all sentient beings do not achieve bodhi or arhatship is entirely due to adventitious [defilements].'"
"Deceived by the afflictions of the dust [of passion], by what means have you all attained awakening and achieved the fruit of sainthood?

Kātyāyana rose and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Among this great assembly, I alone have gained renown for my understanding. It was by awakening to the two characters 'guest' and 'dust' that I attained this fruit.
What is meant by 'guest-dust'? It is like a traveler who stays overnight at an inn; once his business is finished, he packs his belongings and departs."
On the road, there is no time for rest. If the actual host has no place to go, I shall take this state of non-abiding as the meaning of "guest," and the state of abiding as the meaning of "host.

Furthermore, it is like the clear sun rising in the sky and its light entering through a crack, where the appearance of dust is seen; while the substance of the dust vibrates, empty space remains tranquil. I shall take this clarity...
Quiescence is termed the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that which is agitated is termed the meaning of dust (*rajas*). The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is.

The guest is a metaphor for the coarseness of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*); the dust is a metaphor for the subtlety of innate [afflictions] (*sahaja*). However, as for the guest in the inn...
To drive away [dust] is easy; to sweep away the dust in a dark crevice is truly difficult.

Thus, the co-emergent afflictions (*kleśa*) must wait until the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are exhausted before they can be completely eradicated. This is explained in detail in the ten fascicles.
At that moment, the Tathāgata bent his five fingers, then opened them after bending them, and bent them again after opening them. He asked Ānanda: "What do you see now? Ānanda...
Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing among the assembly. The Buddha said, "Is it my hand that opens and closes, or is it your vision that opens and closes?
Ānanda said, "It is the Tathāgata’s hand; it is not because of my vision. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
First, by asking about opening and closing, I clarified the dust of movement. Next, by asking about motion and stillness," [he proceeded].
This clarifies that the guest does not abide. Thus we know that movement, stillness, opening, and closing all reside in the object and not in the mind;
this is also very clear. Thereupon, the World-Honored One raised his palm and sent forth light to illuminate Ānanda.
Ānanda looked left and right, his head moving incessantly. The Buddha said, "Is it your head that moves, or is it your vision that moves? Ānanda—
[Ānanda] said, "My head moves, yet my nature of seeing remains without even a moment's cessation; who, then, is it that stirs?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: "...in this cycle of saṃsāra, they themselves take up the turning of the wheel."
Furthermore, if sentient beings regard that which is shifting and wavering as "dust" and that which does not abide as "guests," they have already recognized the luminosity;
they must now seek a clear understanding at this very moment. Observe Ānanda: though your head and eyes shift and move, your vision remains unmoving;
observe my hand: though the fist opens and closes, the seeing has no contraction or expansion. Thus, that [vision] is unmoving.
It wavers. That which neither rolls up nor unrolls—what thing is this? Is it not, in itself, your true nature?
Why is it that sentient beings take movement to be the body, failing to realize that the unmoving is not the body;

they take movement to be the object, failing to realize that the seer of the object is not the seeing? They identify external things as themselves, thereby losing their true nature and transmigrating in saṃsāra.

To undergo the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) by one's own taking is indeed appropriate. This is because they blame [the mind] for recognizing adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*) while neglecting its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Wénlǐng says: "The myriad phenomena of mind and objects all possess a fundamentally quiescent essence. Apart from this fundamental essence, everything is adventitious dust.
It is like the opening and closing of a hand or the movement and shaking of a head; when these cease, the fundamental essence remains as it is."
In stillness, there is nothing else; thus, all ordinary delusions and movements are fundamentally unobtainable. Yet you sentient beings take movement for your body and movement for your environment;
this is merely to recognize adventitious dust while neglecting true nature. Acting in such inversion, you wander through the cycle of saṃsāra—its very omens begin here.
It is said that within this very state where one takes hold of true nature, it is originally...
There is no transmigration; each takes [their state] for themselves. This is intended so that they may awaken at the very place where they are deluded.

△ Third: The Permanence of the True Nature.
Following the preceding discussion on how one loses the true nature and acts in delusion, this section explains the causes for such loss and delusion.
This essence of seeing, clear and bright, is my true nature; it is profound and eternally abiding, fundamentally without loss.
It is only due to inverted views that it appears as if lost.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [from "until" they] leaped for joy with the great assembly.
Having heard the Buddha’s instructions, Ānanda felt serene in body and mind, reflecting that since beginningless time he had lost his original mind.
Having falsely identified with the objects of the senses and discriminated between reflected phenomena, you have now attained awakening.

I pray that the Tathāgata will reveal the true and the false, the real and the unreal, regarding the body and mind, as well as the present processes of arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing.

Therefore, the Sūtra again uses King Prasenajit to raise this point, clarifying that the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is fully present even within the state of bondage. The King cites the non-Buddhist teacher Kātyāyana...
Katyāyanīputra said, "Annihilation after death is called *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha said, "You have never experienced cessation;
how then do you know of cessation? The King said, "I observe that preceding moments pass away and new ones do not abide, like fire turning to ash, gradually dissolving and perishing.
I am certain that this body must likewise reach total extinction. The Buddha said, "The King observes..."

"Your body changes with the years and transforms with the months; it shifts and alters without ceasing. Do you realize that while you perish, you also know that within your body there is something that does not perish at the time of death?
I shall now show you this nature of non-arising and non-perishing. Your age has passed from childhood to old age;
look at these waters of the Ganges—do you see them as they were when you were a child? The King replied, "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said, "O King, although your face is wrinkled, this essence of vision has never been wrinkled in its nature. That which is wrinkled undergoes change;
that which is not wrinkled does not change. Since that which does not change is fundamentally without birth or extinction, how could you undergo birth and death within it?"
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the King suddenly awakened to the true and eternal, and no longer clung to the view of annihilationism.
Ānanda then rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and [continued] until the Tathāgata declared him to be one who is worthy of compassion.

Ānanda rose and addressed the Buddha, saying, "If this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion? Thereupon, the Buddha extended his arm;
with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda and said, "Do you see my hand? Is it upright or inverted? Ānanda replied, "According to worldly convention..."
Sentient beings generally take this to be inverted; yet I do not know who is right and who is inverted.
To take what hangs down as upright and what stands vertical as inverted is truly a perverted view. However, this inversion is merely a matter of exchanging the head and the tail.

The arm and the body are originally one; it is through the attachments of deluded sentiment that they appear as distinct. By this analogy, the Dharma-body is fundamentally identical, yet it appears different due to inversion.
When this principle is revealed, one knows that the body of the Tathāgata is that of Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), whereas your own bodies are termed "inversions of nature.
Nature itself is without loss; it is only because of the inversion of nature that it is lost. Furthermore,
By what standard do you designate something as "inverted"? Is it not the delusion within awakening that you have failed to recognize?

I have always taught that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and the various objects of perception (*ālambana-dharma*), are manifested solely by the mind. "Form" refers to the six sense organs; "mind" refers to the mental consciousness;
and "mental factors" refers to the two types of fruits—wholesome and unwholesome—as well as the two kinds of retribution: the primary and the secondary. These are the *dharmas*.
This refers to the myriad dharmas; that is, these various phenomena all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-citta*).
They are like images appearing in a mirror: the entire substance is the mirror itself. Your current illusory and deluded body and mind are both manifestations of this wondrously luminous mind-mirror.

You ought not to identify with the illusory and deluded, but instead awaken to the wondrous luminosity. Yet, on the contrary, you have abandoned the fundamental wondrousness and clung to the illusory and deluded.
Is this not delusion? Those who have attained awakening regard that essence of nature as empty and tranquil, yet they take it to be wondrously luminous rather than dark and obscure;
regarding those phenomenal forms, they take them to be conditioned reflections rather than truly existent.
It is because the perfectly wondrous and luminous mind is fundamentally neither emptiness nor form; it is entirely one true awakening.

Due to the sudden arising of delusive objects, the five aggregates obscure and cover it, forming a state of dark obscurity. Thereupon, the essence of awakening is transformed into inert emptiness, and the wondrous luminosity is obscured into delusive form.
Once emptiness and form are established, conceptual appearances compete to arise; as form and concept intermingle, the physical body subsequently comes into being.
There is delusory vital energy (*prāṇa*) that accumulates therein; internally it fluctuates according to mental appearances, and externally it rushes toward sensory objects.
This state of confused agitation—how could it be recognized as the essence of the mind? The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says:

"To delusively take the four elements to be the appearance of one's own body, and the shadows of conditions from the six sense-objects to be the appearance of one's own mind—is this not solely delusion? To be further deluded within that delusion."

Consequently, you claim that this mind definitely resides within your physical body; yet you do not realize that this mind is vast, pervading the sands of the universe, and subtle, beyond compare. It is like the great ocean, while you now identify a single bubble as the entirety of the tide. To exhaustively search the depths of the vast sea [for it] is surely to double one's confusion. For the bubble has no substance; to take it as such— [The text continues: ...is to mistake the wave for the water itself. How could this be anything other than a profound delusion? If you wish to understand the true nature of the mind, you must first abandon all such attachments. Only when you have severed the root of these delusions will you be able to perceive the original source. This is why the Buddha said: "The mind is originally pure; it is only due to adventitious defilements that it appears otherwise. You must now diligently cultivate yourself to remove these obstacles.
