Together with the seeing, they constitute a cataract of the eye; therefore it is said: "The shadow and the seeing are both cataracts. However, that which perceives the cataract is not itself a cataract;
therefore it is said: "Perceiving the cataract is not a disease. Why is this? When the eye has the disease of a cataract, one sees a circular shadow;
yet that which perceives the presence of that cataract-disease is my wondrously luminous true essence, which is fundamentally free from disease and does not suffer from cataracts.
This is the disease of illness. Therefore, one is able to see clearly. My eyes now have the ailment of cataracts;
if this cataract is removed, the true vision will naturally return to its original essence, which is suchness (*tathatā*), eternally abiding and immovable.

One should ultimately not say that these cataracts are the lamp or the vision, nor that within them there is something that is neither lamp nor vision. It is just as there is only one moon in the heavens. To see the truth—
Regarding the moon, how could one further say that there is a second moon? For what reason? That second moon is produced by pressing upon the eyes;

it is entirely illusory and should not be subjected to exhaustive inquiry as to whether it has form or lacks form, or whether it is produced apart from seeing or is not produced apart from seeing. The meaning of this lamp-shadow is also like this.
This is so. Since one realizes that [phenomena] have no inherent substance, what need is there to apply the mind?
Why is this called "deluded vision of the same portion" (sabhāga-viparyāsa-darśana)? [It refers to] the pure fundamental mind, which is the eternally abiding original enlightenment.
What is meant by "shared delusory vision"? It is like the various lands within Jambudvīpa.
If the people of a single nation collectively encounter adverse conditions, then among that multitude they will perceive all manner of inauspicious phenomena:
the sun, moon, and stars; shifts in yin and yang; and various signs of malevolence and calamity—all of these they will see without exception. And yet, those...
To sentient beings of other lands, this has never been seen before, nor has it ever been heard of; this is what is called the deluded vision of shared karma (*sabhāga-viparyaya-darśana*).

I shall now, for your sake, distinguish the karmic actions of shared karma through both principles and metaphors, clarifying them through mutual illustration and through both positive and negative reasoning.

Just as those who experience the separate karma see a circular shadow within a lamp, this arises solely from a cataract in the eye and is not produced by the lamp itself; it is a particularity of the sense organ.
This is a delusion of the seeing itself; it is not a delusion of the objects seen. Therefore it is said: "The cataract is the exhaustion of seeing; it is not created by external forms.

However, one who does not have a cataract will never suffer the fault of such seeing. By this analogy, you should understand that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the lands, and sentient beings that you today observe with your eyes are fundamentally without reality, appearing like the circular reflection in the lamp. One who sees the reflection in the lamp is as one who has a cataract.
As for illness, this unreal realm may also be called that which is produced by the disease of vision since beginningless time.
Why is this? Because both are equally unreal. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All sentient beings have, from the beginningless past, illusory ignorance;
it is like flowers in the sky, appearing as forms based upon space. The meaning is roughly as follows. Now, as for my faculty of sight:
This vision, although appearing before one as the object perceived by that [defective] sight, cannot itself produce the cataract.

This cataract was originally produced by that which perceives the objects of my enlightened awareness (*jue-ming*). When awareness conditions external objects and gives rise to discrimination, it becomes that which is conditioned by awareness;
this is what truly produces the cataract. It is only my fundamental enlightened mind (*ben-ju ming-xin*) that is aware of all things.

That which serves as the condition is not itself the cataract. Fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is like a healthy eye; the clarity of awakened awareness is like an eye disease; the sense organs and their objects are like a lamp and its shadow.
If one simply perceives the cataract of that which is perceived, then this awakening has already not fallen into the midst of the cataract.

This is what is meant by "seeing the illness is not the cataract"; it is truly the seeing of seeing. How could one further use the faculties of awakening, hearing, knowing, and seeing to [perceive] the cataract within?
To name it according to its function! As previously stated: "At the time of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not [the true] seeing. This directly answers this question.
Therefore, you now merely see people seeing me and all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world;

these all belong to the "seeing-illness" (*jien-sheng*). They are not the one who sees the illness. Indeed, each person inherently possesses their own "seer of the illness," which is the primordial [nature].
The essence of seeing is called the true nature of the seeing-essence; it cannot be termed "seeing. The previous statement, "seeing is not seeing," intends precisely this.
As for the phrase "common deluded seeing," this uses individual karma as an illustration, referring to that single person.
Take this one country as an example: when a single person suffers from eye disease, the shadows of lamps appear; when the whole country is afflicted by pestilence, calamities arise in succession.

Seeing these shadows and seeing these calamities, they all equally return to false perception. Furthermore, using this one country as an analogy for that great trichiliocosm: [the same principle applies].
This same awakened clarity, the immaculate and wondrous mind, relies upon the Truth to give rise to delusion. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the illusory conditions of disease;
through their conjunction, there is illusory birth, and through their conjunction, there is illusory death.

If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction, then one eliminates the causes of all birth and death, perfects Bodhi, and realizes the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing—pure.
"Purify the fundamental mind. Fundamental enlightenment is eternally abiding. Wénlǐng says: "The various conditions of conjunction arise from objects to produce the coarse marks of deluded thought.
Those that do not conjoin are the solitary realization apart from conditions; yet these constitute the subtle marks of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
They can impair *bodhi*, give rise to birth and extinction, defile the pure mind, and cause one to sink into fundamental enlightenment. Therefore, one must distance oneself from them."
△ Chapter Six: Awakening Is Not a Conjunction.
Ānanda had previously realized that fundamental awakening is wondrously luminous, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature;
yet he still did not clearly understand that this source of awakening is neither born from conjunction nor from non-conjunction. This constitutes the awakened mind.
Because there were still remaining doubts regarding external objects, the World-Honored One again clarified them for him. He brought up the previous external objects once more and asked:
"Ānanda, although you previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment... [and so on] ...even all the various obstructed things are likewise thus."
Ānanda, you harbor doubts based on the deluded conceptions of all the world, regarding the nature of the conjunction of various causes and conditions.
You suspect that the realization of the Bodhicitta arises from such conjunction;

yet, if you hold this view, then as for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing, does it conjoin with light, or does it conjoin with darkness, or does it conjoin with openness, or does it conjoin with obstruction?
If there were any blending with something else, one would be entangled in delusory objects rather than being wondrously pure.

If it were blended with clarity, then since clarity is already manifest before you, where would the seeing be intermingled? Seeing and its characteristics can be distinguished by direct observation. If clarity and seeing were mixed together, what form or image would they take?
If you claim that clarity is not seeing, how could you see clarity as if it were intermingled? If clarity...
One sees immediately. But who is it that performs this seeing? Furthermore, it appears not to be mixed [with light]. If there were mixing, there would necessarily be blending;
yet this substance of seeing is complete and perfect—wherein could it blend with light? The substance of light is also complete and perfect, and by itself does not blend with seeing.

This seeing must be distinct from light and does not mix with light. If it were mixed, it would lose its wondrous, luminous, and pure nature; yet you claim that seeing and light blend. This is not so.
Its meaning is thus. The examples of darkness versus clarity, and obstruction versus penetration, can be understood from this very principle;
it is likewise so. Furthermore, Ānanda, as for you now—[from "you now" up to] "and all the various obstructions"—it is also like this.
"Harmony" means being mixed yet not indistinguishable; "union" means being joined yet not separated. The former clarifies the meaning of harmony, like water blending with soil;
the latter clarifies the meaning of union, like a lid fitting onto a box.
Furthermore, Ānanda, that wondrous, pure essence of seeing does not conjoin with light, darkness, penetration, or obstruction.

If it were to conjoin with light, then when darkness arrives, the characteristic of light would have already ceased; this seeing, having conjoined with light, would likewise have to perish along with it.
How then could it conjoin with darkness and yet perceive darkness? If, when perceiving darkness, it does not [conjoin with it]...
If seeing were conjoined with darkness, then one who sees light should not be conjoined with light; if not conjoined with light, then one would not see light.
If one does not see light, how can it be said that seeing is conjoined with light while simultaneously discerning that light is not darkness?
It is the same for that darkness, as well as for openness and all manner of obstructions.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I reflect upon this—[up to] the various classes of obstructing beings—it is likewise so.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I now reflect, is this wondrous source of enlightenment not in a state of conjunction with the various conditioned objects and the mental deliberations?
The Buddha said: "It is also not the case that it is not in a state of conjunction. 'Conjunction' means being with..."
Brightness and darkness, penetration and obstruction, and so forth, are all in harmony. Generally, when things are not in harmony, both sides possess distinct boundaries.
You should observe this carefully: where is the brightness? Where is the seeing? Within the seeing and within the brightness, from what do they take their boundary?
If you search for the boundary and cannot find it, it is not that they are not in harmony. Not only can you not find the boundary, but even the very concept of a "boundary" is unattainable.
This is not established. If, within the limit of light, there were necessarily no seer, then this seeing and the light would not reach one another.
To reach one another constitutes having a boundary. Now, since you do not even know where the characteristic of light is located, how can a boundary be established?
Since the meaning of a boundary is not established, it is not the case that they are not in harmony. This is likewise true for darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.
Furthermore, if you claim that seeing does not conjoin with light, darkness, penetration, or obstruction, then seeing and light would be as discordant as the sense organ and its object;
they would be as utterly non-contacting as the ear and light. In that case, for now, one would not know where the characteristic of light resides.
How does one discern the principle of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*)?
Now, since the perceived object is not at odds [with the sense organ], and yet it appears as if it were not non-conjoined, the same logic applies to darkness, openness, and various obstructions.
△ Manifesting the Nature of the Store:
From the beginning of the seventh fascicle, the nature of awakening is elucidated, and the distinction between the real and the false is extensively debated.
Upon reopening the eyes of wisdom and once again sweeping away remaining dust, the body and mind become liberated and both the real and the false vanish; thus, the Tathāgata-garbha can be manifested.
The nature of the ālayavijñāna causes one to know that the faculties, objects, sense bases, and elements are each perfectly luminous; every phenomenon is clearly manifest.
This is called the root of creating awakening and cultivating realization.
Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all floating dust [of phenomena], up to and including delusion and enlightenment, birth and death, are utterly unattainable.
Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all these floating dusts and illusory transformations arise at the very place they appear and perish at the very place they exist.
Fundamentally, they have no arising, nor do they have any combination; they are merely called "phenomena" based on illusory falsehood. To trace their origin...
The fundamental nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightenment and clarity. For illusions have no self-nature; they depend upon the True to exist.
They are like flowers arising from space—their entire substance is space itself; or like bubbles arising from water—their entire substance is water itself.

Therefore it is said: "Its nature is truly wondrous enlightenment. The essence of clarity is thus. This applies even to the five aggregates and six sense bases, from the twelve entrances up to the ten [realms].
The eight realms arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are called "extinction" falsely when causes and conditions disperse.
Yet one does not realize that this is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrous function, immovable and all-pervading, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this true and eternal nature, it is utterly impossible to find coming or going, delusion or awakening, birth or death. Question: Regarding True Suchness—

"Nature is possessed by every person. Fundamentally, there is no birth, death, coming, or going. Why, then, do these appear to exist in reality today? He replied, "They exist because they are not true and permanent;
if they were true and permanent, they would not exist. It is like flowers in the sky or bubbles on water: when the eyes are diseased, one sees flowers;
when the wind stirs, bubbles form. How could these be true and permanent? If the vision were clear and limpid, one would seek for those flowers and bubbles in vain."
Can it be attained?
△ The form of the five aggregates is like flowers in the sky; sensation is like touching one's own palm; perception is like describing a plum.
The formations are like a torrential stream; consciousness is like a bird soaring through space.
Ānanda, how is it that the five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously?
What are the five aggregates? They are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.

This is because illusions have no self-nature and exist in dependence upon the Real, just as flowers depend upon space and bubbles depend upon water. The Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrous nature of the human Dharmakāya.
It is called "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) in reference to its fruition; it is called "Garbha" (Womb/Treasury) because it encompasses all virtues; it is eternally abiding.
It is immovable, omnipresent, perfect, and wondrous. Although the myriad things reach the divine nature, it is not different in all of them;

thus it is called "wondrous. The nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is able to perceive this nature; once this is perceived, delusion, awakening, birth, and death can no longer be found. What are the five aggregates (skandhas)?

They are form (rūpa), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna). These five constitute the body and obscure the wondrous luminosity. By means of form...
This is spoken of in terms of the *skandha* of form (*rūpa-skandha*). For example, suppose there is a person who, with clear eyes, gazes upon a bright, cloudless sky.

Seeing only the empty sky, vast and devoid of anything at all, that person, for no reason, fixes their gaze without moving their eyes; through this staring, they become fatigued and then perceive within the void various illusory flowers (*keśoṇḍuka*).
Furthermore, there are all manner of other such delusory appearances. One should know that these are the non-characteristic *skandha* of form.
It is also like this. A clear sky with pure eyes is used as a metaphor for pure wisdom, because one contemplates the wondrous nature; thus, there is ultimately nothing at all.
The flowers that weary the eyes in the sky are used as a metaphor for delusive causes and conditions and delusive forms; therefore, one separately perceives these mad appearances.

Yet, these forms of the aggregate (rūpa-skandha) do not exist because of external objects, nor do they emerge from the sense organs themselves. This is analogous to how those mad flowers do not arise from the sky, nor...

If it were to come from space, then there would be entering and exiting. That which has entering and exiting does not possess the characteristic of empty space. If it were not empty, it would be substantial;
being substantial, it could not accommodate the arising and ceasing of its illusory manifestations, just as Ānanda’s own body cannot accommodate another Ānanda.
Thus, one can see that the flowers do not arise within space. If they were to emerge from the eyes, then the eyes must be capable of seeing; yet, how could they emerge?

Since you see flowers when looking out, you ought to see your own eyes when looking in. If there were no seeing, then just as [the vision] obscures the sky when looking out, it ought to obscure the eyes when looking in.
Furthermore, if the eyes see flowers when looking out, the eyes should be free of obscuration. An eye that is free of obscuration is a healthy eye; why then must it necessarily see a clear sky?
It is only when there are no flowers that it is called a healthy eye. That [the vision] does not emerge from the eyes itself is evident through these three points of analysis. This is so.
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of form is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
It is, in fact, the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The following four aggregates should all be understood by this same analogy.
Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet (up to: ... are neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature).
Speaking in terms of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*): suppose there is a person whose hands, feet, and hundred bones are at rest and in perfect harmony;
suddenly forgetting his body, he originally has no sensations. For no reason, that person suddenly rubs his two palms together against empty space, and immediately [a sensation] arises.
The various characteristics of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat—these are all illusory touches. They do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm.
If they came from space, then since they can touch the palm, why do they not touch the body? How could it be that empty space selects the palm to be touched?

If it were to emerge from the palm, it should not depend upon your closing and rubbing [the hands] for its production. Furthermore, if it were to emerge from the palm itself, then as there is an emergence, there must also be an entry;
since the palm possesses cognition at the time of emergence, the arm should possess sensation at the time of entry, such that one would both know the emergence and know the entry.
If there were inherently a single entity that comes and goes within the body, why would it require the joining of palms before it could be perceived?

Thus, it is clearly demonstrated through these three examinations that the aggregate of sensation is empty and false, fundamentally neither arising from causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.
Ānanda, it is like a person speaking of [the five aggregates] up to [the aggregate of perception], which are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
To speak of the aggregate of perception is like a person speaking of sour plums, where water flows from the mouth;
or thinking of treading on a precipice, where the soles of the feet feel a stinging ache. This water in the mouth does not arise from the plum, nor does it enter from the mouth. If one were to say...
Master Mei: Even Master Mei himself cannot speak of this water; how could he cause others' mouths to salivate?
If it were to enter through the mouth, the mouth would close of its own accord—why wait for the ears? If one hears this water with the ears alone, why does it not emerge from the ears themselves?
To contemplate treading upon a precipice is analogous to this principle. Therefore, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally not the cause.
Conditioned, not of spontaneous nature—this is made clear by the threefold analysis.
Ānanda, it is like a torrential stream and its waves (up to) being fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

Speaking in terms of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): it is profoundly clear yet delusively moving; it pursues objects and shifts about, changing and passing away from moment to moment, with nothing new remaining still.
It is like that torrential flow, where waves succeed one another. Such a nature of flowing does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water;
it is neither the nature of water, yet it is not separate from space and water. If it were produced because of space, then throughout the ten directions there would be no...
Pervading all of space, they form an inexhaustible flow; the worlds naturally and simultaneously undergo submersion.

If [this flow] exists because of water, then the flow should exist apart from water, possessing its own distinct essence, characteristics, location, and spatial dimensions, and it should be manifest right now. If, on the other hand, it is identical to the nature of water, [then...]
Then, at the time when it is clear and still, there is no separate flowing substance. Furthermore, it cannot be separated from space, nor can it be separated from water.
Space is not obstructive; the water flows within it. Outside the water, there is no flow; the flow ultimately depends upon the water.

Thus, the falsity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—that it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature—is clearly demonstrated through these four points.
Ānanda, it is like a person who takes a *pingala* jar, [fills it with air, and carries it]—up to the point that it is neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

Speaking in terms of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it is like a person who takes a *pingala* jar, plugs its two openings, and carries it full of empty space for a journey of a thousand li.
The empty space within the jar is a metaphor for the aggregate of consciousness. The true awakening of the nature of emptiness is all-pervasive.
The Dharma-realm: when deluded as one, it becomes consciousness, confined within the false body like space contained within a jar.
Although the space has no coming or going and cannot be carried away, because it conforms to the jar, it appears to travel a thousand li when the jar moves;

this is a metaphor for how the nature is without birth or extinction and without abandoning or receiving, yet because it relies upon the false body, it hides its form therein and undergoes experience.
The body is in that [space]; deluded by its nature, it forms consciousness and falsely follows the cycle of rebirth. The principle is likewise so.

However, this empty space does not come from that direction, nor does it enter here from this direction. If it came from that direction, then since that direction would have carried the space away with it, there should be a deficiency of space in that direction.
If it entered here from this direction, then when the bottle is opened here, one should see the space emerging from that direction.

Space has no substance; to calculate its coming and going is entirely false and delusive. The consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is likewise false and delusive; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This is clearly demonstrated through the threefold analysis. Now, the body, mind, and all phenomena are the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
Because the Great Awakened One intends to cause beings to awaken to this, at the beginning of this fascicle, he provisionally clarifies what is inverted and what is correct.
Discernment. Through the discerning vision of the reflected image, it precisely reveals the true measure.

First, addressing their deluded attachments and emotional calculations, it brushes away the dust and cataracts from the eyes of the mind and washes the filth and turbidity from the liver and intestines, causing the mind and its objects to fall into a state of refreshing liberation where truth and falsehood are both forgotten.
Only then does one harmoniously merge into the Tathāgatagarbha, thereby realizing that the faculties, objects, locations, and elements are none other than the wondrous.
The nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This constitutes the general purport of these second and third fascicles.

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Three.
Recorded by the Buddhist disciple from Huaihai, the Layman Yun Kong, Lu Xixing.
Collated and verified by the later scholars of Huainan (Xia Fan and Gong Yange).

△ The six sense bases take the faculties as their conditions and give rise to cognition in relation to objects; abiding therein, it is called the "nature of cognition. This nature of cognition is apart from objects.
They have no substance; they are entirely false and illusory. Who is it that knows this illusion? It is the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the six sense bases said to be neither produced by causes and conditions nor by spontaneity?
Regarding the statement "from the eye-entrance": it is when those very eyeballs become fatigued that empty flowers appear in a state of madness;

these are identical to Bodhi, being merely the signs of fatigue produced by staring. These signs arise from the two conditions of light and darkness, while the faculty of seeing abides in between, drawing in these sensory objects.
This is called "seeing the nature. If this seeing were separated from the two objects of light and darkness, it would ultimately have no substance.
How could this seeing, which lacks substance, be anything other than delusion? Furthermore, this delusive seeing comes from nowhere;

it does not come from light or darkness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced by the sense organ. If it came from light, it should be extinguished upon encountering darkness. It should...
If there were no seeing of darkness, then when one comes from darkness and encounters light, that seeing would cease accordingly, and one should not see the light.
If it were produced from the sense organ itself, it would certainly not depend on light or darkness; yet apart from this light and darkness, such a visual essence has no self-nature.

Furthermore, this [perception] seems to arise from light and darkness, rather than from the sense organ itself. If it were to emerge from space, then since space belongs to the external objects (*viṣaya*), it would ultimately belong to the seeing faculty (*indriya*).

Moreover, if space were observing by itself, what connection would that have with your sensory entrance? Since there is no source from which it arises, it is neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Thus, the false nature of the eye-entrance (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is self-evident; its falsity has no inherent reality.
The nature is the entirety of reality; it is true. To thoroughly understand that [phenomena] are illusory, the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is revealed.
As the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Once the flowers in the sky have vanished, the nature of space does not vanish."
Ānanda, it is like a person who uses two fingers [to block his ears]... (up to) "it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
Speaking in terms of the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*): suppose a person blocks both ears with his fingers;

the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) gives rise to fatigue, and he then hears sounds within his head. This, too, is a sign of the fatigue of Bodhi; it arises from movement and stillness, and the ear inhales [these sensations].
The nature of hearing is designated by the names of sensory objects. This hearing is illusory; apart from these two kinds of delusive objects—movement and stillness—it ultimately has no substance.
This very nature of hearing does not come from movement or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced spontaneously from empty space.
They are fundamentally without self-nature. You should know that the ear-entrance is illusory. Having realized its illusoriness, who is it that hears?
It is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches his nose (until... fundamentally neither due to causes and conditions nor by way of spontaneity.

Speaking in terms of the "nose-sphere" (*ghrāṇāyatana*): suppose there is a person who forcefully pinches his nose; after pinching for a long time, he becomes fatigued, and then within the nose he perceives a sensation of cold.
Based on that sensation, he discriminates between permeability and obstruction, emptiness and solidity, as well as various fragrances and stenches. All of these are...

The characteristic of the *bodhi-lau* (nose) arises from the two kinds of false objects, namely penetration and obstruction. When the faculty of hearing is activated within, it inhales these objective phenomena;
this is called the nature of smelling and hearing. Apart from these two objects, it ultimately has no substance.

You should know that this hearing does not come from penetration or obstruction, nor is it produced in the sense organ, nor does it emerge from space. It originally has no self-nature; the nose-faculty is a虚妄 (false delusion), arising from...
This should now be understood: delusion has no self-nature; it does not depart from original enlightenment. Is this not the wondrous true suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha?
Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue... [up to] "it is neither a nature produced by causes and conditions, nor a spontaneous nature."

Regarding the sense-base of the tongue: suppose a person licks their lips with their tongue. By licking repeatedly until it becomes fatigued, one who is ill perceives it as bitter, while one who is healthy perceives it as sweet.
When not licking, the nature of neutrality remains constant. Yet, both the tongue and its fatigue are likewise the wearisome characteristics of Bodhi.
Their cause arises from two kinds of false objects—sweetness and bitterness—which trigger the faculty of cognition and dwell therein.
Inwardly inhaling these sensory objects of taste is called the nature of knowing taste. This nature is distinct from those two objects—sweetness and bitterness—and from the neutral (mild) object;

it ultimately has no substance. It does not exist because of the neutral, nor does it arise from sweetness or bitterness. It does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced by the organ itself.
Fundamentally, it lacks intrinsic nature. The tongue-faculty is illusory; it cannot be said that it is known. Who is it that knows taste? It is not like...
Is it the wondrous true suchness-nature of the ālayavijñāna?
Ānanda, it is like a person who, with one cold hand [and the other warm]... [it is] fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
To enter into discourse by means of the body: it is like a person who touches one hot hand with a cold hand.
If the power of the cold is greater, the hot becomes cold; if the efficacy of the heat prevails, the cold becomes hot. This is the nature of contact:
cold and heat contend with one another, having no fixed power from the outset. When joined, there is sensation; when separated, there is no cognition. Thus, they likewise lack a fixed nature.
Thus, by means of this contact that unites through cognition, the state of separation is revealed. How could there be any inherent nature here? It is merely the momentum of mutual interaction;
once it is established, whether cold or hot, both are equally the laborious touch of *bodhi*. Its cause lies in the two types of union and separation.
Through the delusion of these two objects, awareness arises in the interim; it inhales these objective images and names them "cognition."
As for this nature of cognition: apart from those two objects of separation and union, or opposition and compliance, it ultimately has no substance.
It does not come from separation or union; it does not exist through opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense faculties, nor is it born from space.

If it were to come from union, then at the time of separation it would have already ceased; how then could one perceive separation? The same applies to the two characteristics of opposition and compliance. If it were to emerge from the sense faculties...
If there were necessarily no four characteristics of separation, union, opposition, or conformity, then the cognition of your body would have no self-nature at all.
If it emerged from space, then space itself would possess self-awareness; what concern would that have with your sense-faculties? What can be seen is entirely false and illusory.
Ānanda, it is like a person who falls asleep when weary and exhausted... [as previously stated] ...it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
The faculty of mind (*manāyatana*) gives rise to recollection and cognition; recollection and cognition give rise to waking and sleeping. Therefore, I rely upon sleep to clarify this point.

Observation gives rise to recollection; loss and forgetfulness constitute cessation. Does it then abide in another place? Within this process, having observed and recollected, one immediately loses and forgets; this is called inversion.
Drawing in and habituating to false objects within the sensory fields, one returns to the mental faculty (*manas*).

From the preceding thought to the succeeding thought, they continue in succession without interruption from object to object; therefore, it is said that they do not transcend one another. This is the entry of the mental consciousness.
Aspects, combined with intention and effort, are likewise aspects of the toil of bodhi. Their cause lies in the two kinds of deluded objects: arising and ceasing.
Consciousness gathers within and draws in the internal realm of dharma-objects; these arise from internal conceptualization and extend to what is reached by hearing and seeing.
It is able to reflexively take the five sense organs as its object, even reaching grounds beyond their range, like recollecting the scenes of a dream. Five...
The faculties cannot reach it. The five faculties can only follow along with present objects; the mental faculty (*manas*), however, can turn back to perceive past objects.
Therefore, it is said that seeing and hearing flow against the current, reaching places where the current does not go. This is called the nature of awareness and cognition.

It is apart from the two defilements of birth-and-death and waking-and-sleeping, and ultimately has no substantial body. Nevertheless, it is the root of awareness and cognition, not [the state of] waking.

Sleep does not come from waking; it does not emerge from the sense faculties, nor is it produced from space. When examined and scrutinized from every angle, it possesses no reality whatsoever. Why is this?

If sleep came from waking, then as soon as one wakes, sleep would immediately cease; with what, then, would one be asleep? If it existed at the time of birth [of sleep], then upon its cessation it would become non-existent;
who then would experience that cessation? If it existed from the moment of cessation, then birth would be non-existent; how could there be such a thing?
Who knows that this arising [of consciousness] occurs? If it arises from the sense organs, then its two aspects—waking and sleeping—open and close according to the body.
As Zhuangzi said: "When one awakens, the form opens; when one sleeps, the form closes. Thus, it is said to open and close according to the body.

Apart from these states of waking and sleeping, this cognitive awareness would be like a flower in the sky, having no essential nature whatsoever. If it were to arise from space, it would naturally be...

Space is merely cognition. What does it have to do with your sense-base? Therefore, you should know that the mental base is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
△ The Twelve Bases (Āyatana)

The six sense faculties and the six sense objects are called the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Whether distinguished according to the faculties or distinguished according to the objects, these two bases both lack intrinsic nature and are equally false and illusory.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the twelve bases (āyatana)? [From] "the eye and the form-base" [up to] "originally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Take, for example, the Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds; are these not all forms?
When my faculty of sight, which is capable of observing, encounters these objects of observation, is it the case that the form produces the visual perception of the eye?
Can the eye produce the appearance of form? If you claim that the visual faculty can produce the appearance of form, then this eye must possess the nature of form.
When one raises the eyes to look at empty space, space is already not form; thus, the nature of form should dissolve. If it dissolves, then there is entirely no appearance of form.
Since nothing exists, with what could one clarify the substance of emptiness? This is because [the distinction between] form and emptiness...

Phenomena manifest through mutual dependence; since there are no objective forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), how can emptiness be manifested? Thus, the calculation that the eye produces the form of color is an error.
If one were to claim that the sensory object of form produces the seeing of the eye, then at the time of contemplating emptiness, emptiness is already not form;
how then could it produce seeing? Once seeing has dissolved away, and having dissolved, there is no seeing—by what, then, would one clarify the distinction between emptiness and form?
Thus, to calculate that the eye-sphere arises from form is an error. The seer and form are both empty; neither has a location.
These two locations are illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, listen further to this Jeta Grove... [up to] ...it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Second, regarding the sense-sphere of the ear and sound: listen further to the sounds of bells and drums within this grove as they continue in succession from beginning to end.
Does the sound come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place of the sound? If the sound comes to the ear, since it has already arrived here, where would that [original sound] be?
The location [of the ear] would then be non-existent. For example, when I beg for alms within the city, I am not present in the Jeta Grove.

Furthermore, if sound comes to the ear of this person, that person should not hear it simultaneously; how then could one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus hear the sound of a drum at once and come together to eat?
If, on the other hand, the ear goes to the location of the sound, it would be like my returning to the Jeta Grove.
Within the city, there is inherently no self. When you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is;
yet when the bell and the drum are struck together, they cannot be heard simultaneously. How much less so for the various sounds within them, such as those of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep?
Furthermore, if that sound does not come here and your ear does not go there, then by its very nature there is no hearing, and the meaning of "hearing" cannot be established. Thus, as for listening—

Sound and its resonance both have no location; calculating their going and calculating their coming, both states are false. Fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, when you again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... [up to] fundamentally they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Third is the olfactory faculty. A single *zhu* of sandalwood incense can be smelled from forty *li* away;
since even this mere fragrance possesses such extraordinary power, there is no need to further mention that the faculties and powers of the Sages are sharp and keen.
Ānanda, you should know that among the various assemblies at these two times, when holding the alms-bowl—[down to]—these are neither caused by conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.

Regarding the four sense bases of the tongue and flavors: when you are on your almsround, if you encounter a superior flavor, does this flavor arise from space, arise within the tongue, or arise within the food? If it were to arise within the tongue, then the tongue would perceive but a single flavor.
How could it shift or change? If it does not shift or change, how can it be called "knowing taste"?

Furthermore, the tongue is not a plurality of entities; how can a single tongue know many tastes? If [the knowledge] arises from the food, the food itself possesses no consciousness; how could it know itself?

Even if the food were able to know, that knowing would not reside in you—what concern would it have for you such that it could be called "your" knowing of taste? If [the knowledge] arises from space...
If you were to eat empty space, what flavor would it have? Even if you were to falsely imagine a salty taste, your tongue would perceive saltiness upon contact;

yet that which touches your tongue also touches your face. Your body would experience this saltiness, and you would become like a sea fish. Having once experienced saltiness, you would no longer know the taste of fresh water.
If one is ignorant of both salt and fresh, how can one be said to know taste? Therefore, you should know that taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting are all [empty].
There is no location; thus, both the tasting and the flavor are equally false. Fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, when you regularly rub your head with your hand in the early morning... [up to] ...fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Regarding the five bodies and the sense-base of touch: if you rub your head with your hand in the early morning, as for this sensation known through rubbing, who is it that performs the touching?
Is it located in the head, or is it located in the hand? If there were no hand, the head would have no cognition; how then could there be contact?

If it were located in the head, then the hand would be useless; how then could it be called "contact"? If one falsely distinguishes between the agent and the object, [it is merely a conceptual fabrication].
Thus, [the sensation] resides in the head and in the hand; each has its own distinct touch. It requires two bodies to be able to determine their respective locations.
You, Ānanda, do you not have two bodies? If the head and the hand each constitute a separate touch, then the hand and the head would have to be a single entity.
The meaning of "touch" must be established through two things; if they were a single entity, touch could not be established.

If they were two distinct entities, then when [the body] is in the hand or in the head, for whom would the touch exist? Furthermore, that which is the agent cannot be the object, and that which is the object cannot be the agent;
it should not be the case that empty space comes into contact with you. Therefore, one should know that both the perception of touch and the body have no location.
Thus, both the body and touch are equally false; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, as for the wholesome, unwholesome, and (up to) indeterminate objects that are constantly taken as focal points by your mind—wherefrom are these established apart from the locus of the mind?

They are established within the six bases of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). These dharmas are produced by the three natures—the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—which are constantly taken as focal points by your mind.
Thus, does this dharma arise as identical to the mind, or does it exist separately from the mind in another location? Good and evil are the mind’s objects of contemplation;

the indeterminate is the mind’s state of dull abiding. The mental faculty (*manas*) contemplates nothing outside these three natures, yet it extracts internal objects to constitute the dharmas that serve as its objective referents (*ālambana*).
If these dharmas arise from the mind, then the dharma is identical to the mind; one cannot say [they are separate].
This dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) is not an object of the mind; how then could it be designated as a sense-field?
If it were to exist apart from the mind with a distinct location, then let us inquire into the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this dharma: is it conscious or is it unconscious?

If it is conscious, it is called "mind" and would differ from what you claim is not an object; it would be identical to the mental measure of another, and thus identical to what you [claim] is... [the self].
The mind is one. That which is not an object is your own intrinsic nature, which does not depend upon dharmas.
That which is the mind as your emotional consciousness arises by depending upon dharmas. How could you have two minds?
Thus, it is clear that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not an object of cognition.

If one says it is not an object of cognition, then since this dharma-object is neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, nor tactile qualities such as contact, separation, cold, or heat, nor is it the characteristic of space—having no location—where does it reside?
Since it is not manifested within either form or space, it should not be said to exist within form or space.
Furthermore, since emptiness itself does not exist outside [of these], the mind’s objectification of the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) ultimately lacks any reality.

Therefore, one should know that dharmas and the mind are both without location; thus, both the mind and dharmas are equally false and illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor possessing an inherent nature.

△ The eighteen *dhātus* (elements) refer to their respective categories or lineages (*gotra*). Just as with the term "element" used for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), each constitutes its own class.
Among the three—faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—each has six divisions; when categorized internally and externally, they constitute the eighteen *dhātus*.
One is distinguished by way of the faculties, one by way of the objects, and one by way of both faculties and objects. All are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

△ First, the visual faculty and its objects within the realm of form. Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the eighteen realms? [Up to: "They are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
Ānanda, as you understand it: with the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises. Does this consciousness, in turn, have a cause...
It is produced by the eye and takes the eye as its constituent element (*dhātu*); it is produced by form (*rūpa*) and takes form as its constituent element.

As you have explained, these are the phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) understood by the Hīnayāna; they are all not substantial entities, yet they fail to realize that they are empty from the very beginning.

Therefore, I challenge you based on their own tenets: if this consciousness is produced by the eye, yet lacks both the empty [nature] and form, then the consciousness would have no object of perception (*ālambana*). How could it see?

There is nothing to manifest, and thus the realm cannot be established either. If [consciousness] were produced because of form, then when you do not see form within emptiness, your consciousness should cease;

how then could you cognize the nature of this emptiness? If it is at the time of seeing [form] that ceases that you alone can cognize its transformation, then it is that form ceases while consciousness does not cease. Your consciousness alone...

It exists. If it were solitary, it would have no neighbor; from what, then, could a realm (*dhātu*) be established? If form ceases and consciousness also ceases, then it changes in accordance with change;

that which changes has no substance, and thus the characteristics of a realm do not exist of themselves. If it does not change in accordance [with form], then the nature of consciousness is eternal and constant.
Since it arises from form, there must be one who perceives form; how could one not know where emptiness resides? Yet this reasoning is also incorrect, for it does not arise from form.

Furthermore, if the sense organ and the object were to combine to produce the realm of consciousness, then half would possess cognition and half would lack it, and they would naturally become separated in the middle.
Thus it is said: "If combined, they separate in the middle. Since they have already separated in the middle...
If they are separated, then that which possesses cognition would not avoid uniting with the sense organ (*indriya*), while that which lacks cognition would unite with the object (*viṣaya*).
Therefore it is said: "If separated, then both [would] unite. Thus, their essential natures are in disarray. When investigated through these two meanings, neither constitutes a "realm" (*dhātu*).

For this reason, one should know that the eye and form serve as conditions to produce the visual consciousness-realm; all three locations are entirely non-existent and are collectively false. All such delusions combined...
[The false views] are removed; True Suchness manifests of itself.
△ Second, regarding the realms of the ear and sound:
Ānanda, as for what you have clarified—that the ear and sound serve as conditions—[it follows that they] are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The ear presides over sound and governs hearing; it gives rise to consciousness based upon the two characteristics of movement and stillness, which abide within it.

Yet, this consciousness does not arise because of the ear. Why is this? If the two characteristics of movement and stillness were silent and did not manifest before it, then the ear would not constitute cognition.

Since cognition itself would not be established, what form or appearance could consciousness have? If one considers the act of hearing by the ear, when there is neither movement nor stillness, the nature of hearing [remains].
It is eternally present. At the time when there is neither movement nor stillness, even "hearing" is not yet established;
how then can the ear-form, which perceives the sensory object of various sounds, be designated as the element of consciousness? Thus, that which is distinguished by relying on the sense organ—
All of these are false and delusory. Furthermore, if one distinguishes based on the object, consciousness likewise does not arise because of sound.
If you claim that consciousness arises from sound, then consciousness would exist because of sound and would have no relation to my faculty of hearing.
If there were no faculty of hearing, how could one know the location of the characteristics of sound? Thus, as for the claim that consciousness arises because of sound, we grant that it may be so.

If hearing possesses the characteristic of sound, then while hearing can hear sound, why does it not hear consciousness? Since it does not hear consciousness, how can the meaning of a "constituent" (*dhātu*) be established?
If one were to grant that the ear can indeed hear consciousness, then when consciousness and sound are heard, consciousness itself would already have been heard.
Furthermore, who would then come to know that "I am hearing consciousness"? For hearing necessarily involves the subject and the object; sound is the object heard, and consciousness is [the subject].
It is capable of hearing. If one claims that it is consciousness (*vijñāna*) that hears, then consciousness would merely be that which is heard; who, then, would be the hearer?

If there were no hearer, then there would be an object without a subject, and it would ultimately be like grass or wood. This, too, is untenable. It is incorrect to discuss [the ear] in isolation from the faculty and the object.
One should not treat the faculty and the object as being conflated with the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*). Rather, [it should be understood as follows:]...

There is no intermediate position within the realms (*dhātu*). If there is no intermediate position, then from what could the intermediate consciousness—the consciousness that arises between the two aspects of internal and external, namely the internal faculties and external objects—be established?
Since an intermediate position does not exist, how can the realms be established? Thus, one knows that for the Śrāvakas and the [consciousness-only] school, [the realms do not truly exist].
In all three locations, there is nothing at all. Fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
△ Third, regarding the sphere of the nose and fragrance:
Ānanda, as you have clarified, the nose and fragrance act as conditions... (up to) fundamentally they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.

Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that with the nose and fragrance as conditions, nose-consciousness arises—does this consciousness arise because of the nose and take the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of fragrance and take fragrance as its constituent element? If the consciousness arises because of the nose, [then...]
Then, within your mind, what constitutes the nose? Is it the physical form of the two fleshy appendages?
Or is it the nature of olfactory cognition that vibrates? If you take it to be the physical form, then as for the substance of flesh, it is the object of the body;

it is touch. Flesh is the substance of the body, and touch is the sensory field (viṣaya) of the body. Since even the "nose" has no name [apart from these], from where could its constituent element (dhātu) be established?
If you apprehend it through smelling, then within your mind, by what do you know? If you take the flesh to be that which knows, then that which is known by the flesh is contact and not fragrance.
If you take space to be that which knows, then space would know itself, and the flesh would have no sensation.
If the knowing were in empty space, then empty space would be your body; yet your body is not the knower. Thus, Ānanda’s body would be empty and non-existent.
This is where it resides. This calculation that consciousness arises because of the nose is false. If you claim that it is known through fragrance, then the cognition belongs to the fragrance itself;

what concern does it have with you? If the scents of fragrance and stench must arise within your nose, then those two types of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not originate from within the *eranda* and *candana* trees. Since these two substances do not come from there, you [must produce them] yourself.

When you smell with the nose, it perceives either fragrance or stench. What is stench is not fragrance; what is fragrance is not stench. These two vapors are opposites. If both could be smelled by a single person, then you would have to possess two noses. Furthermore, there are two people here facing me who are asking questions.
