Ānanda, what constitutes the true substance here? If the nose were merely a single faculty, how could its objects be two? Since what is foul becomes fragrant, and what is fragrant becomes foul, these two natures cancel each other out;
from what, then, could a sensory realm be established? Therefore, you should know that the nose and fragrance act as conditions to give rise to the nose-consciousness realm.
In all three locations, none of these exist inherently; they are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
△ 4. The Sphere of the Tongue and the Sphere of Taste.
Ānanda, as for what you understand regarding the tongue and taste acting as conditions (up to): "fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
If this consciousness were produced because of the tongue, then among all the things in the world such as yellow myrobalan, ginger, and cinnamon, there would be none at all [that could produce it].
Taste. Taste your own tongue with your tongue: is it pungent or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste that bitterness?
The tongue does not taste itself; who then provides the cognition? Question: Of these two, which one clearly reveals the existence of a cognizing nature?

If the nature of the tongue were not bitter, then taste would have no source of arising; since there would be no object to correspond to it, how could the sense-field (dhātu) be established? If you say:

Consciousness arises because of flavors; consciousness itself constitutes the flavor; thus consciousness and flavor are identical. Yet, it cannot taste itself, being just like the faculty of the tongue.
How then can one know whether something is sweet or bitter? Furthermore, if consciousness were to arise because of flavors, then since worldly flavors are many, consciousness should also be many.
If the essence of consciousness is unitary, how could it also distinguish the various variations of flavors?
If there were no characteristic of non-identity and no discrimination, it would not be called "consciousness. How, then, could it be called the "element of tongue-taste-consciousness"?
When the tongue and taste come together, there is therein no intrinsic nature. How, then, can an element be established?

Therefore, one should know that the tongue, the taste, and consciousness—these three locations—are all non-existent; they are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
△ 5. The Sphere of Body and Tangible Objects.
Ānanda, regarding what you have clarified—that body and tangible objects serve as conditions [up to] "fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature":

if this consciousness were produced because of the body, it would necessarily exist neither when separated nor when joined. Why then does it exist when there is contact and cease when there is separation?
If it does not exist, then because there is no object, consciousness does not exist; thus it is clear that consciousness depends on the object and not on the sense organ.
If one were to distinguish [consciousness] based on its support, then where there is no body, there is none; yet that which knows union and separation depends on the organ and not the object.

Furthermore, if one distinguishes by the conjunction of organ and object, contact does not know itself; it is only when there is a body that it is known. Thus, this bodily consciousness must necessarily arise from the organ.
The characteristics of the object manifest through conjunction. Through conjunction, one knows that the body is contact and that contact is the body.
If the body were identical to contact, then the body could not be singularly designated as "body. If contact were identical to the body, then contact could not be singularly designated as "contact.
In this way, body and contact mutually cancel each other out; therefore, there is no location. When conjoined with the body, the body lacks the status of being contact.
Contact has no intrinsic nature; for apart from contact, the body would have no function of contacting, and thus it would be identical to empty space.

Consequently, neither the internal, the external, nor that which is between them can be established. Even if consciousness were to arise from contact, from what could the "element" (dhātu) be established?

Thus, with the body and contact as conditions, the element of body-consciousness arises; yet these three locations are all non-existent. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
△ Sixth, the Mind and Dharma Realms:
"Ānanda, as for the mind and dharmas that you have identified as conditions... (up to) they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

With the mind and dharmas as conditions, mental consciousness arises. If consciousness arises because of the mind, then the mind constitutes its realm; if it arises because of [dharmas], then dharmas constitute its realm."
"Phenomena arise; phenomena serve as their boundary. Now, I shall further clarify that this is not so.

If consciousness arises dependent upon the mind, then within your mind there must be something being contemplated, which serves to manifest your mind. That which is contemplated is a phenomenon; it is an object.
If this object did not exist, then the mind would have nothing from which to arise; what, then, would consciousness be used for?

Furthermore, is your conscious mind, along with the various faculties of deliberation and the nature of discernment, identical or distinct? The "conscious mind" is the *manas*; the "various deliberations" are the mental objects (*dharma*);
and the "nature of discernment" is consciousness (*vijñāna*). If they were identical, how could the *manas* arise? If they were distinct, [consciousness] could not function.
The consciousness arises. If these three were identical, then which would be the producer and which would be the produced?
Therefore it is said: "If they are identical, then it is simply the mind; how then could the mind arise? If the three were distinct, then the three natures would be mutually contradictory.

How could consciousness arise? Therefore it is said: "If the mind were different [from consciousness], they would not be the same; there would be nothing to cognize. Without cognition, one would be the same as grass and trees.
How then can the mind give rise to consciousness? Since the mind is fundamentally formless, how can consciousness perceive the mind?
Whether in terms of identity or difference, these two natures cannot be established. How then can the realms (dhātus) be posited? If consciousness arises dependent on dharmas, then all worldly..."
The dharma-element does not exist apart from the five sense objects. Observe that visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are all equally termed dharmas;
their characteristics are distinct, corresponding to the five faculties and each belonging to its own respective domain, rather than being subsumed by the mental faculty.
You have concluded that consciousness arises based on the dharma-element. Now, observe carefully: what is the appearance of this dharma-object? If it were separate...
Form is empty; all marks are ultimately unobtainable. When arising, form-emptiness and all dharmas arise together; when ceasing, form-emptiness and all dharmas cease together.
Since they are not grasped by the mind and possess no substantial appearance, and since their cause is non-existent, how could consciousness arise from such a cause?
As for its marks and appearances, they do not exist. How, then, can the realms be established? Therefore, one should know that the mind—
With dharmas as conditions, the mental consciousness-element arises. Since all three locations are entirely non-existent, both the mind and the dharma-element are equally illusory;
fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

First, one uses the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to dismantle the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*); although this involves dismantling them through the confrontation with sense objects (*viṣaya*), the primary intent lies in the faculties themselves.
Next, by means of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), although the faculties and objects mutually dismantle one another, the primary intent lies solely in the objects.

Finally, by means of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), one dismantles them by analyzing the three characteristics of faculty, object, and consciousness; here, the primary intent lies solely in consciousness.

△ First, prior to the seven great matters, he takes his own body as a proximate object to reveal the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it is elucidated by means of the four categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and realms (*dhātu*).
Although one may awaken to this single body, one has not yet harmonized the myriad dharmas; the faculties and their objects remain distinct, and the vision of the nature is not yet perfect. This...
Furthermore, he takes up various objects from afar and demonstrates the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha) through them.

Thus, by means of the seven great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, sight, and consciousness—he clarifies that sentient beings and objects share a common root, and that the dharma of non-duality is one and the same.
These dharmas perfectly manifest as sensory objects, and these objects pervade the entire dharma-realm. A verse says: "If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, within the body..."
Just as it returns to pervade the external, the sentient and the insentient share a single essence; everywhere they are identical with the True Dharma-realm.
This is the purport of the "Seven Greats. As for why they are called "Great," it is because their nature is perfectly pervasive, encompassing and containing the ten directions.
As for why there are seven: the generation and completion of the myriad dharmas do not depart from the four great elements, upon which they depend.

Space is established. Because of seeing, there is sensation; because of consciousness, there is cognition. The first five [elements] are possessed by insentient things, while the latter two are shared by sentient beings.
All seven great elements arise from the transformation of consciousness; therefore, they are subsumed under consciousness.

Consciousness is that which, within the nature of awakening, falsely manifests as luminous cognition. Once that which is falsely manifested is established, it gives rise to the false capacity of the subject.
Thus, there are the seven great elements. These seven elements were originally neither water nor fire, nor were they space or consciousness;
they are entirely the substance of the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting in accordance with karma alone.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, as for the Tathāgata... it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water.
The Buddha told Ānanda, “It is as you have said. That the four great elements combine to produce the various transformations of the world is truly a provisional teaching.
Although it speaks of combination, it has no real substance. For the nature of those four great elements is, in fact, [empty].”
If it were not in conjunction, it would be like empty space, which does not combine with various forms; yet this is hardly the case.

If it were indeed in conjunction, it would be identical to those myriad transformations, mutually forming and continuing in a succession of shifting delusions, like a whirling firebrand that has no substantial reality and knows no rest;
yet this too is not so. Furthermore, it is because the nature of the Great [Self] is neither in conjunction nor in combination.
In principle, let us take an analogy: it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water. How could water combine to become ice? How could ice blend to become water?
It is not through combination or blending; rather, they manifest according to karma. Such is their nature.
△ First, regarding earth:
Observe the nature of earth; that which is coarse is "great earth" (down to the point where it is said) that there are only words and no real meaning.

Observe the great earth: that which is coarse is "great earth," while that which is fine becomes subtle dust, down to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle), until it is analyzed to its ultimate limit.
Subtle. Even an atom of the ultimate minute particle still possesses subtle form; this is called the characteristic of the limit of form.
If one further analyzes the *paramāṇu* (neighboring-void) into seven parts, that subtle form becomes the *paramāṇu*. That *paramāṇu* is itself the nature of true emptiness.
If this *paramāṇu* is analyzed until it becomes empty space, one should know that empty space and the production of the characteristics of form share the function of a single *paramāṇu*-dust.
How many atoms of space are combined to constitute it? Furthermore, when analyzing the atoms of matter to reveal space, by means of how many material characteristics are these spaces synthesized?
From this, it is clear that these manifested phenomena are not composite entities.
Moreover, if matter were to combine, it would be purely a single mass of matter and could not be called "empty space. If space were to combine, it would be purely a single mass of space.
It cannot be called "form" (rūpa). Form can still be analyzed, but how could emptiness (śūnyatā) be combined?

You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, essential form is true emptiness, and essential emptiness is true form. To say that emptiness can take form as its essence means that form is also the essence of emptiness.
This "essence" is the essence of all mental states; it should be viewed as something living and dynamic. That emptiness can take form as its essence means:

To arise from non-existence is to exist; that form (*rūpa*) is also empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to return from existence to non-existence. Because it is the nature of form, it manifests various appearances;

because it is the nature of emptiness, when analyzed through the senses, it becomes empty. Yet all are fundamentally pure and inherently so, pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). They do not require synthesis;
they arise according to the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of what is known, and manifesting in accordance with karma. And thus, the world...
The interim state of ignorance takes delusion as its causal condition and its inherent nature; all of these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning mind.
They exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever. Why is this? Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness;

yet, following karma, they appear as if diverse, resulting in the names of the "Seven Great Elements. These are merely different designations for the distinction between essence and function. The true nature of form...
Emptiness is the essence of suchness. The true form of the empty nature is the function that follows from its manifestation.
Form is fundamentally illusory, yet it is also expressed through the True Word (mantra). Because essence and function are non-dual, they rely upon one another and are raised up together.
This is intended only to let people know that they are not separate from the wondrous nature. It is just as when water freezes into ice; the ice is not separate from the water. Sentient beings...

Turning one's back on awakening and joining with the sensory dust, one gives rise to worldly toil (*rajas*). However, if one causes the dust to cease and unites with awakening, the true *tathatā* (suchness) and the measure of the mind will manifest, arising in accordance with conditions;

this is what is meant by "the ten thousand dharmas are of one suchness. Such is the intended meaning. Yet, when observing appearances, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described.

When observing the nature, it is fundamentally empty, being only the wondrous luminosity of awakening. This principle transcends emotional conceptualization and admits no room for [dualistic] thought.
To attempt to measure it falsely is to err the moment the mind is directed toward it; it is to deviate the moment a thought is stirred.
Rather, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts and do not employ the discriminating consciousness; only then will you be in accord.
△ Second, regarding the fire element:
Ānanda, the nature of fire is without self; it relies upon various conditions. (Up to: "There are only verbal expressions, but no real meaning.
Ānanda, the nature of fire is without self; it relies upon various conditions. Observe the houses in the city where people seek food; with their hands—
Holding a sun-gem (*sūryakānta*), one obtains fire from before the sun. Yet, this characteristic of fire is neither produced by blending nor by conjunction.
Generally speaking, when we speak of "blending" (*saṃyoga*) or "conjunction" (*samavāya*), if one examines them, each has its own fundamental basis.

For example, although you and I, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty people, form a single assembly gathered in one place, if one examines us, each of our fundamentals has its own name, clan, and lineage.
If this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, you should test it:
since each lacks a fundamental source, does it arise from the mirror, emerge from the moxa, or come from the sun? If it comes from the sun, it should be able to burn the moxa in your hand by itself;
furthermore, all the forests from which it originated should likewise be consumed by fire. If it emerges from the mirror, it should be able to emerge from the mirror by itself.
Yet, why does the mirror not melt? Though held in your hand, it still shows no sign of heat. If the fire were produced from the moxa, why would it depend on the sun and the mirror?
It is only when the light of the sun and the mirror meet that the fire is then born. If you say it is neither a blending nor a combination, then observe closely again:
the mirror is held by your hand, the sun comes from the sky, and the moxa grows from the earth; from what direction, then, does the fire come?
As you wander here, the sun and the mirror remain far apart; they are neither joined nor blended, yet fire does not arise from them. Nor can it be said that the flame arises spontaneously of itself.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire.

It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. In accordance with the minds of sentient beings and according to the measure of their cognition, if one person holds a mirror in one place—
Fire arises from its locus; it grasps the entire dharma-realm and manifests throughout the world. Since it arises pervading the world, how could it have a fixed location?

It appears according to karma; such is the general principle. To regard delusion as a cause and condition, or as having a spontaneous nature—all these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning mind.
They exist only as verbal expressions and possess no fundamental reality from the outset.
△ Third: The Water Element of Mahānāma is Indeterminate; Its Flowing and Ceasing Are Without Constancy. (Up to: "There is only verbal expression, but no real meaning whatsoever.
Ānanda, the nature of water is indeterminate; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy. It is like the great illusionists of Śrāvastī who seek..."

The essence of the Great Yin, combined with various illusory elixirs, is used on a day during the bright fortnight; one holds the *fangzhu* (the "square pearl" lens) in the hand to receive the water from the moon.

Does this water emerge from the pearl, or does it exist in space, or does it come from the moon? If it comes from the moon, it is already capable of causing the pearl to produce water from such a great distance;
even the trees and forests it passes over should all discharge their fluids. Why, then, must one wait [for the moon to be directly overhead]?
Furthermore, the forest trees do not flow; thus, it seems this water does not descend from the moon.
If it were to emerge from the pearl, the pearl should constantly produce flowing water—why wait for midnight to face the moon? If it were produced from space, the nature of space is boundless.
Water should be boundless. From humans up to the heavens, all should be submerged; how then could there still be those that move on water, land, or through the air?
One can see that this is fundamentally pervasive and not a product of combination. If you say it is neither combined nor joined, observe this closely again:
the moon ascends from the sky, the pearl is held in hand, and the basin of water that receives the pearl is a human creation. Water—[is it not likewise so?]
From what direction does it flow here? The moon and the water-crystal are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the water-crystal exists of itself without a source.

You still do not know that the nature of water is true emptiness, and that the nature of emptiness is true water—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognition. In one place there is the grasping of the crystal, in another place...
Water emerges. It fills the dharma-realm and is grasped; from within the water that fills the realm, it arises and fills the world. How could there be any fixed location?

It manifests according to karma; the meaning is roughly like this. To claim that delusion is caused by conditions, by nature, or by anything else, is entirely the conceptualization and calculation of the conscious mind.
These are merely words; they possess no real substance whatsoever.

△ Fourth, the Great Element of Wind: Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant. (Up to: It is merely verbal expression and entirely devoid of real meaning.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant. When you adjust your robes to enter the assembly, [observe] the corner of your saṃghāṭī.
When it moves and affects bystanders, a subtle breeze brushes their faces.

Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*, or does it arise from empty space, or is it produced on the faces of those people? If it comes from the corner of the robe, you must be wearing the wind;
in that case, as the robe flutters, it should detach from your body. I am now sitting with my robe draped over me; look at my robe—where is the wind?

If it were located in empty space, your robe would not move; for what reason, then, is there no brushing against it? Since the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, the wind should be constantly arising.
If there were no wind, empty space would have to perish. If the perishing of wind could be seen, what would the perishing of empty space look like?
If there were arising and ceasing, it could not be called empty space. Since it is called empty space, how can wind emerge from it?
If the wind arises naturally on the surface that brushes against you, then it should brush against you; you yourself have adjusted your robe—why does it brush against it instead?
If you say it is not a result of conjunction, then observe carefully: the adjustment of the robe is with you, while the face belongs to the other person.
O person, empty space is tranquil and does not participate in movement. From what direction does the wind come? The natures of wind and space are distinct; they are neither blended nor joined.
It cannot be that the nature of wind exists of itself without a source. Yet when one seeks its origin, it is profound and beyond investigation.
One must believe that it is fundamentally all-pervasive, manifesting according to karma. You, however, do not realize the nature of wind within the Tathāgata-garbha.

The true emptiness is the wind of the nature-emptiness. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings and responds to the measure of their cognition.
When one person moves their robe, a subtle breeze arises; when robes are moved throughout the realm, they sweep across the entirety of the lands.
Pervading the world, how could there be any fixed location? These arise in accordance with karma.

To deludedly regard them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature is entirely the false calculation and discrimination of the conscious mind; it is merely words and possesses no real meaning whatsoever.
△ Fifth, the Great Emptiness of Ānanda:
Emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form. (Up to: There are only words, but no actual reality.
Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form. For example, Śivara, in a place far from the river... all.
Suppose a member of the Kṣatriya caste has newly established a dwelling and digs a well to seek water. When he has removed one foot of earth, there is one foot of empty space within;
when he has removed ten feet of earth, he obtains ten feet of empty space. The depth of this space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth removed.
Is this space produced by the removal of the earth, or does it exist because of the digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
If it were produced without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth had been excavated? One sees only the vast expanse of the great earth, with no passage through it.
If it arose because of the earth, then at the moment the earth is excavated, one should see space entering;
yet if the earth comes out first while space does not enter, how can you say that space arises because of the earth? If there is neither entry nor exit, then space and earth must be identical.
They merge into a single entity; fundamentally, there is no distinct cause for their separation. When the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?

If space emerges because of digging, then the digging itself must produce space; it should not be that space emerges from the earth while the digging does not produce space. Conversely, if space does not emerge through the digging, then the digging itself must produce the earth.
"How do you perceive emptiness? It is because it cannot be separated from its cause; yet that cause is also not [independent]. You must again examine and contemplate this with utmost care:
the chisel follows the hand, moving in various directions, while the earth shifts according to the ground.
From what source does such empty space arise? The chisel is substantial, whereas the space is void. These two—void and substantial—do not function for one another, yet they are not separate."
It is neither identical with nor separate from [the physical realm]. It is not the case that empty space arises spontaneously without any source.

Through these skillful arguments, all false conceptualizations of the discriminating mind are dispelled to reveal the perfectly interfused true essence. One should know that the nature of this empty space is perfect, pervasive, and omnipresent.
It is fundamentally immovable. One should know that the present earth, water, fire, and wind are collectively termed the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*).

These are equally interfused and all-pervasive; they are all the *tathāgatagarbha*, fundamentally without arising or ceasing, neither caused by conditions nor dependent on causes, and yet not produced spontaneously.
All such false conceptualizations and deliberations are merely your consciousness-spirit; they are not the true meaning of ultimate reality.

However, Ananda, you are deluded and confused in mind; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should observe empty space: does it emerge from something, or does it enter into something?

This is not a matter of coming or going. If you realize that the nature of empty space is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally has no coming or going, then you will realize that the true nature is inherently perfect and harmonious, and fundamentally has no arising or ceasing.
You do not at all understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding according to the minds of sentient beings.
Know the measure. It is like the emptiness of a single well: as emptiness arises within one well, so it is with the empty space of the ten directions;

it fills the ten directions completely—how could it have a specific location? It manifests according to karma; the meaning is roughly like this. The emptiness of one well is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (nature) of a single phenomenon;
the emptiness of the ten directions is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* of all phenomena. By means of one, one observes the many; by means of oneself, one observes others. This is the nature.
There is no duality or distinction; it is merely a false discrimination based on specific forms and vessels. △ Sixth:

Ānanda observes that the faculty of perception is devoid of knowledge, arising due to form and space (*rūpa* and *ākāśa*)... (up to) ...there is only verbal expression, and it is entirely without real meaning.
Ānanda, seeing and awareness are themselves devoid of cognition; they exist only because of form and emptiness. When you were in the Jeta Grove, it was bright in the morning and dark by evening;
even if you were in the middle of the night, there would be light during the bright fortnight and darkness during the dark fortnight.
Since these distinctions arise through seeing, is this faculty of seeing then one with the phenomena of light and darkness, as well as with great empty space? Or is it not one with them?

Are they the same? Are they not the same? Are they different? Are they not different? If they were originally one substance, then the two substances of light and darkness would mutually exclude one another:
when there is light, there is no darkness; when there is darkness, there is no light. If it were necessarily one with light, then light would perish;
if it were necessarily one with darkness, then darkness would be extinguished. How could one see both light and darkness? If light and darkness...
Furthermore, if one perceives no arising or ceasing, then it cannot be established as a single entity.

If this essence of seeing is not a single entity with darkness or light, then try to separate it from light, darkness, and space, and analyze the source of seeing: what form or appearance does it take?

If brightness, darkness, and emptiness—these three things—are all distinct from one another, from what basis could "seeing" be established? Furthermore, they are not of different substance [from seeing].
Now, brightness and darkness are mutually opposed; how can they ever be the same? Apart from these three, there is no seeing; how can it ever be different?
To distinguish between space and seeing, there is originally no boundary; how can they not be the same? Seeing brightness and seeing darkness, the nature [of seeing] does not undergo change. How...
How could it not be different? You should examine this further with meticulous scrutiny: light comes from the sun; darkness comes from the dark moon;

openness belongs to the void; and obstruction returns to the great earth. From what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise? Seeing is aware, while emptiness is inert; they are neither blended nor joined.
It cannot be that the essence of seeing emerges of its own accord without a source. You should know that the nature of seeing is perfect and pervasive.
It is all-pervasive, fundamentally unmoving, and likewise without arising or ceasing. Yet you continue to sink into delusion without awakening.
Your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. Simply observe this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: do they arise or cease? Are they different or the same?
Are they neither arising nor ceasing? Are they neither different nor the same? For arising and ceasing, sameness and difference—all are due to delusory objects.
It is neither born nor different; it is not separate from false conceptualization. To be free from this false conceptualization is the Tathāgatagarbha.
You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing is luminous awareness, and luminous awareness is pure seeing. It is inherently pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
According to the minds of sentient beings, it accords with the measure of what they know. Just as with a single faculty of sight, seeing pervades the Dharma-realm, so too does hearing.
Smelling, tasting, and touching—these are the perceptions of touch and the awareness thereof. Their wondrous virtue is luminously pure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm and filling the ten voids;

how could they have any fixed location? They manifest according to karma. Those in the world are ignorant, deludedly regarding them as having the nature of causes and conditions or as being spontaneous.
These are all merely discriminations of the conscious mind; they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real substance.
△ The Seven Consciousnesses. "Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises because of the six kinds [of sense objects]. (Up to: It is merely words and has no real meaning.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no objective condition; it falsely emerges from the six kinds of faculties and objects. You should now examine this thoroughly."
When you assemble the assembly of saints and observe them with your eyes, they appear as if in a mirror, without any further differentiation or analysis;

this is their true nature. As for your consciousness, which sequentially identifies and points them out—saying "this is Mañjuśrī," "this is Pūrṇa"—does this consciousness arise from seeing, from forms, from empty space, or does it arise without any cause?
Does it emerge suddenly? If you say it arises within seeing—just as there are the four factors of ignorance, darkness, form, and space—then your seeing would not exist.
Since the nature of seeing itself would be absent, from what could consciousness arise? That the visible object arises within seeing is incorrect.
If you say it arises within the objective mark and does not arise from seeing, then since you do not see light nor do you see darkness, [how can it arise?]
When light and darkness do not strike [the eyes], there is neither form nor space; since even those characteristics do not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

To say that it arises from the characteristics of the visible is incorrect. If you claim it arises from empty space—neither from seeing nor from characteristics—then, being "not seeing," there is no discernment, and being "not characteristics," conditions are extinguished.
Situated between these two absences, if you say consciousness arises from space...

Then it would be identical to that which cannot be distinguished. If you say there is consciousness, yet it is not identical to the characteristics of objects, then even if you were to activate your consciousness, what object would you wish to distinguish?
Furthermore, the claim that "what is visible is neither seeing nor a characteristic, but arises from emptiness" is also incorrect.
If you say that it arises suddenly without any cause, why do you not suddenly see the bright moon during the day? You should examine this more minutely and carefully:

when the visual faculty relies upon your pupils and projects toward external objects, that which can be characterized becomes "existent," and that which cannot be so characterized becomes "non-existent.
Thus, from what source does consciousness arise? Consciousness— *Note: The final character "識" (consciousness) appears to be a fragment of the original text.*
The movement of cognition and the clarity of vision are neither conjoined nor combined. Hearing, listening, sensation, and awareness are likewise so.
What is meant by "the movement of cognition and the clarity of vision"? Cognition possesses discrimination; this is termed "movement. Vision lacks discrimination; this is defined as "clarity.
Movement stirs its inherent nature, while clarity returns to its true purity. Thus, they are neither conjoined nor combined. Hearing, listening... [is likewise so].
The same applies to the awareness of cognition. All are neither produced by combination nor are they spontaneous.
The nature of what is visible is truly perfect, profoundly still, and does not involve any delusions; it fundamentally has no origin. Furthermore, the seven elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha.
Fundamentally, there is neither arising nor ceasing. Your mind is coarse and restless; you have never attained awakening.

You merely observe the six sense bases with your consciousness, yet you do not discern whether the conscious mind is identical to or different from them, whether it is empty or existent, or whether it is neither identical nor different, nor both empty and existent.

This is because you fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminously aware, and the true consciousness of awakened clarity is wondrously enlightened and profoundly still, pervading all phenomena.

The realms encompass and breathe forth the ten voids; how could they have a fixed location? They manifest according to karma. The world is ignorant and deludedly regards them as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously;
these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind. There are only words, but no real meaning.

When one’s fundamental nature and consciousness are clearly aware, that which is called "nature" is this very consciousness; all that is clearly known by me is my own clear awareness. This clear awareness is itself the Good.
Regarding the meaning of "knowing": "Awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Although consciousness is a fault of awakened clarity, its essence (*tǐ*) is truly real.
Therefore, it is called "awakened clarity as true consciousness. Essence and function are non-dual; truth and delusion are of one suchness.
For this reason, they are mentioned alternately. In the text, first it says, "You originally did not know"; next, "still"; next, "yet"; next, "clearly"; next, "entirely"; and next...

The terms "once" (zēng), "originally" (yuán), and so forth all possess a sequential progression of depth. First, saying "originally did not know" means that he was fundamentally deluded from the beginning, which is why he did not know.
When he was further given clear instruction, he still did not understand; hence the subsequent term "still" (yóu). Later, when he was again given clear instruction, he knew even less;
hence the subsequent term "yet" (shàng). Because his ignorance became increasingly profound, the term "completely" (wǎn) is used.
Because one does not know at all, it is said "entirely" (quán). Because one knows very little, it is said "ever" (céng). Because one never knows, it is said "originally" (yuán).

The initial intention is to forgive; the final intention is to reprove. Such is the sequence of lightness and gravity. To discern deeply is called "examination" (shěn); to deliberate with examination is called "detail" (xiáng);

to accord with principle is called "reality" (di); to look with reality is called "contemplation" (guān). At the beginning, regarding the great element of earth, it speaks of you alone: "You contemplate. Regarding...

The fire element said, "It is true. Its words were even more true; it observed with scrutiny and examined with careful discernment. It reached the great element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and spoke repeatedly;

it reached the great element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) and spoke in succession. Its meaning was the same as the words "wonderful" (*wan*), "ancient" (*zeng*), and so forth, because [the other elements] did not understand its transformation, understood nothing at all, and understood it most profoundly.
△ Chapter Eight: Expressing Gratitude through Verses of Praise.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [up to] spoke verses before the Tathāgata to praise the Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, felt their bodies and minds become purified.

Nevertheless, from the initial discernment of the mind and its perceptions, up to the final section on the aggregates, bases, and the seven elements, [the text] elucidates these through manifold methods to cause one to realize that the myriad phenomena of the vessel-world are, in their very essence, entirely true—the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha. This is what is called the subtle and wondrous revelation.
Having realized that the nature of the vessel-world is truly perfect and harmonious, body and mind become vast and open, equally free from obstruction.

Having realized that wondrous enlightenment is profound and still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, each person comes to know for themselves that their own mind extends throughout the ten directions.

As this wondrous enlightenment is profound and pervasive, encompassing and containing the ten voids, one perceives the emptiness of the ten directions as if looking at leaves in one's hand. Thus, the true nature of all phenomena is revealed.
Since this is the Tathāgatagarbha, all that exists is none other than the wondrous mind.

Having realized that the measure of one’s fundamental mind is as vast as this, one looks back upon the deluded body: it is as minute as a speck of dust and as illusory as a bubble, suddenly becoming nothing at all.
Thus, the fundamentally wondrous and eternal mind was clearly realized and attained; thereupon, he rejoiced deeply and spoke a verse in praise and gratitude:
"The Sovereign of the Śūraṃgama Samādhi, the King of Worldly Rarities, is wondrously profound, all-holding, and immovable."
"Sublime, profound, and total retention" is the very essence of the Tathāgata-garbha.
This is what was previously described as "sublime awakening, profoundly still and unmoving, pervading and encompassing the ten directions.

Although all beings inherently possess this, it must be brought forth through the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi. That a Buddha is a Buddha is solely due to maintaining this; thus, Ānanda praised the Buddha on this account.

Furthermore, when the ocean of awakening is perfectly clear and still, such that external objects cannot disturb it, it is called "wondrously profound. When the hidden mind is perfectly pervasive, encompassing the ten directions, it is called "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*).
When its essence is quiescent like space, eternally abiding and never perishing, it is called "immovable. Possessing these qualities, it alone is honored as supreme within the three realms;
by virtue of this, it serves as the King of all Dharmas. To seek such a thing within the mundane world, it is truly rare indeed.
"May my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas be extinguished, so that without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I may attain the Dharma-body.
Having been deluded regarding the Truth since beginningless time, one falsely identifies with the shadow of conditions; this is what constitutes the inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas.

Once one receives this instruction, one realizes and attains the original mind; thus, without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Dharma-body is attained immediately. *Asaṃkhyeya* here means "immeasurable number."
Kalpa. May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King (until) never taking *nirvāṇa* here.

Having realized my own nature, I am deeply moved by the thought of [the Master’s] illumination; therefore, I vow that once I have attained realization, I shall propagate the Way and benefit sentient beings.
To praise the Buddha’s mind and repay his kindness above is the aspiration for the attainment of fruition; this is the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*).
To further deliver sentient beings is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*). To unite wisdom and compassion in a vast and immeasurable manner is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*).

To vow to enter the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) without seeking personal nirvāṇa is the ultimate limit of the profound mind. Relying upon this repayment of kindness, I therefore request the Buddha to act as my witness.
"O Great Hero, Great Power, Great Compassion... (up to) "...sitting in the place of enlightenment throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having offered this praise and gratitude, he requests once more that the teaching be further expounded, so as to completely eliminate the obstacles of delusion and fulfill the vows of fruition.

Previously, the manifestation of the mind-ground revealed the *tathāgatagarbha*, thereby breaking the coarse delusions of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). Next, one must resolve lingering doubts and obstructions to open [the path].

The Gate of Cultivation and Realization: By severing the subtle afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and eliminating them through thorough investigation, one ascends to supreme awakening.
The fourth fascicle resolves doubts and obstructions and subdues discursive clinging; this is precisely the method for investigating and eliminating subtle afflictions.

Having thus eliminated inverted perceptions and suddenly attained the *dharmakāya*, one might suspect that the fruit has already been realized, yet one still harbors further desires and seeks to eliminate even more subtle [afflictions].

Regarding those who are deluded: there are seven aspects of the Buddha-fruit, namely: bodhi, nirvāṇa, true suchness (tathatā), buddha-nature, the amala-vijñāna, the empty tathāgatagarbha, and the great perfect mirror wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna).
That which is called the attainment of the dharma-body is the partial realization of bodhi.

It is simply a matter of seeing one’s own Buddha-nature. After seeing this nature, one must carefully eliminate subtle delusions so that both arising and ceasing, as well as the cessation of arising, are stilled, thereby harmonizing with the *nirvāṇa* of true suchness (*tathatā*). Being pure, white, and perfectly concentrated, one harmonizes with the *amala-vijñāna*.
Being vast, perfect, and illuminating, one harmonizes with the empty *tathāgatagarbha* and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). (7)
When the fruits are fully perfected, one attains supreme enlightenment.
"The nature of Śūnyatā may perish, but the *śakala* mind does not waver.
*Śūnyatā* here means "emptiness"; *śakala* here means "solid" or "firm. This refers to the fact that the nature of emptiness is without substance; even so—

They may perish, but my mind is firm and resolute; it shall never waver. This is based on the power of concentration from the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, binding my previous vow to take a personal oath to reach the ultimate goal without ever falling back.
When the vow is thus established, the fruit of sainthood can then be expected, and the Buddha’s grace can be repaid.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,

Recorded by Layman Yunkong Lu Xixing, Disciple of the Buddha from Huaihai;
verified by the junior scholar of Huainan, Jiang Yiqi.
△ Section Nine: Thoroughly Investigating the Myriad Dharmas.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... (up to) "...I have constantly heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having now heard from the Tathāgata..."
The Sublime Meaning and the subtle, wondrous sound of the Dharma have been proclaimed and made clear, causing me to eliminate my delusions;
yet, I still do not fully understand the ultimate meaning of this principle and have not yet reached a ground free from doubt.

World-Honored One, if all things in the world—the faculties, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements—are all the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and inherently so, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) undergo successive transformation and flow, ending and beginning again. If they were pure, there should be no such characteristics;
if they were primordial and natural (*tathatā*), there should be no such successive flow. This is the first doubt.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that the intrinsic nature of earth, water, fire, and wind is perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding. If [it were as described], then regarding earth...
"Nature is all-pervasive. How can it accommodate water? If the nature of water is all-pervasive, then fire cannot arise.

Since the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space, how could they not conflict with or extinguish one another? Furthermore, the nature of earth is obstructive, while the nature of space is open and penetrating;
how can both be universally pervasive? I do not understand the principle underlying this. This is my second question. Thus it was said. All.

This arises from the preceding text concerning the four categories and the seven elements. The intent is that because nature and characteristics contradict one another, and phenomena and principle obstruct one another, ordinary people harbor doubts and stagnate;
thus, they seek a definitive resolution. In the Buddha’s response to the first question, he states: "It is fundamentally pure."

"How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that 'the nature-awakening is wondrously luminous' and 'fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous'?
'The nature-awakening is wondrously luminous' and 'fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous' are alternative designations for the essence and function of the myriad dharmas.
That which can take all things as its nature is called 'nature-awakening. The wondrousness of this nature-awakening manifests as luminosity; this is precisely the self..."
It is that which awakens and manifests within the myriad dharmas. The fundamental source of its nature is called "original awakening" (*mūla-awakening*).

The luminosity of original awakening is hidden within the wondrous; it functions spontaneously and returns to merge with the single reality. One who understands these two meanings [attains realization].
Thus, essence and function are one awakening; things and self are one wondrousness. There are no longer any differences between various characteristics.
Furthermore, Gushan said: "Original awakening is also intrinsic awakening; it is merely a variation in the phrasing.

Since the fundamental original nature is such that both subject and object are simultaneously transcended, and stillness and illumination are mutually fused, it is therefore explained in two phrases. Tianru said: "This was because the Buddha wished..."
The manifestation of mountains, rivers, and the great earth arises from deluded awareness;

therefore, the text first designates true awareness, wherein essence and function mutually manifest, yet from the very beginning there is neither subject nor object, establishing the fundamental ground. The subsequent text then introduces both true and deluded awareness.

The Buddha said, "When you speak of 'awakened clarity,' do you mean that the nature itself is clear and thus clarity is called awakening? Or do you mean that because the awakening is not clear, it is called 'clear awakening'?
Pūrṇa replied, "If this lack of clarity were what is called awakening, then there would be nothing at all to be made clear. The Buddha said:

If there were nothing to be illumined, then there would be no illumination-consciousness (*vijñapti*). That which has an object is not consciousness; that which has no object is not illumination. Furthermore, non-illumination is not the nature of the profound clarity of consciousness.

The nature of consciousness is necessarily luminous; it is through delusion that it constitutes "illumination-consciousness. Consciousness itself is not something to be illumined; it is because of illumination that an object is established.
Once the "object" has been falsely established, it gives rise to your false "subjective capacity. Within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is created.

Based on that which is different from the object, identity is established through difference. As identity and difference manifest, one further establishes "neither identity nor difference. Thus, there is this turmoil.

Mutual dependence gives rise to weariness; long-standing weariness produces dust, which turbidly muddies one's own characteristics. From this, the afflictions of dusty toil are incited. The Buddha said:
"Regarding what you call 'awakened clarity' (*jue-ming*), do you designate it as 'clarity' because its nature is inherently clear?
Or do you designate it as 'clear awakening' because it is awakened yet not inherently clear? Briefly take up these two terms, 'awakened' and 'clear,' and examine what you understand by them. Fu...
Pūrṇa replied: "If this lack of illumination is what you call awakening, then there is nothing being illuminated;
how can that be considered awakening? To not know while having even the slightest thing illuminated is to fall into deluded awakening.
This was the error in Pūrṇa’s understanding. The Buddha said: "If there is nothing illuminated, then there is no awakening through illumination. Is this not unfortunate? For illumination..."
The delusion of awakening arises from that which it itself illuminates. Therefore, that which has something to illuminate is illumination, not awakening;
that which has nothing to illuminate is awakening, not illumination. Yet, having nothing to illuminate is not the absence of illumination.

If there were no illumination, it would further not be the nature of the profound clarity of awakening. Why? Because the nature of awakening must necessarily illuminate that which is illuminated; [otherwise], it is delusion.
It is only for the sake of clarifying awakening that delusion is spoken of as "that which is clarified. Thus, Wu-xing said:

"The awakening of the fundamental nature must inherently possess the nature of profound clarity. Because one does not understand this, delusion arises as the 'clarity that clarifies' and the 'awakening that awakens.
Wen-ling [Liu Yong] takes the forceful arising of cognition as "necessary clarity"; having already spoken of the "clarifier" and "the clarified," he further establishes...

It must be "illumination. Ultimately, it is not like that which is merely "seemingly settled" in Wuxing. Therefore, one realizes that what is illuminated is not the object; rather, it is the fundamentally inherent true essence.
Because illumination establishes an object, the deluded consciousness of the person arises. Once the object has been falsely established, your deluded subjectivity is produced.
When subject and object are established, the mind and its environment are divided. Within that state where there is neither identity nor difference, a blazing diversity comes into being. Indeed!
As for "difference," it is merely that which is different from that [original awakening]. The essence of original awakening is not necessarily different.

By reversing difference into identity, identity and difference stand in opposition; they mutually illuminate one another and shift back and forth. Consequently, one further establishes the state of "neither identical nor different."
One does not realize that within the true essence, these things fundamentally do not exist; they are all falsely established through the opposition of subject and object.

This agitates and gives rise to the emotions of the mundane world, thereby causing the wondrous luminosity to become turbid and the wondrous clarity to become muddied. From this point on, the signs of obscured darkness and the manifestation of form and color began to emerge.
Consequently, this gave rise to worldly toil and affliction: being stained is "dust" (*rajas*), and being disturbed is "toil" (*lao*); thus, sorrow [arises].
"Torment" refers to vexation; "affliction" refers to delusive confusion. Tianru said: This chapter of questions and answers is truly significant.
The preceding Buddha enumerated the seven elements to encompass all phenomena; thus, the world, empty space, sentient beings, and karmic fruits are all contained therein.
When he discussed the characteristics of these seven elements, he stated that they manifest within the *tathāgatagarbha* according to one's karma.
When discussing the nature of the seven elements, it was said that they are all-pervasive, perfectly interfused, and fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

At this point, Pūrṇa had not yet attained an understanding of the meaning of their sequential arising and universal interfusion; consequently, from these two doubts, he raised two questions. His first question was:
"If they are fundamentally pure and quiescent, how is it that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise? How can they be fundamentally pure and quiescent?"
This refers to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth" refers to the world and space.
"And conditioned phenomena" refers to the karmic fruits of sentient beings. Because they have not yet realized the principle of following conditions to arise, it is asked:
"How could they suddenly come into being? These four characters constitute a crucial question. The Tathāgata then took up the delusion within the fundamental awakening of nature...

To clarify what constitutes "luminosity" (*ming*), he instructs and resolves [the doubt], saying: "Based on luminosity, the objective realm is established. These four characters constitute the essential answer.
For "luminosity" here refers to deluded luminosity; deluded luminosity is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).

"The objective realm" refers to the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth—the source from which they manifest. To summarize: "Based on luminosity, the objective realm is established" means...
This means that it is due to ignorance (*avidyā*) that the world, space, sentient beings, and the fruits of karma arise.
Thus, both the doubt regarding the manifestation according to karma and the question of how they suddenly come into being are simultaneously resolved; there is no need for further explanation.

Now, I shall clarify this point by following the sequence of the text: "Based on clarity, the objective field is established. Since the objective field has been falsely established, your delusion arises."
"Yes. This section refers specifically to ignorance (*avidyā*). Within that which is neither identical nor different, it blazes forth to create difference;

yet here, once again, it establishes that which is neither identical nor different. This section poses the question: how is it that, due to the aforementioned ignorance, the world, space, and sentient beings are formed?
Thus there is turmoil, and through mutual dependence, weariness is produced. Through long-standing weariness, dust is stirred up, and their own characteristics [manifest].
"Turbid. The first two phrases emphasize ignorance as the basis for establishing the objective world (*bhājanaloka*) and so forth;

the latter two phrases emphasize the blazing [of afflictions] as they form various distinctions. "Dust" refers to the world and sentient beings. Because the world and sentient beings exist, there are karmic fruits;
therefore, it is said that "from this, the dust-laden afflictions are incited. This section summarizes the preceding meanings while remaining implicit.

This, however, demonstrates the three types of emotional states (*kleśa*). From "arising as the world" up to "truly existent conditioned phenomena," the text restates and synthesizes the preceding meanings regarding identity and difference, thereby revealing the names and characteristics of the three types. Yet, this is still a general exposition;

it is only from the passage beginning with "the clarity of self-awakening and the darkness of emptiness" that the text separately opens three sections to provide a detailed sequence of the three types.
The continuity [of these states]. Having completed the detailed exposition, it further states: "These three kinds of inverted continuities are all the luminous awareness;
they are the nature of cognition. Because of this cognition, appearances arise; they are born from deluded vision.
The mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena flow on in succession; because of this falsity, they end and begin again. This, moreover, is a summary conclusion.
Chapter One: Response to the Intent.
△ Section Thirteen: The Threefold Continuity.
"Threefold" refers to the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits. That which arises spontaneously constitutes the world; from its inception until its conclusion, it recurs again.

This begins with the account of how [the world] is bound by conditions. All are clearly and luminously aware of their own nature; yet because they perceive characteristics through this awareness, these arise from deluded vision.
They emerge as the world and, in stillness, become empty space... (up to) "by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession."
Pūrṇa had not yet realized the principle that within the Tathāgatagarbha, phenomena manifest according to karma; thus he asked how they could suddenly arise.
The Buddha explained the causes of his confusion and bondage: all are due to the delusion of enlightened awareness, which arises as the world and, in its stillness, becomes empty space.
He said that when deluded awareness moves, it gives rise to agitation and stirs up dust, thereby manifesting as [the phenomenal world].
When false awakening is suppressed, it becomes stubbornly dark and vast; thus, stillness constitutes empty space. Empty space is the same, while the world is different.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, which is pure and spontaneous, there is fundamentally neither sameness nor difference.
That which blazes forth as difference is truly the conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Now, let us speak from the perspective of the initial arising and establishment of the world.
Thus it is. Generally, the world’s arising begins with the clarity of awareness (*jue-ming*), which relies upon wind, metal, water, and fire to produce the myriad things.
This corresponds to the meaning found in Confucian texts regarding how yin and yang and the five elements transform and give birth to the myriad things.

When the clarity of awareness and the obscurity of emptiness interact, they produce agitation; hence there is the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) that supports the world. The clarity of awareness is yang.
The emptiness and obscurity are the yin. Yin and yang stand in opposition; through their alternating transformation and union, they produce movement.
From this movement, wind is generated; thus there exists a wind-circle that revolves beneath the nine earths. That world rests supported upon this wind-circle.
Therefore, it is called "maintaining and holding. The *Poem on the Seal of Verification of the Golden Elixir* by Longmei Zi says:

"The primordial abyss is without light; the Great Ultimate precedes the wind. The wheel strikes and moves, producing true lead from emptiness and obscurity. This refers to the meaning of the "primordial abyss being without light.
When the wind-wheel strikes and moves, it is the movement of Yang. Producing true lead is the sprouting of Yang; it is the Mother of Gold.
Yang (the active) is inconstant; inconstancy belongs to the delusory. Yin (the passive) is quiescent and eternally abiding; eternal abiding is the Real.

This is discussed from the perspective of cosmic transformation (*zaohua*). Wēnlíng’s commentary says: "The bright and the dim oscillate against one another, and one is unaware that the mind is moving.

Does cosmic transformation also possess a mind? This does not realize that the former was discussing it from the perspective of human nature. Indeed, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth exist within the scope of human nature.
It has indeed existed inherently from the beginning. For now, let us provide an explanation based on the process of cosmic creation (*nirmāṇa*), applying it point by point to the nature of humanity.
Because of emptiness, movement arises; because of firmness and clarity, obstruction is established. That which is the "golden treasure" is the firmness established by luminous awareness;
thus there is the Golden Wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*) that maintains the realm. Because of emptiness, movement arises; as this movement does not cease, the energy of vigorous Yang (*yang-qi*) coagulates.
It reaches the state of solidity. Solidity, when clearly manifest, establishes obstruction; its nature is firm and rigid.
That which is the "precious metal" is the solidity established by clear awakening within the human nature. Therefore, beneath the great earth, there is further a wheel of gold that sustains the land.
Firm awareness forms the jewel; the oscillation of clarity gives rise to wind. As wind and metal rub against one another, fire-light is produced. Thus, for the person—
Within the nature [of these elements], transformations occur in an instant, flashing and flickering without ceasing. From the brilliance of the jewels, moisture arises;
from the fire, heat ascends. Through this steaming, water is produced; thus there is a water-wheel that encompasses the great earth. Therefore, it is said to contain the worlds of the ten directions.
Water is the water of love within human nature. Fire ascends and water descends; they interact with the solidity established by metal.
Moisture becomes the great ocean, and dryness becomes the islands and sandbanks.

For this reason, within the great ocean, flames constantly arise, and within the islands and sandbanks, rivers and streams constantly flow. The power of water is weaker than that of fire; thus, fire does not [extinguish it].
It undergoes subjugation and coagulates to form earth, which transforms into high mountains. For this reason, when mountain rocks are struck, fire issues forth;
when melted, they become water. The nature of earth is weaker than that of water, so water does not undergo subjugation by it. The vapor of water rises upward.
The citron is a plant; for this reason, forests and thickets, when encountered by fire, become earth, and when subjected to pressure, become water.
Within the process of cosmic transformation (*zaohua*), it first begins with the movement of Yang. Through mutual interaction and illusory conjunction, the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*) are formed.

These act as seeds for one another, giving rise to things without end. By these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession. Within human nature, luminous awareness undergoes illusory movement, giving rise to...
The drawing forth of afflictions is likewise so.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, [you have explained] that delusion is not caused by another... (up to) ...by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
Furthermore, if we speak from the perspective of the origin of sentient beings: the aforementioned "shaking clarity" and "solid clarity" are both clarities of delusion.
How could they exist apart from original enlightenment? They are all the clarity of original enlightenment; it is simply that [sentient beings] have incurred blame for this.
It is not that they dislike enlightenment, but rather that they dislike clarity. If one were enlightened but lacked clarity, there would be no delusion of something to be clarified.

Once what was falsely established has taken root, the essence of awakened clarity consequently acquires spatial dimensions. Being obstructed by these barriers, it can no longer be perfectly integrated or all-pervasive;
thus, the principle of clarity does not transcend its limits. Consequently, the six sense-faculties are falsely localized: hearing cannot reach beyond sound, and clarity cannot surpass form.
Form, fragrance, taste, touch, and the other objects are divided by these six false distinctions, each remaining confined to its own root faculty, failing to achieve perfect penetration.

What is called "clearly understanding principle without transgression" is precisely what this means. The six sense-objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) are false defilements; the six consciousnesses (ṣaḍ-vijñāna) are false distinctions.
From this nature of karma, false karmic actions subsequently arise. Bound by common karma, beings undergo transformation through union and separation within the six realms and four modes of birth.

All arise from this. Those of "common karma" are the class of womb-born and egg-born beings; because the three—father, mother, and self—share common karma, they are entangled with one another and thus born.
Those of "union and separation" are the class of moisture-born and transformation-born beings; some take form by uniting with moisture.
This refers to crawling insects and the like. Or, there are those who undergo transformation through separation and alienation, such as those in the heavens, the hells, and the realm of ghosts.

What is meant by "seeing clarity gives rise to form"? To see clarity is to perceive that which is illuminated. Since there is already deluded clarity, the mind gives rise to objects, manifesting deluded forms;
hence it is said, "seeing clarity gives rise to form. Because one gives rise to seeing based on clarity, one generates attachment toward the perceived object; therefore...
Perception arises from seeing. When what is seen differs, the emotions are discordant; thus, differing views give rise to aversion. When perceptions accord, the mind is compliant;

thus, concordant perceptions give rise to craving. The mutual persistence of these three cravings is called "flowing" (*āsrava*); the mutual convergence of these three perceptions is called "receiving" (*upādāna*).
Since craving is the root of saṃsāra, the flowing of craving constitutes the seed. Since perception is the medium for transmitting life, the receiving of perception constitutes [the cycle].
The womb is produced through sexual union and drawn forth by common karma; it is here that the reception of birth and the entrusting of a physical substance begin.
Thus, due to causes and conditions, there arise the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.

*Kalala* is translated here as "coagulated mucus," which is the state of the embryo during the first seven days in the womb. *Arbuda* is translated here as "bubble," referring to the second seven-day period within the fetal membrane.

This is their characteristic mark. Among the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—each follows its own appropriate course: those born from eggs arise through thought; those from a womb result from emotional attachment;

those from moisture are produced by contact; and those born by transformation respond to separation. These states transform and shift into one another, and according to the karma they have received, beings follow their respective paths of flight or descent.
By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession. Disordered thinking is called "thought" (saṃjñā), while the binding of craving is...
It is said that when emotion (*qing*) is joined with vital energy (*qi*), it is called "conjunction" (*he*); this arises from dampness. When form (*xing*) withdraws, it is called "separation" (*li*);

this means that what is born here departs for there. As for further transformations and changes, sometimes emotion transforms into perception (*xiang*), and conjunction becomes separation; there is no fixed karma.
Eggs may easily become embryos; moisture-born beings may easily become transformation-born. There is no fixed substance. Receiving retribution according to karma, they may either ascend or sink;
there is no fixed destination. This is the cause for the continuity of sentient beings.
Pūrṇa, conceptual attachment and craving are bound together as one; one cannot separate from craving. (This continues until: Because of this delusion, it ends and begins again.
This is spoken of in terms of the arising of karmic fruits. "Conceptual attachment and craving are bound together;

one cannot separate from craving" means that within all worlds, fathers, mothers, sons, and grandsons are born in succession without interruption. These are rooted in sensual desire and greed. This refers to the condition.

Affection gives rise to desire; craving and affection nourish one another. When greed cannot be restrained, then all beings of the world—born from eggs, transformed by heat, born from moisture, or from wombs—devour one another according to the strength or weakness of their power. These acts are rooted in the greed for killing;
this speaks of how killing arises conditioned by greed. Thus, when humans eat sheep, the sheep dies and becomes a human, and when the human dies, they become a sheep, as they prey upon one another.
They consume [their victims] as food; this evil karma arises simultaneously with them and persists until the end of the future.
These beings take greed for theft as their root, and they give rise to theft by means of killing. What is meant by greed for theft? To take what is not given is called greed for theft.
"You owe me my life; I shall repay you with your debt. By reason of these causes and conditions, they remain constantly in birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. This is killing.

This is the cause for the continuity of stealing. You love my heart; I cherish your form. By reason of these causes and conditions, one remains constantly bound throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
This is the cause for the continuity of lustful craving. Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct alone constitute the root.
By reason of these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession. These three types are thus inverted characteristics.

[Continuation: All these are the luminous clarity of awareness (*jñāna-prakāśa*). The nature of clear cognition gives rise to appearances through its own act of discernment; they arise from deluded vision.

The various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—mountains, rivers, and the great earth—successively flow and change. Because of this false fabrication, they end and then begin again. This restates what was previously mentioned to provide the final answer:
the worlds, sentient beings, and their karmic fruits are all the fault of the luminous clarity of awareness. Yet, this does not mean that one should lay the blame upon awareness itself.
It is clarity. To be awakened and yet perceive this clarity as a fault is precisely what constitutes a transgression.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous awakening is thus, then it is the same for bodhi and nirvāṇa."
Because of the Buddha’s previous words regarding the fault of "awakened clarity," Pūrṇa again harbored this doubt, saying:

"This fundamentally wondrous, awakened clarity—the mind of sentient beings—is essentially no different from the Tathāgata’s wondrous awakening; there is originally no increase or decrease between them.

Yet, for no apparent reason, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena have suddenly arisen. Since the Tathāgata has realized the emptiness of awakening, when could these things ever arise again?"
"There is. The Buddha established an analogy for this: it is like that deluded person who, in a certain village, mistakes south for north.
Is this delusion produced because of further delusion, or is it produced by means of awakening? Pūrṇa said, "This delusion originally has no root.

How can it be produced because of delusion? Awakening does not produce delusion; how can it be produced because of awakening? The Buddha said, "It is like that deluded person who, while actually [in the village]..."
"When one is deluded, there suddenly appears an enlightened person who points it out to bring about awakening. Once this person has awakened, would they become deluded again? No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise thus. This delusion has no origin; its nature is ultimately empty.
Originally there was no delusion, yet it appeared as if there were an awareness of delusion. Now that the delusion regarding delusion has been extinguished, original awakening..."
No delusion arises. It is like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky; once the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Having understood this analogy, why do you still harbor your previous doubts? Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold:
once the gold is pure, it can never again become mixed. Or like wood turned to ash: it cannot become wood again. So it is with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Bodhi and nirvāṇa are likewise so. The above section responds to the question: "How can the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise?
The following section further responds to the question: "Since the four great elements each pervade everywhere, how can they be mutually contained?"
Pūrṇa, as for what you asked regarding earth, water, fire, and wind—up to the point where you spoke of cherishing the Lesser Vehicle and being satisfied with meager attainment—Pūrṇa, you also asked:
"The fundamental nature of earth, water, fire, and wind is perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm."
One might doubt that the natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another.
Furthermore, it is questioned how empty space and the great earth—both of which pervade the entire Dharma-realm—can coexist without conflict. To illustrate this by analogy:

just as the substance of empty space is not identical to its various phenomena, yet does not obstruct the manifestation of those phenomena, why is this so? Because when the sun shines upon that vast empty space, it becomes bright; yet when clouds gather...
When it is dark, it is obscured; when stirred by wind, it moves; when clear after rain, it is pure; when the vapors coalesce, it becomes turbid;

when earth accumulates, it forms a haze; and when water is still, it forms reflections. As for these various appearances, are they produced because of those external conditions, or do they exist inherently within space itself?
If clarity arises because of the sun, then at the time the sun shines, the empty space of the ten directions would all take on the color of the sun. How could this be?
When the sky is seen again with the full orb of the sun, if this light were inherently present within space, then space itself should illuminate itself;
