why then does it fail to produce radiance during the hours of midnight when shrouded by clouds and mist? One should know that this light belongs neither to the sun nor to space.
They are no different from the sun in the sky. When one contemplates their characteristics, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described;
how, then, can one question their mutual overcoming or extinction? When one contemplates their nature, it is fundamentally true—merely the wondrously enlightened clarity.

This mind of wondrously enlightened clarity was not originally water or fire; why, then, do you again ask how they could be mutually incompatible? Furthermore, this true awakening and wondrous clarity manifest according to conditions; therefore, you...
When space is clear and bright, there appears the manifestation of emptiness. When earth, water, fire, and wind each manifest individually, they appear individually.
If they manifest together, they appear together. "Together" means at one time; "individually" implies a sequence of before and after. How can they appear together?
It is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water, which two people observe simultaneously. In the water—
The sun: if it moves east, there is an east; if it moves west, there is a west. If each person has their own sun that follows them, one should not raise the objection:
"This is but a single sun; how can it travel in different directions? Since there would be two suns for each person, why do we perceive only one?
Such arguments are merely circular and illusory, providing no reliable basis. True awakening is like the sun: when following conditions, it is like the sun following the movements of people.
The characteristics of the seven elements vary according to conditions; such is the general meaning.

You regard form and emptiness as mutually exclusive and antagonistic, yet within the Tathāgatagarbha, the Tathāgatagarbha itself manifests as form, emptiness, and so forth, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within this, the wind moves and the void is clear; the sun is bright and the clouds are dark. Such is the wondrousness of their perfect interfusion.

Sentient beings lose their way in this wondrous clarity, discriminating between the shadows of conditions; they turn their backs on the dust and unite with awakening, thereby giving rise to worldly toil.
There are worldly appearances that are cramped and obstructive; it is no wonder, then, that they give rise to doubts of resistance and rejection.
I, however, through my wondrous clarity, merge with the Tathāgatagarbha; within this Tathāgatagarbha, there is only wondrous, enlightened clarity, which perfectly illumines the entire Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one; the small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small.
The one and the many respond to one another; the large and the small contain one another. One manifests jeweled lands upon the tip of a hair, and turns the wheel of Dharma within a speck of dust.
Every phenomenon is unimpeded; every dharma is suchness. Therefore, the manifestation of signs is fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described.
The wondrous nature is fundamentally true; there is nothing it does not encompass. It is simply by extinguishing deluded dust that one spontaneously accords with wondrous enlightenment.
Yet, within the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and complete mind of True Suchness (tathatā), there is not a single thing, nor is there even the slightest dharma to be obtained.
It is neither space nor mind; it is neither earth nor water, neither wind nor fire. That which is called the seven elements and the five aggregates are all not it.
It is neither eye nor ear, neither nose, tongue, body, nor mind; it is neither form nor sound, neither odor, taste, touch, nor mental objects;
it is neither the eye-consciousness, nor even the consciousness-element of the mind. And that which is called the eighteen elements and the ten...
The eight bases are all non-existent. They are neither ignorance nor the cessation of ignorance, up to and including neither the cessation of ignorance.
They are neither old age and death nor the cessation of old age and death; yet the Pratyekabuddha contemplates the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination as being entirely non-existent.
They are neither suffering nor its origin, neither cessation nor the path, neither knowledge nor attainment; yet the Śrāvaka’s dharma of the Four Noble Truths is likewise [non-existent].
It is not so. It is not dāna (giving), nor śīla (precept-keeping), nor vīrya (patience), nor kṣānti (diligence), nor dhyāna (meditative concentration), nor prajñā (wisdom), nor pāramitā (perfection).
Thus, all the six perfections of the Bodhisattva are "not so. Likewise, it is not tathāgata (Tathāgata), nor arhat.
The Arhat (*Arhat*), the Samyak-saṃbuddha (*Samyak-saṃbuddha*), and the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyak-saṃbuddha—all these are not [existent].
Neither is Nirvāṇa; they are neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure. Yet, they constitute the fruit of Buddhahood, as well as all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Nor is it otherwise. Yet it is neither identical to nor separate from [these phenomena]. Furthermore, when spoken of in terms of the wondrous mind of original luminosity, this very mind is it;
emptiness is it; earth, water, fire, and wind are it; and the six perfections are it as well.
It is the faculties, the objects, the elements, and consciousness; it is the twelve links of dependent origination;
it is the four noble truths; it is the six perfections; it is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
and it is the Great Nirvāṇa of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This is because, within the Tathāgatagarbha, when discussed in terms of its essence, [it is thus].
It is said that the fundamental, wondrously perfect mind, when discussed in terms of its function, is called the "primordially luminous, wondrous mind. This mind is not the dharmas;
it is both the dharmas and the mind. Since it is neither yet is, and is yet is neither, it ultimately culminates in the "wondrously luminous, primordial mind.

Furthermore, speaking in terms of the unity of essence and function, it is detached from both "is" and "is not," being both "is" and "is not," and neither "is" nor "is not. When one reaches this state of wondrous perfection, then—
Truly, when both essence and function are simultaneously extinguished, emotional conceptualizations are severed, and the wondrous nature of the hidden mind becomes vast and free from all blemish.
Yet, as soon as one attempts to conceive of it through the deluded calculations of the mind, one immediately deviates from the true nature of the Dharma.

How could the sentient beings of the three realms of the mundane world, or the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the supramundane realm, ever fathom the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata with their minds of limited knowledge?
To employ worldly language to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is like the lute, the zither, the pipa, and the konghou:
though they possess wondrous sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce them. You and all sentient beings are also like this;

the precious, awakened true mind is fully complete in each and every one of you, just as these instruments each have their own wondrous sounds. [The text compares] the lutes, zithers, and so forth to sentient beings.
It is the wondrous sound, the nature of the treasury. "Wondrous" refers to true wisdom. It is like when I press my finger, the Sea-Seal manifests its radiance;
yet when you briefly raise your mind, the afflictions arise first. This is because you do not seek supreme Bodhi, but instead cherish the Lesser Vehicle, taking little as sufficient.
Wēnlíng says: Although the lute possesses the sounds, they do not manifest without a finger; so it is with the human mind.
Although it is perfect, one does not awaken to it without a teacher. The various methods mentioned previously to reveal the *tathāgatagarbha* are the Buddha’s pressing of his finger.
That body, mind, and the myriad dharmas are manifest in their very place is the radiance of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

That Pūrṇa and the others gave rise to interpretations according to the words, resulting in a proliferation of doubts and anxieties, was the initial arising of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). The great meaning of this passage is to explain [this].
Ānanda raised an objection, saying: "If all things are identical to the true self, why is it that their wondrous function does not match that of the Tathāgata?

The present explanation states: "Although you possess the precious, awakened true mind, you do not attain its wondrous function because your defilements and deluded thoughts have not yet been purified."
△ Chapter Eleven: Requesting an Investigation into the Cause of Delusion.
Pūrṇa, following upon the previous statement that each [of the four elements] is individually complete, had already realized the Unsurpassed.
This further revealed the depth of his immersion in delusion; however, he did not yet know the origin of this delusion, and thus requested an investigation into its cause.
Pūrṇa said, "I and the Tathāgata... [until] I finally realized that the divine jewel was not obtained from without.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa, "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unexhausted.

To illustrate this, I shall cite the case of Rāvaṇa in the city of Śrāvastī, who, upon looking into a mirror, became attached to the head in the reflection—where the eyebrows and eyes were visible—and grew resentful toward his own head."
Failing to see one's own face, one mistakes it for a *chīmèi* (a mountain-demon). Without cause, one runs about wildly. The mirror is used as a metaphor for the deluded mind;
one loves the head seen within the mirror and becomes attached to illusory objects. Illusory matters are easy to cling to, like the eyebrows and eyes in a mirror;
true reality is difficult to know, like failing to see one's own head. Turning away from awakening and remaining in delusion is like running about wildly without cause. Pūrṇa replied:
This person’s mind is deluded; they run about wildly for no reason. To know that their running is causeless is to know that the delusion has no cause.

The Buddha spoke clearly to explain that delusion has no cause. Now, the wondrous enlightenment is perfectly complete; its fundamental nature is originally bright and wondrous. It is inherently free from delusion.
Since it is already designated as "delusion," how could it have a cause? If it had a cause, it would not be called delusion.
From these various deluded thoughts, they arise in succession, each depending upon the other. Such causes of delusion exist only because of delusion itself; in reality, there is no cause.
Since delusion has no cause, what can the false have to rely upon? Since there is not even arising, what could there be to cease?
One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream; though the mind may be sharp and clear, for what cause or condition would one grasp at them?
Objects in a dream—how much more so those that lack a cause? How could they have ever existed from the beginning? As for that person, Pūrṇa, did he have any causal conditions for his behavior?
He was merely terrified and running about wildly; when his madness suddenly ceased, his head was not obtained from outside. Even had his madness not ceased, what would his head have lost?
Thus we know that delusion is fundamentally without cause and there is nothing to be extinguished; one need only allow the conditions for delusion to subside, and delusion will then cease.
You have seen truly. You need only not follow the threefold continuity of worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings.
Because these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise; then the madness within your mind will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself *bodhi*.
For the supreme, pure, and luminous mind is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm and is not obtained from others. What need is there for toil or laborious effort?

As for cultivation and realization, it is simply because subtle and minute delusions have not yet been eliminated. Once the causes of delusion are extinguished, the knots of affliction will naturally unravel;
what need is there for laborious cultivation and realization? It is like a person who has a wish-fulfilling jewel tied within their garment, yet remains unaware of it.

Wandering abroad in poverty and destitution, they run about begging for food. Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to them, and all their wishes are fulfilled according to their heart’s desire.
Greatly wealthy, he finally realized that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.
△ Chapter Twelve: On the Doubts Regarding External Conditions, Causes, and Spontaneity.
At that moment, Ānanda was among the great assembly... (up to) "Because the three conditions are severed, it is the Bodhicitta."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, you have just stated that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise;
thus, Cūḍapanthaka’s madness subsided of its own accord within his mind. This subsiding is itself Bodhi, not obtained from without. This, then, is the severing of conditions."
Yet, [if] causes do not arise, how can this teaching of the true causes and conditions be suddenly abandoned by the Tathāgata?
We and all the members of this great assembly have all resolved their minds and attained awakening through causes and conditions; now you speak of Bodhi.
If it were not dependent on causes and conditions, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) taught by those heterodox teachers such as Kauṣārī would constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
I pray that you will deign to instruct me. The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just like the case of the city-dweller Yaśodara, whose state of madness was caused by certain conditions;
once that madness is eliminated, the state of non-madness emerges spontaneously. This is what is meant by 'causes and conditions.'"
This is a matter of natural principle; this analogy exhausts the logic. It is because once the nature of madness has ceased, the nature of spontaneity emerges.
Prior to the state of madness, both the causal conditions and spontaneity were non-existent. How, then, could you have first applied the two characters "spontaneous" (zìrán)?
Viewed from this perspective, all that is called "causality" or "spontaneity" is fundamentally non-existent; they are all established merely through deluded狂妄 (madness).
Therefore, it is said that their logic is exhausted. Thus, one uses causality to refute spontaneity: if the head were originally spontaneous, there would be nothing for it to be ignited by;
yet it is not spontaneous. Furthermore, why rely on the causal conditions of looking into a mirror to be afraid?
"Does it run madly about because it has lost its head? If this were so, then the principle of spontaneity (*ziran*) would be undermined.

Furthermore, you use spontaneity to refute dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If the head were originally spontaneous, why does it not lose itself spontaneously when it sees its reflection and becomes terrified and runs mad?
It is not that the head is originally lost; rather, the delusion of terror arises falsely, while the head itself never undergoes any change."
What need is there for causes and conditions? If this were so, the doctrine of causes and conditions would fall into error.
If you say that madness is fundamentally natural and fear is also inherently present, then on days when one was not yet mad, where did the madness lie latent?

If you take non-madness to be natural, since the head was originally not lost, by what cause and condition does one run about in a frenzy? This is the matter of causes and conditions versus the natural.

These doctrines are all established falsely. If one awakens to the original head, then one recognizes that the frantic running was false, and that both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity are merely frivolous arguments (*prapañca*). Therefore, I say: when the three conditions are severed, that is the *bodhicitta*.
If one awakens to the original head, this is the ability to know one's own original face; thus, all illusions and falsities are fully understood.
This is irrelevant. It is for this reason that great practitioners of the Way, having suddenly and completely eradicated all delusive conditions, attain great liberation.
△ Chapter Thirteen: Reproaching Idle Discourse (Prapañca)
The phenomena of arising and ceasing are fundamentally not bodhi. Once duality has departed, names and words vanish of their own accord.
Though one may uphold many sutras, it only serves to increase frivolous proliferation.
"When the bodhicitta arises, the arising-and-ceasing mind ceases"—how can you deceive yourself by still lingering in observation and listening?
What is meant by "proliferation" (*prapañca*)? If one says, "When the bodhicitta arises, the arising-and-ceasing mind ceases," this is merely a phenomenon of arising and ceasing;
it is not bodhi. If one says, "When both cessation and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*), wherein only spontaneity remains."
Thus, when the mind arises spontaneously and the arising mind ceases, this too is subject to arising and ceasing; it is not Bodhi.
Now, you instead point back to that which is without arising or ceasing, clarifying it as "spontaneous nature" (zìrán). How does this differ from the mundane world?

That which is formed by the blending and combining of various characteristics is called the nature of combination (héhé xìng); that which is not a combination constitutes the nature of original suchness (běnrán xìng). Why is this so?
All phenomena are not in harmony; each possesses its own inherent nature, and thus they can be designated by names.
However, this Dharma-gate of non-duality is devoid of all opposition and naturally transcends words and names. To further apply designations to it—is this not mere conceptual proliferation?
To directly address whether it is so or not so, whether it is a union or not a union—both "union" and "so" are equally non-existent.
Even the mind that distinguishes between union and separation is likewise non-existent. This accords with the intent of the *Daodejing*, which states that even "non-being" is non-existent.

Furthermore, [the Buddha] rebuked Ānanda for his lack of benefit despite his extensive learning; though he maintains many scriptures, they only increase his frivolous disputations. For this reason, he could not escape Māraṇḍa.
Without this divine mantra of my Buddha-Usnīṣa, how could it suddenly cause that lustful mind to cease, dry up the river of craving, and bring you liberation?
Therefore, Ānanda, practicing and maintaining [the mantra] throughout kalpas is not as good as cultivating untainted karma for a single day;
untainted karma is precisely the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. It can cause one to leave behind the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.
Its efficacy is swift and profound; it can cause Māra’s daughter to emerge from her entanglements and bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon Yaśodharā.
Why do you deceive yourself by still lingering to watch and listen, allowing craving and attachment to remain within your mind and eyes?

To personally discern the true from the false, to illuminate the nature of awakening, and even to profoundly investigate the myriad dharmas and decisively resolve all doubts and obstructions—all these serve as the primary expedient means to bring this about.

This true and correct faith and understanding serves as the mind of the causal stage. Since the causal mind is already authentic, one can thereby perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage;
therefore, the preceding sutra concludes here. What follows begins a new section.

△ Chapter Fourteen: Determining the Two Meanings First is the false root of birth and death, which depends upon arising and ceasing. Second is the fundamental root of afflictions, which arises from the faculties and their objects.
When Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha’s instruction, they all attained the pure and wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*.

Ānanda, following upon what had preceded, again requested: "Although I know that the ground of practice requires entry through the gateway of causes, I pray that I may set aside the Lesser Vehicle and ultimately attain the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
As for the path of my original aspiration, by what means shall I tread upon and subdue my past habits of objective clinging?"
They attained great *dhāraṇī* and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Buddha said: "You must resolutely resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Regarding the wondrous *samādhi* of the Buddha-Tathāgata, do not give rise to weariness.

You should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) and the awakening of the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*) are the same or different. If, at the causal ground, you take a mind of arising and ceasing as the basis for your cultivation..."
To seek the Buddha-vehicle through causes that are subject to birth and death—this is impossible.
To unite with the Tathāgatagarbha by means of what is unborn and undying is to be identical [to it]. To seek the eternally abiding fruit with a mind subject to birth and death is to be different;
therefore, it is impossible. Ānanda, you see that all conditioned phenomena in the world undergo change and extinction. Who is it that...
It does not perish; yet, one never hears of empty space rotting or decaying. Why is this? Because emptiness is not something that can be produced.
Therefore, from beginning to end, it neither perishes nor ceases. Now, as for one's own body, it possesses the characteristic of decay:
that which is solid is earth; that which is moist is water; the sensation of warmth is fire; and movement is wind. By means of these four entanglements, [the body] is divided.
Your perfectly湛 (zhan) and lucid awareness—whether as seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing—from beginning to end has been fivefold turbid, entangling you in the root of birth and death.
Turbidity constitutes the root of delusion and karma. What is meant by turbidity?
It is like clear water and sand or soil; the natures of these two substances are fundamentally not compatible. For the sake of worldly people...
Take that sand and soil and cast it into pure water. Because of this, the earth loses its solidity and the water forfeits its clarity;
their appearance becomes turbid, which is termed "turbidity. There are five layers of turbidity in your body: the first is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
The second is the turbidity of views; the third is the turbidity of afflictions; the fourth is the turbidity of sentient beings; and the fifth is the turbidity of lifespan.

What is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*)? You see that empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions; yet upon awakening, it is neither emptiness nor form. Due to a single moment of non-awakening, one falsely perceives the appearance of space.
Because the arising [of delusion] causes pervasive confusion, the seeing of emptiness and [the nature of] emptiness are not distinguished; thus, although one sees emptiness—

It is not the substance of original emptiness; though there is seeing, it is not the wondrously luminous awareness. These two interweave to form delusion—this is the appearance of the chaotic void when ignorance first arises.
Therefore, it is called the first layer of the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). What is meant by the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*)?
Your body currently manifests as a compacted aggregate of the four great elements as its substance. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing encounter this...

Obstructed and congested, they become impediments. Water, fire, wind, and earth revolve and combine; perceptions and cognitions interweave, forming deluded views. This constitutes the second layer of turbidity:
the turbidity of views. What is meant by the turbidity of afflictions? Furthermore, within your mind, there is the recollection, chanting, memorization, and cultivation [of teachings].
From this, within the internal divisions of the nature, they arise as cognition and view; externally, within the objective fields, they manifest as...
The six sense objects and the faculties form a complex entanglement. Apart from the objects, there are no marks; apart from cognition, there is no nature.
Nature and marks are interwoven, forming a delusive falsehood; this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). What is meant by the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*)?

Furthermore, you are born and perish morning and evening without ceasing, thereby creating the conditions for karma. You are attached to the three realms, and your knowledge and views remain perpetually within the world.
Rebirth occurs according to one's destiny, and the karmic forces constantly shift from one land to another; these phenomena interweave to form delusion.
This is called the fourfold turbidity of sentient beings. What is meant by the turbidity of lifespan? All that you see and hear is but a portion of the profound, perfect stillness.

Originally there is no distinct nature. Due to the separation of various particles, they interweave to form delusion, giving rise to what appears to be diverse without any actual basis for such difference.

Therefore, within their fundamental nature, they recognize one another; yet in their functional manifestation, they oppose one another. Their mutual recognition means that originally there is no distinct nature. Their mutual opposition means that diversity arises without any actual basis.
When identity and difference lose their standard, they interweave to falsely constitute delusion. What is meant by "identity and difference losing their standard"?
"Standard. When you speak of their agreement, their functions are yet contrary; when you speak of their contrariety, their natures are yet mutually cognizant.
Therefore it is said: "The standard is lost. This is the fifth stage of the turbidity of life-span.

If you wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to accord distantly with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should first select the very root of birth and death. Seeing and hearing... [text truncated]
To be aware and perceive is the sensory enjoyment of the six faculties of human beings. "Permanence, bliss, self, and purity" are the wondrous virtues of the Buddha’s nirvana.

The root of birth and death is precisely the karmic activity of the five turbidities. If one wishes to turn back from delusion to accord with the Truth, one must first select and eliminate the delusive root of birth and death;
relying upon the nature of non-arising and non-extinguishing perfect stillness, one must revolve away from that which is false and illusory, so as to—
Returning once more to original enlightenment, one attains perfectly luminous enlightenment and takes its nature—free from arising and ceasing—as the ground for practice.
Thereafter, one fully realizes the cultivation and realization of the ground of fruition. It is like settling turbid water in a clean vessel:

if it remains still, deep, and unmoving, then the sand and silt will naturally sink, and the clear water will appear before you. This, however, is merely called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions.

When the mud has been removed and only pure water remains, one attains perfect, luminous enlightenment; thus, the root of ignorance is forever severed, and the nature of awakening becomes profoundly still and luminous in its essential purity.
All transformations and manifestations no longer constitute afflictions, but are entirely in accord with nirvana.
It is like water from which the mud has been removed; it may be stirred and scooped at will, yet it can never again become turbid.

When the ground [of practice] is thus, then at the stage of fruition, there will be no lack of perfection in cultivation and realization, and nothing that does not accord with the wondrous virtue of Nirvana.
The second meaning is that you must all desire to simultaneously purify those six bases of cognition.
The second meaning is that you should resolve upon bodhicitta, give rise to great courage within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, abandon all conditioned marks, and carefully examine the root of afflictions;
this has been the source from which karma has been produced since beginningless time.

"Runsheng, who creates and who receives? If you do not examine this with thorough scrutiny, you will be unable to know that the sense bases and their objects are illusory, nor where the inversion occurs.
If you do not even know the location, how can you subdue it and attain the rank of Tathāgata? Observe those in the world who untie knots;
if they do not know what was knotted, how can they know how to untie it? Have you never heard that space possesses any knots that could be tied?"
As for "untying": why is this? Because emptiness has no form or characteristics, and thus there is nothing to be untied. Yet, the knots before you are many:
the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as the body and mind—these six act as intermediaries for thieves, plundering the treasures of your own home.
From this beginningless time, sentient beings have been bound by these entanglements within the world, such that they cannot transcend the vessel-world (the physical environment).

This correctly describes the locus of false speech, the inversion of sense organs and objects, where one plunders the family treasure for oneself and plunders one’s own true nature, giving rise to the inversions of entanglement.
The world of sentient beings is precisely the root-body; the vessel-world is the triple realm.
"Entanglement" has the meaning of fetters. "World" (*loka*) refers to flux and transition; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation: east, west, south, and north.

The four intermediate directions, above, and below constitute the realm (*dhātu*); the past, future, and present constitute the world (*adhvan*). There are ten spatial directions and three temporal flows;
these are all the manifestations formed by the interweaving of the delusions of all sentient beings. Within the body, they exchange and shift; worlds intersect one another. Why is this?
It is because when one speaks of the principle inherent within a single sentient being’s body, that principle itself interpenetrates other bodies. Furthermore—

Where there are realms, there are antecedents and consequents, as well as left and right. The body also possesses a temporal dimension—that is, the four and three below, and the four and three above—which revolve and undergo transformation.
However, this provisional reliance on worldly discourse is intended to manifest wondrous function; such is the general outline.
If one understands that the six directions vanish within the single [point], and they are mutually employed in perfect illumination, how could this possibly be reached by calculation?
For now, let us discuss it in terms of traversing the world: in the world there are only east, south, west, and north; as for above and below, they have no fixed position.
In the center there is no fixed direction; there are merely the four numbers: east, west, south, and north. Once these four directions are established, they interact with the world.
Three times four and four times three revolve into twelve; through successive transformations and layering, these become ten, a hundred, and a thousand.
To summarize from beginning to end: this generally enumerates the increasing numbers. Increasing one makes ten; increasing ten makes a hundred;
increasing a hundred makes a thousand, thus forming three layers in total. The first layer concerns the four directions, each discussing the three periods of time, totaling twelve.
The second layer takes the three periods of time in the eastern direction and transforms "one" into "ten," thereby forming thirty. [The same applies to] the south, west, and north.
The directions are likewise thus. There are thirty in each of the four directions, which together form three times forty, or one hundred and twenty.
In the third stage, there are thirty in the eastern direction; by transforming ten into a hundred, they become three hundred.
The southern, western, and northern directions are likewise thus. There are three hundred in each of the four directions, which further form three times four hundred, or one thousand two hundred.
If one uses the phenomenal world to engage with the noumenal principle, then by this same logic, one may use the noumenal principle to engage with the phenomenal world;
the pattern is thus evident. When the Buddha spoke of "this," he was likely referring to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

As the faculties and their objects interweave, and the worlds interpenetrate, the afflictions (*kleśa*) that arise—from the coarse to the subtle—are as numerous as these. Zhuangzi said: "The myriad transformations have no beginning and will never reach an end. Furthermore...
Based on the fact that the nature of discernment through the six sense organs is identical, each possesses one thousand two hundred merits.
However, because the functions of discerning the six objects differ, there are distinctions of superiority, inferiority, completeness, and deficiency.
Taking the eye as an example, it possesses only eight hundred merits; it can only see clearly when facing forward, while its peripheral vision to the left and right covers only two-thirds.
Speaking of the ears, they possess a full one thousand two hundred merits; when listening all around, nothing is missed in the four directions, and when hearing in stillness, there is no limit.
Speaking of the nose, it possesses only eight hundred merits; while it governs the passage of inhalation and exhalation, it lacks the central intersection.
As for the tongue, it possesses a full one thousand two hundred merits, capable of discerning flavors.
It is said that its wondrous function further awakens throughout all worlds; while mundane and supramundane wisdoms have their spatial limits, this principle is inexhaustible.
If it were merely a physical body, it would possess only eight hundred merits, capable of awakening when in conjunction with others but unable to know when separated from them.
The faculty of mind is thus perfected with one thousand two hundred merits.
It encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time, including both the ordinary and the sagely, reaching to their very limits.

Ānanda, if you now wish to investigate the stream of birth and death and trace it back to its root until you reach that which is neither born nor extinguished, you should verify these six faculties of experience in relation to those [objects].
Regarding true nature: who is conjoined with it and who is separated from it? Who is deep and who is shallow? Which constitutes perfect penetration, and which is not complete?
If one can awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration therein, then one can reverse that beginningless deluded consciousness and cause the stream of karma to follow its proper course.
The single gate of perfect penetration; entering deeply into this one entry, there is no delusion. Those six faculties of cognition become pure all at once.
△ Chapter Fifteen: The Six Organs Become Still and Perfect.

Now, because the six organs cling to stillness to give rise to delusion, when that one [faculty] becomes still, the other six vanish. Since both the organs and their objects have been eliminated, how...
"Why is it that cognitive clarity does not achieve perfect wonder?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how is it that one flows against the current... [and so on] ...how is it that cognitive clarity does not achieve perfect wonder?"
Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One: "How is it that by flowing against the current and entering deeply through a single gate, one can cause all six sense faculties to become pure simultaneously?

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Although you have already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and have extinguished the afflictions of the three realms belonging to the world of sentient beings that are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), you have not yet severed the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). These have accumulated over beginningless lifetimes..."
This habituation must be severed through the three fruits; it is not something Ānanda can know. When these delusions are completely exhausted, the six depths will become perfect.
Now, you should observe for yourself: are the six faculties before you one, or are they six? If you say they are one, why does the ear not see, and why does the eye not hear?
If they are established as six, then listen now as I proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to you.

"Among your six sense faculties, which one comes to receive [the sound]? Ānanda said, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "If it is your ears that hear, what concern is this for your body or mouth?
It is the mouth that comes to inquire about the meaning, and the body that comes to receive and uphold [the teaching]. Therefore, they are not one, yet they ultimately constitute six;
they are not six, yet they ultimately constitute one. Ultimately, they are not your roots; the root is one, while the six are its manifestations. You should know that these faculties are not one."
It is not six. Due to beginningless inversion, one has been submerged in the perfectly湛 (zhan) [luminous] state, and the meanings of "one" and "six" have arisen.

Although you, having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), have achieved the dissolution of the six, you have not yet forgotten the one. The "six" refers to coarse afflictions and deluded knots; the "one" refers to subtle afflictions and attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Having severed the coarse afflictions, the *srotāpanna* no longer enters into sounds, forms, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; this is what is meant by "attainment."
The six [consciousnesses] have been dissolved, yet one still lingers in attachment to dharmas; thus, "one" has not yet perished. This is proven by the subsequent text.

Here, one has merely attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but has not yet achieved liberation from dharmas (*dharma-vimokṣa*). Only when both are empty and non-arising can it be said that "one" has perished, like the great void.
When this merges with all categories of phenomena, although it is called "different emptinesses" due to the differences in the shapes of their vessels, if one removes the vessel and contemplates...
"Space. To speak of space as 'one'—how could that vast void possibly constitute for you either identity or difference?
How much less can it be called 'one' or 'not one'? Thus, your understanding is that the six faculties of sensory reception are likewise so.
When you know the identity and difference of the great void, and when right and wrong find no footing, then both 'one' and 'six' vanish together, and the perfect, profound stillness remains."
Although they were originally undivided, now that the "one-sixth" has vanished, the six sense organs currently exist; this arises because the turbid stillness (*zhan*) adheres to delusion.
Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrously perfect state, the turbid stillness adheres and gives rise to seeing.

The essence of seeing reflects forms, and by binding with these forms, it constitutes the organ. The source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason, it is called the eye.
At this stage, it is like a cluster of grapes; although the substance is complete, consciousness has not yet flowed forth.
When it flows outward and rushes toward objects, it is renamed due to defilement as the "floating roots" and the "four sensory objects," and is no longer called the "pure four great elements.
This occurs because the two aspects of movement and stillness strike against one another within the wondrous perfection, causing the clarity to coagulate and give rise to acuity.
The faculty of hearing reflects sound; when sound is rolled up, it forms the root-organ, which is called the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*), like a newly unrolled leaf.
When it reaches the floating organ, its flow becomes dissipated as it rushes toward objects, transforming into the four sense-objects and no longer being pure.

Due to the manifestation of the two conditions of openness and obstruction, within the wondrously perfect state, it adheres to stillness and gives rise to the sense of smelling. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance, and by incorporating the tongue, it completes [the faculty of taste].

The root source is called the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like two pairs of hanging claws. When they reach the floating faculties and flow outward to pursue objects, they transform into the four sensory dusts and are no longer called "pure.
Because the two aspects of tranquility and transformation intermingle, within this wondrous perfection, the clarity adheres to stillness and gives rise to tasting.
The essence of tasting reflects upon flavors, and by churning flavors, the faculty is formed; its original name was the pure four great elements.
It is like the crescent moon at its beginning. When the floating faculties flow outward and rush toward sensory flavors, they transform into the four objects;
thus, they are no longer called "pure. Through the mutual friction of the two aspects—separation and union—within the wondrous perfection, the stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to cognition.

The essence of cognition reflects upon contact, and contact transforms into the faculty, like the head of a waist drum. Flowing outward and rushing toward contact, it transforms into the floating faculty of the four [objects].

They are called "defilements" (dust) and are not termed "pure. Due to the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrously perfect [nature], the stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to cognition.
This essence of cognition reflects the dharmas, and by grasping the dharmas, it forms the sense organs. Originally, these were the four great elements of purity, like seeing within a dark chamber.
However, when the floating roots flow outward and rush toward the dharmas, they transform into the four defilements and are no longer termed pure, Ānanda.
Thus, regarding these six sense faculties: through that awakened clarity (*jue-ming*) there is "clarity" (*ming*); when this clarity-awakening loses its essence, it becomes attached to delusion.

From this attachment, the luminous awakened clarity—the true clarity—manifests. When there is "clarity within clarity," it is deluded clarity. What was stated previously—that "the nature of awakening is necessarily clear, yet it is falsely made into 'clarity-awakening'"—is fully explained by this.
Therefore, at this moment, you are neither separated from darkness nor separated from light, and yet there is no seeing.

The substance [of the body] is free from motion and free from stillness; fundamentally it lacks the quality of hearing. It is neither permeable nor obstructed; the nature of smelling does not arise. It is neither changing nor tranquil;

tasting has no point of emergence. It is neither separated nor joined; the perception of touch is fundamentally non-existent. There is neither cessation nor arising. To understand where [consciousness] rests:
one realizes that all six [senses] are empty and false, and that apart from their objects, they all lack intrinsic substance. You need only not follow after them...

Movement and stillness, union and separation; tranquility and transformation, penetration and obstruction; birth and death, light and darkness—all such conditioned phenomena—may be resolved by uprooting a single sense-faculty.
By detaching from external clinging and withdrawing inwardly, by gathering the hearing and turning back the gaze, one returns to the fundamental reality.

When the innate radiance is manifested, this luminous nature shines forth, and all other fivefold attachments are simultaneously severed and liberated in their totality. This clarity does not depend upon the cognitive perceptions arising from external objects.
They do not follow the sense organs; rather, they rely upon the organs to manifest clearly. Thus, the six organs function interchangeably for one another.

When they adhere to delusion, they follow the floating objects of the external environment and consequently become obstructed. When they adhere to the profound stillness, they neither follow nor depend on anything, but merely rely upon the organs.
Therefore, the ear can also see, and the eye can also hear; they function interchangeably, for the six functions share a single source.
Do you not know that within this assembly, Raudrākṣa sees though he has no eyes; the Naga King Bhadrananda hears though he has no ears;
the Goddess of the Ganges smells fragrances though she has no nose; Gavāmpati knows flavors though he lacks a tongue; and Kāśyapa of the Void perceives touch though he has no body?
Thus, within this assembly, Mahākāśyapa’s faculty of mind has long been extinguished, yet it is perfectly complete.
He understands with clarity, not by means of mental recollection. Now that your faculties have been completely uprooted, they shine forth from within with inner brilliance.
Thus, these superficial, illusory appearances will melt away like ice dissolving in hot water, becoming a single, perfectly fused, pure, and precious awakening.

Therefore, it is said that one is "transformatively born by thought. Such is the supreme, perfect, and wondrous state of awakened awareness. It is like the way worldly people gather their perceptions.
Regarding the eye: if one forces it to close tightly, the appearance of darkness manifests before it; the six sense-faculties become dark and indistinct, and the head and feet appear as one.
If, without relying on external light, there were an internal radiance that shines forth, this would mean that the lack of light is self-originated.

In that case, all appearances of darkness could never cause obscuration. Such is its wondrous nature. If the faculties and their objects have already been eliminated, how could the awareness-illumination not [manifest]?
The Perfection of the Sublime.
△ Chapter Sixteen: Cultivating the Ultimate Cause.
Ānanda mistakenly identified the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as his own mind-nature; therefore, he doubted that liberation from these objects would lead to extinction.
By what cause shall one establish [this truth]? It is for the sake of seeking unsurpassed enlightenment. The Buddha sent Rāhula to strike the bell to provide verification:
although the faculties and their objects are severed, the nature of hearing does not perish. Taking this as the cause, the fruit of the sevenfold permanence can then be established.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said [up to]: 'Why would one not achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said: if, on the ground of the causal stage, the mind of awakening desires to seek that which is eternally abiding...'"
If this seeing were to be heard, it would be devoid of light and darkness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction;
ultimately, it would have no substance. It would be like the thinking mind, which, apart from external objects, fundamentally has no existence.

How can you take this ultimate annihilation as a cause for cultivation, seeking the fruit of permanence? How could such a thing be consistent [with the goal]? (7. The "fruit of permanence" refers to Bodhi and Nirvana.)

Suchness-Buddha-nature (*tathatā-buddhadhātu*), the *amala*-consciousness, the empty Tathāgata-garbha, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—these are what the Buddhas have attained and are called *bodhi*.

That which is quiescent and eternally blissful is called *nirvāṇa*. That which is non-false and unchanging is called Suchness. That which is free from faults and transcends all defects is called Buddha-nature.
That which discerns all things without defilement or attachment is called the *amala*-consciousness. Not a single dharma...

Established, the total exhaustion of afflictions is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (empty womb of the Tathāgata). To illuminate all phenomena through and through without discrimination is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
Because Ānanda mistakenly took the reflected images of the six sense-objects to be his own mind-nature, it is said: "If there were no light or darkness, the seeing..."

Ultimate emptiness is like the absence of external objects; the nature of thought itself is extinguished. Through repeated cycles of analysis and subtle investigation, one finds that fundamentally there is no self-mind nor any mental factors associated with the self. With what, then, could one establish a cause to seek supreme enlightenment? Thereupon, the Buddha, to clarify their delusion, first had Rāhula strike a bell to test their sensory faculties. He asked, "Did you hear it? The assembly replied, "We heard it. He asked again, "Is it still ringing? They replied, "It has already ceased. He asked once more, "Can you still perceive its cessation? They replied, "Yes, we can perceive it. He then asked, "When the bell was struck, you perceived its sound; when the sound ceased, you perceived its cessation. What is it that perceives this? They replied, "It is our hearing faculty. The Buddha said, "If your hearing faculty is truly constant, why does it not perceive the cessation when the sound has stopped? If it does not perceive cessation, how can you say it is constant? If it perceives both sound and cessation, then it must have two distinct natures—one for perceiving sound and one for perceiving cessation. Since these two natures are different, how can you claim the hearing faculty is one and constant? Thus, he led them to realize that the sense organs are not inherently real. Furthermore, he had Ānanda strike the bell again. While the bell was ringing, he asked, "Do you hear it? They replied, "Yes, we hear it. When the sound had ceased, he asked, "Do you hear it? They replied, "No, we do not hear it. He asked, "When the bell was struck, you heard the sound; when the sound ceased, you did not hear it. What is it that hears the sound and what is it that does not hear it? They replied, "The hearing faculty hears the sound, and the hearing faculty does not hear the sound. The Buddha said, "If your hearing faculty is truly constant, why does it hear when there is sound and not hear when there is none? If it does not hear when there is no sound, how can you say it is constant? If it hears when there is sound and does not hear when there is none, then it must have two distinct natures—one for hearing and one for not hearing. Since these two natures are different, how can you claim the hearing faculty is one and constant? Thus, he led them to realize that the sense organs are not inherently real. [The Master] said: "When the bell has ceased and there is no sound, do you hear it now? The assembly replied: "We do not hear it. He struck the bell once more and asked: "Do you hear it? They replied: "We both hear it. From this we know that hearing arises because of sound; therefore, when the sound ceases, hearing ceases as well. Furthermore, he commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked: "Now the sounds are not simultaneous. After a short while, does the sound exist? They replied: "It exists. He then asked: "Is there still hearing? They replied: "There is hearing. He struck the bell again and asked: "Is there still hearing? They replied: "There is hearing. Aniruddha rose from his seat... (until) "turning back the vision and tracing its source; this is the foremost.
Regarding those who attain awakening through the faculty of the eye:
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat... [until]... returning the breath to circulate through emptiness; this is the foremost.
This is one who attains awakening through the faculty of the nose.
Gavāmpati immediately rose from his seat... [until]... returning the taste to revolve within the cognition; this is the foremost.
Regarding those who enter through the faculty of the tongue:
Pilindavatsa immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...this is the foremost for the pure awakening that leaves the body behind.
Regarding those who enter through the faculty of the body: knowing this profound pain in a few phrases—“knowing” is itself awakening. It says:
Although one uses awareness to perceive pain, my pure mind of awareness is of a single flavor of pure awareness;
there is no perception of pain within the perception of pain. Thus, the perceptions of pain and the perceptions of the perception of pain all arise directly from delusion.

One must simply cast off this illusory body and purely maintain fundamental awareness. Consequently, before long, as he gathered his mindfulness, his body and mind suddenly became empty. By means of this, he attained realization.
"Without further training.
Subhūti then rose from his seat (up to) "turning the Dharma back into non-existence; this is the foremost.
This refers to those who enter through the faculty of mind. All marks enter into non-mark; that is to say, all marks enter into the absence of marks.
The absence of marks is the true mark.
Śāriputra then rose from his seat... [until] ...the light of supreme knowledge and vision is foremost.

This refers to those who enter through visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Because visual consciousness is clear and sharp, one penetrates it upon the very first sight; thus, consciousness is purified.
Therefore, they attain various penetrations and proficiencies; because the mind is boundless, their vision and awakening are perfectly luminous.
Bodhisattva Samantabhadra then rose from his seat... [up to] ...this mastery in discernment is the foremost.
Regarding this entry through the auditory consciousness: the "mind-hearing" that brings forth illumination is internal realization; the "discernment with mastery" is external application.
Sudhana and Nanda then rose from their seats... [up to] "...this perfect clarity that extinguishes outflows is the foremost."
Regarding this entry through the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*): previously, one relied on the sense organ (*indriya*) for counting the breaths in order to collect the mind;
here, one relies on consciousness for observing the breath in order to stabilize the mind. The breath arises from wind and fire, which agitate the turbidity of afflictions;

therefore, its appearance is like smoke. When the six [elements] interact and fire is seen to burn, the breath can manifest as various smoky purple flames—all of which are produced by the turbidity of afflictions.

When pure contemplation brings forth illumination, then turbidity and defilement are thereby dissolved. Thus, the interior is luminous while the exterior is empty, like smoke vanishing to become white.
Upon the exhaustion of outflows, there are no further afflictions; the inner clarity emits radiance, so that every inhalation and exhalation becomes pure light.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (up to) was foremost in the total extinction of all outflows (*āsrava*). Those who enter through the consciousness of the tongue:

Pūrṇa was foremost in preaching the Dharma; his eloquence was unimpeded, and by means of this he eliminated Māras and extinguished the outflows—all of which was due to the power of the consciousness of the tongue.
What is meant by "turning the wheel"? The Buddha, by means of body, speech, and mind...
The three wheels: the wheel of speech is that which adapts to sentient beings with unimpeded sound and voice.
Upāli then rose from his seat... [until] ...he was foremost among those who possess all-pervading benefit.
Regarding those who enter through realization by means of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*): there are the fundamental karmas, namely killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;

and the derivative karmas rooted in these fundamentals, namely the prohibitions against secondary transgressions. As for the cessation of faults due to causes, as established in the *Upāliparipṛcchā-vinaya*, all attain liberation by means of the body-consciousness, reverently upholding the three thousand eight hundred thousand precepts without the slightest error.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat... [until] "having long since attained clarity and purity, he is foremost.
This refers to the profound meaning of the causal conditions for entering through the mental consciousness; it means that this is not a coarse phenomenon produced by worldly conjunctions.

This brings forth the realization of both mundane and supramundane dharmas; thus, by means of this, one arouses the bodhicitta and attains great penetration, supernormal powers, and mastery according to one's will.

As for "revolving the stillness," one enters the wondrous stillness from the mental consciousness; therefore, after a long time, one achieves clarity and transparency, with perfected and pure supernormal powers that are luminous, clear, and sovereign.
Ucchuṣma was foremost among those who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
Those who enter through the element of fire are those of excessive lust; for such people, desire-fire originally arises from the sensation of warmth.
Death is the fire of karma. When the power of karma intensifies, it becomes a mass of fierce flames. One observes that all four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are merely objects of sensory contact:
the hundred parts of the body and the four limbs are earth; the various sensations of cold and warmth are water, fire, and wind.
Once one is established in *samādhi*, it is said that "divine light condenses within. Because the fire element is pervasive and intense in those with many desires, it transforms [the practitioner].
The fire of desire becomes the fire of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder then rose from his seat... [omitted] ...and attained the Unsurpassed Way; this is the foremost.
This refers to those who awaken through the element of earth: the two types of sensory objects within the body-realm, up to and including weapons, are all the element of earth.
The derived forms of matter are phenomena produced by causes and conditions; they are no different from sensory objects—they are empty.

They are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Their self-nature is untouched. This means that because one knows them to be illusory and give rise to sensory dust, there is not the slightest defilement or contact.
When the dust is eliminated and wisdom is perfected, one then achieves unsurpassed enlightenment.
The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to bring about the perfect awakening of Bodhi;
this is the foremost. This is the realization through the water element.
The Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to transmit the single wondrous mind; this is the foremost.

This refers to those who enter through awakening by means of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). Those who transmit the single wondrous mind know that the power of the wind has no basis and that all myriad movements are illusory;
thus, they are able to personally realize the unmoving nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat... [omitted] ...this supreme perfection of wondrous power is the foremost.
This refers to those who awaken through the great element of space. Regarding the simultaneous manifestation of clarity:

it means that within the perfectly hollow mind, there is an inner lucidity that emits light, such that they interpenetrate and merge in harmony. The pearl represents form; the mirror represents the mind. Form is created from the mind.
The entire body is mind; therefore, it emits jewel-light that灌 (irrigates/infuses) the ten directions and so forth.
Maitreya Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [up to] ...attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost.
This refers to the entry into awakening through the great consciousness (*vijñāna-mahā*). It concerns the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*): 1.

**The nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*):** This is so called because one horizontally clings to the notions of a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), a self (*ātman*), and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*); furthermore, it is so called because one conceptually constructs the existence of substantial entities throughout the distinction between the animate and the inanimate.

Thus, it is "pervasive conceptualization. 2. **The nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*):** This is so called because one calculates that there are causes and conditions, and that the world is a combination [of these].
[This is] the synthesis. One establishes names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), and clings to these provisional marks. [One holds that] these definitely arise from seeds;

although there is no self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), by the natural seed-nature, one takes provisional form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) and so forth as seeds to produce the dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth.

The *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is the essence of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for consciousness entering the *pariniṣpanna* through its perfect luminosity: it is due to...
The wondrous, perfect consciousness-mind realizes and enters true wisdom; it no longer becomes deluded by the pursuit of objects through various attachments.
Among those of his same class, the Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta has attained samādhi, which is foremost.

Regarding this entry through the great awakening by means of the faculties (*indriya*): mindfulness belongs to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). If the mental faculty is pure, all the other faculties are naturally restrained; thus, there is no need for selection.

As for "attaining the patience (*kṣānti*) of mindfulness of the Buddha," it means that through pure mindfulness one eliminates turbid thoughts, and through right reception (*samādhi*) one extinguishes false reception.

Once the false and turbid are dispelled, the mind and its objects are empty and tranquil, and nothing arises; this is called the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). It is as follows: [text continues].
This is because the Buddha-land of self-nature is pure; thus, it can gather the practitioner back [to the source]. The *Contemplation Sutra* states:
"Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must not, for even the duration of a finger-snap, dwell upon the five worldly desires. This is called 'binding the mindfulness.
If one can remain thus, without interruption or distraction, then immeasurable nature-light will spontaneously manifest. This is what is meant by not relying on external directions."
Thus, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.

The Sixth Fascicle of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,

△ Specifically Highlighting the Ear-Faculty, Twenty-First.
This fascicle specifically highlights the twenty-five gates of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty. This is most appropriate for the present occasion; therefore, it must [be studied].
Special Note: At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat... [up to] "...entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

This means entering perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) via the three types of wisdom. "Hearing" refers to reaching the ears; "contemplation" refers to fixing the mind; "cultivation" refers to practice.
To practice this is called cultivation. These three are perfect clarity; they are known as the three types of wisdom.
First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object; once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered. The present text says, "entering the stream while losing the object.
This indicates that this Bodhisattva has likewise cultivated from the first fruit of the srotāpanna; hence it says, "firstly. Thereafter, he advances through the stages in succession.

Regarding the phrase "hearing the middle and entering the stream": "hearing" refers to the sense-object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*), and "stream" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). That is to say—
Initially, one takes the sensory object of sound and enters into my Dharma-nature; yet in reality, there is nothing entered.

That "nothing entered" is precisely what the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* means by "entering the stream while having nowhere to enter. When there is nothing entered, external objects do not enter.
"Object" (*suǒ*) refers to the locus of the subject-object duality; whereas "entering" involves both subject and object, here we merely eliminate the object. However, as for the Dharma—
Within this nature, the essence is inherently and eternally quiescent; fundamentally, there are no moving dusts. How, then, could there be a mark of stillness?
Since that which enters has perished, one perceives that the two marks of movement and stillness clearly do not arise. "Clearly" means awakening. One awakens to their non-arising.
At this stage, there is still the presence of discernment (*vijñāna*). There is entering and departing; there is stillness and discernment. This is not yet the ultimate.
Thus, as [insight] gradually increases until what is heard and what is to be heard are exhausted, and when arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction (*śānti*) manifests before one.

External objects are easy to eliminate, but internal faculties are difficult to exhaust. Through such practice of eliminating the object, one gradually progresses until both the faculty of hearing and the object heard are simultaneously exhausted.
Thus, both the internal and external are eliminated, and both object and wisdom are merged into stillness.

Nevertheless, in fundamental awakening and true emptiness, not even the slightest dharma can be obtained; the exhaustion of the object and the cessation of hearing are specifically the method of contemplation and cultivation.
[The ear. Now, as for the dharma of hearing all sounds, it likewise does not abide. When one realizes that both the perceiver and the perceived are empty, then emptiness-awareness is perfected.

Yet, there is still awareness remaining. When awareness perceives that the perceived is empty, and emptiness itself is extinguished along with what was emptied, then birth and death are extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Having reached this ultimate attainment, the essence of perfect penetrating wisdom is thereby [realized].

Upon examining this passage, its meaning is that one reaches the state where all is lost, exhausted, empty, and extinguished. Yet, there are varying depths in this practice, which constitutes the gradual stages of the Sage’s cultivation.

This precisely accords with the intent of the *Qingjing jing* (Sutra of Purity) in such passages as "observing emptiness, [one finds] even emptiness is quiescent, and there is nothing to be quiescent.
"Exhausted" (*jin*) means exhausting that which was lost; "empty" (*kong*) means emptying that which was exhausted.

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the cessation of that which is empty. There are two meanings of "cessation": there is cessation spoken of in relation to arising, and there is cessation spoken of in terms of non-arising.
Therefore, it is said: "When arising and cessation have both ceased, quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*) manifests before one.
This is what the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* means when it says: "When arising and cessation have been extinguished, quiescent extinction is bliss. Wénlǐng divides this into four meanings.

First, the extinction of external objects; second, the purification of internal faculties; third, the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness; fourth, the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). These meanings are indeed correct.
Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds... (up to) the thirty-two manifestations entering all lands.

Because the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, neither the mundane nor the supramundane can obstruct them; thus, throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, they are perfectly luminous and penetratingly aware.

For this reason, when they harmonize upward with all Buddhas, they take pity on sentient beings and give rise to compassion, responding to capacities to bring them to fulfillment—this refers precisely to the thirty-two manifestations described below. When they harmonize downward with the multitudes of living beings, they understand their sorrowful longing.
To provide rescue and deliverance accordingly refers precisely to the fourteen fearlessnesses mentioned below.
World-Honored One, if various bodhisattvas enter samādhi... [up to] ...the World-Honored One expounds the Dharma for them so that they may attain liberation.

Regarding those indicated by the thirty-two manifestations: they comprise the four classes of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings. The four noble ones are: first, the Buddha; second, the *pratyekabuddha*; third, the *vidyādhara* (or *pratyaya-buddha*); and fourth, the *śrāvaka*.
Among the ordinary beings, there are four types of liberated ones. As for the Buddha: having cultivated right concentration and attained the right fruit, his supreme resolve is fully perfected.
Those from the *pratyekabuddha* downward are all termed "learners" (*śaikṣa*) or "lesser *śrāvakas*. They possess tranquil, wondrous clarity and are supreme.

The marvelous manifestation of perfection is called the Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer). As for the Pratyekabuddha, they awaken to the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination;

through the nature of the conditions and that which is conditioned, the marvelous manifestation of perfection is supreme. The Śrāvaka (Hearer) attains the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths and enters cessation by cultivating the Path;
through the supreme nature, the manifestation of perfection is realized. Liberation and accomplishment are different: liberation involves transcendent progress, whereas accomplishment is merely...
It is simply the accomplishment of their capacity for action; this is the teaching of the Sage who "intensifies the instruction according to the material.
If sentient beings desire to clarify and awaken their minds, they shall attain the sovereign accomplishment of the wondrous power of non-action.
