△ Regarding the Three Heavens of the First Dhyāna: the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā.
Ānanda, all those people in the world who cultivate their minds [to this level]—this class of beings is called the Brahmakāyika Heaven.

Regarding the phrase "without relying on dhyāna," etc.: this means that although such a person does not correctly cultivate the true samādhi and lacks correct wisdom, they merely practice the six modes of conduct to subdue desire, thereby preventing the arising of passionate attachment.

Consequently, they do not remain within the coarse afflictions of the desire realm, and as they are untainted by the retribution of purity, they are reborn in the Brahma world through the power of mindfulness. Initially, they are called the Brahma-parṣadya (Assembly of Brahmās). Then...
The multitude of beings is merely this. Those in the Brahma-purohita [Heaven] are the ministers of the king; those in the Mahābrahmā [Heaven] are the celestial kings.
Once the habituation to desire has been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests—reaching such a state as this—a class of beings is named the Brahma-purohita Heaven.

The gods of the first heaven are merely able to restrain their bodies and subdue desire; these gods, however, have attained the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and practice the virtue of Brahma (*brahmacarya*) in accordance with the code of discipline (*vinaya*), and thus they surpass them.
With body and mind wondrously perfected and majestic deportment unimpaired—[as described up to] "this class of beings is called the Great Brahma Heaven.
Previously, they advanced through pure mind, majestic deportment, and preceptual conduct until reaching wondrous perfection and purity;
furthermore, by adding clear awakening and transcendent penetration, they reach the height of sublime virtue and thus become Brahma Kings.
Ānanda, these three superior streams are free from all suffering and affliction (up to) being unmoved by any outflows; this is called the first dhyāna.

The stream of desire leads toward birth and death; although the six heavens of the desire realm exist, they cannot be considered superior, for these [first dhyāna] devas have already transcended desire.
Turning one's back on the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and hastening toward the supreme purity, all four dhyānas are thus called "supreme flows" (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).

Having already departed from the eight sufferings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is said that "afflictions (*kleśa*) do not oppress. Having already departed from the distracted and agitated mind of desire, it is said that "all outflows (*āsrava*) are unmoving."
△ Second Dhyāna: Three Heavens—Parīttābha (Limited Light), Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light), and Ābhāsvara (Radiant Sound).
Next is the Brahmakāyika Heaven, which governs the Brahma-puruṣas. ... [up to] ... this class is named the Parīttābha Heaven.
This refers to those who advance by following the practice of Mahābrahmā. Because they are endowed with precepts, concentration, and wisdom, they are said to be "perfected.
Being perfected, they are able to clarify and solidify their minds so that they do not move in accordance with external objects; thus, from this profound stillness, light arises.

However, at this initial stage, they are merely able to detach from clinging and restore the state of stillness; since their light is still inferior, it is called "Limited Light" (Parīttābha). In the second dhyāna and above, there is no...
There are verbal expressions, yet they merely manifest light through a concentrated mind. This light varies in degree of excellence, thereby distinguishing their relative heights.
Each light kindles the next, shining forth without end; such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābhā).

The power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly luminous, and wondrous light flashes forth in succession. As the objective realm follows the light, it becomes pure and transforms everywhere into lapis lazuli.
By absorbing and sustaining this perfect radiance, the essence of the teaching is accomplished. Thus, this class of beings is called the Heaven of Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara).

In various worlds, the substance of the teaching differs; thus, in Sahā, it is by means of written characters, whereas in the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) world, there are no written characters or verbal speech, but rather the Dharma is proclaimed through various fragrances.
In this heaven, sounds are produced from the circular radiance [of the Buddhas], and thus it is named "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara).
Ānanda, these three superior classes [of beings] have already subdued all anxiety and [even] coarse outflows (*āsrava*); this is called the Second Dhyāna.
It is only upon entering the First Dhyāna that the mind first attains stability from outflows, yet it has not yet been able to subdue them.

Since these devas have already subdued the coarse outflows, their karma gradually becomes inferior and their conduct gradually superior; thus, while they still experience anxiety, compared to suffering and affliction, it is ultimately slight.
△ Third Dhyāna: The Three Heavens of Limited Purity (Parītta-śubha), Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇa-śubha), and Universal Purity (Śubha-kṛtsna).
Ānanda, such celestial beings whose radiant halos produce sounds [as described]—this class is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parītta-śubha).
From the teaching-essence of the aforementioned radiant halo, the subtle principle is revealed, giving rise to refined practice. Departing from the prior agitation of joy, pure bliss is produced;
this bliss is not an external object, but emerges from the pure nature. It is tranquil, placid, and quiescent, and is thus called the bliss of nirvana (*śānti-sukha*).
However, because the power of purity is still inferior, it can only serve as a passage and has not yet reached fulfillment. This is because it remains inferior.
Therefore, it is called "Limited Purity" (Parittasubha).
When pure space manifests before one and induces boundlessness—extending in this manner to such a class—it is named the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha).
As for "pure space," it is a state of meditative concentration that is free from the movement of joy and does not take objective objects as its focal point. From this, it is expanded.
By causing the pure marks to be boundless and to accord with the wondrous nature, the body and mind become light and at ease, and the joy of the nature is thus perfected.
Because they are boundless, it is called "Immeasurable Purity."
The worlds, bodies, and minds are all perfectly pure; such a class [of beings] is called the Śubhakṛtsna (All-Pervading Purity) Heaven.
Because the pure space is boundless, the worlds, bodies, and minds are all perfectly pure. When the accomplishment of pure virtues is attained, their nature takes refuge and entrusts itself therein.
"Entrusts" means to rely upon this in order to return to quiescence.
Ānanda, these three superior streams, being fully endowed with great compliance (up to) complete joy, are called the third dhyāna.
△ The fourth dhyāna consists of nine heavens: the four fundamental [heavens], the Heaven of Merit-Born, the Heaven of Merit-Loved, the Vast Fruit, and the Unconscious;
and the five non-returners: the Without-Affliction, the Without-Heat, the Good-Vision, the Good-Appearance, and the Cloudless.

Up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven (the apex of the form realm), the meditative practices prior to the four fundamental dhyānas can only benefit oneself; they have not yet been able to benefit others. Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, one concurrently cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The altruistic minds of compassion, joy, equanimity, and benefit are called the "immeasurable virtues.
All untainted contemplative wisdom and various dhyānas and samādhis emerge from these; therefore, they are named the four fundamental heavens.
Ānanda, furthermore, when gods and humans are no longer oppressed in body or mind—up to this point—one such class is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).

Because suffering and pleasure are suddenly abandoned, it is called the cessation of the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness. Since equanimity and mindfulness are purified, the nature of pure merit arises.
The mind of equanimity is perfectly integrated and resolute understanding is pure (up to: such a class is called the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*).
Because both suffering and pleasure have been forgotten, the mind of equanimity is perfectly integrated; because the mind is free from all burdens, resolute understanding is pure.
Consequently, merit is unimpeded and one attains sublime conformity. From this contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*), the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is brought forth.

They practice until they reach the ultimate. Therefore it is said: "Exhausting the limits of the future, their merit is fixed as such; because it is worthy of being cherished and delighted in, the heaven is named 'Beloved Merit' (Puṇyaprasava)."
Ānanda, from this heaven there are two diverging paths... (up to) such a class is named the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
From the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, it branches into two paths: one is a direct path leading toward the Bṛhatphala; the other is a circuitous path leading toward the Āsaṃjñika.
Those who, due to their prior state of mind, do not harbor divergent attachments, directly cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to bring about their own immeasurability.

From the Ābhāsvara Heaven up to the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the merit cultivated by those who dwell therein is perfectly luminous; thus, because the fixed merit of these heavens is exceedingly vast, they are called the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).
If, from their previous state of mind, they simultaneously loathe both suffering and pleasure—up to this point—one such class is named the Heaven of Non-conception (Asaṃjñisattva).

The Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is a point where paths diverge. Although one’s prior mind was able to suppress afflictions and cultivate dhyāna, it involved delusion and carried heterogeneity:
taking the presence of mind to be birth-and-death, and taking the state of no-thought to be *nirvāṇa*.

Thereupon, one simultaneously detests both suffering and pleasure, focusing exclusively on cultivating the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) to hasten toward the state of no-thought. As objects settle upon the body, this extends even to mental conceptions; thus, all [are stilled].
They abandon all [perceptions]; their mental deliberations become ashen and solidified, forming the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

By this, they receive retribution and are born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), with a lifespan of five hundred *kalpas*. When first born in this heaven, they have not yet entirely ceased to conceive;
it is only after half a *kalpa has passed that thought ceases. As their retribution is about to end, they again experience thought for half a *kalpa*, and only then does their retribution expire.
Ānanda, these four superior streams, which reach all throughout the world through the full maturation of their functional effort, are called the four dhyānas.

As for the mind of conceptualization and recollection: the coarse is called *vitarka* (applied thought), and the subtle is called *vicāra* (sustained thought). These two are both present in the three heavens of the first dhyāna; in the Great Brahmā heaven, there is no *vitarka* but only *vicāra*;
in the second dhyāna, there is neither *vitarka* nor *vicāra*, but there is joy and bliss; in the third dhyāna, one is detached from joy and bliss, yet there is still inhalation and exhalation.
Inhalation and exhalation give rise to fire; joy and bliss give rise to water; and the inhalation and exhalation of breath give rise to wind.

The fourth dhyāna transcends and is free from these, and is therefore unmoved by the three calamities; thus it is called the "Unshakable Ground" (Acala-bhūmi). Nevertheless, its receptacle world is not truly eternal, for it arises and perishes along with sentient beings.
Although it is not the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) ultimate realm, the conditioned (saṃskṛta) efficacy of practice has here reached full maturity.
[End of section].
△ Five: The Non-returner Heavens.
Ānanda, herein there are further five non-returner heavens (up to) where they establish their dwellings within their respective homogeneous classes (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The person of the third fruit, having exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is reborn in this heaven and will no longer take birth in the desire realm;

therefore, they are called "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*). They are also called "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*). Both the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) are completely extinguished.
This refers to the absence of karma that leads to continued rebirth in the desire realm. With both suffering and pleasure forgotten, it also refers to the four dhyānas. Because...

The lower [heaven] is where karma through desire is extinguished. These five heavens are established separately from the Fourth Dhyāna; they are collectively named the Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).
Ānanda, because both suffering and pleasure are extinguished and the conflicting mind does not arise, this particular class is called the Heaven Free from Affliction (*Avṛha*).
There is weariness and relinquishment; this is still the mind contending with its objects, unable to be free from vexation. Only when both mind and objects are dissolved do afflictions cease.
When the mechanism functions alone and the point of intersection is nowhere to be found—this class of beings is called the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).

Intense heat is called "affliction" (fan); slight affliction is called "heat" (re). Although the upper [minds] may contend, their intentions do not intersect; yet there still remains a ground for intersection. In this state, however, the mental mechanism has no counterpart;
thus, one investigates the intersection and finds no ground for it. Being able to extinguish the shadows of conditions, one attains freedom from heat.
In the worlds of the ten directions, the wondrous vision is perfectly accomplished... [up to] this class is called the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*).

Because they can extinguish the shadows of conditioned objects, their wondrous vision is perfectly clear and limpid. Thus, the images of defiled mental dust and the accumulated impurities of the nature are entirely absent.
Seeing the ten directions with perfect clarity, it is therefore named "Good Vision."
When refined vision manifests before one, and there is unimpeded mastery in forging and smelting [the elements], such a class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
When concentration and wisdom are brilliant and refined, and one possesses sovereign mastery in fusion and refinement,
reaching the ultimate limit of all subtle phenomena and exhausting the nature of form— such a class of beings is called the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

"Ji" (ji) refers to the subtlety of form; "xing" (nature) refers to the foundation of characteristics. If one has not yet thoroughly investigated and realized this, one remains confined by form and characteristics, creating limitations and obstructions for oneself.
By being able to investigate and exhaustively penetrate this, one transcends physical constraints and enters the boundless.
This is the ultimate limit of name-and-form.
Ānanda, from those gods of the Non-returners in the four dhyānas down to this point, it is called the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The lower heavens cultivate impure, mundane concentrations, whereas these gods cultivate pure, noble karma; thus, there is a difference between them in terms of coarseness and subtlety.

One cannot perceive [them]. "Walking alone without companions" means being free from the defilement of desire. "Not yet having exhausted the burden of the physical form" means that there still remains a material substance.
△ The four heavens of the Formless Realm: the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and the Sphere of Nothingness.

In the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), there is no matter resulting from karma, but there is matter resulting from meditative concentration (dhyāna-phala-rūpa). This applies equally to both the primary body and its environment; thus, one extinguishes the physical form and returns to non-existence.

It is the dwelling place of those Śrāvakas of fixed nature, or the distinct retribution of non-perceiving outsiders (asaṃjñi-bāhya), or the mixed state of those who have abandoned their aversion toward gods and humans.
Their locations are manifold, yet all are devoid of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
△ Further, regarding the branching and transcending:
next, Ānanda, from this Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) [up to] what is called the Great Arhat who has turned his mind back.

The Akaniṣṭha Heaven resides at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and borders the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it is called the "limit of form" (*rūpānta*). There are two divergent paths:

one leads out of the three realms, which is this present section; the other enters the formless realm, which is the subsequent section. All four dhyānas are cultivated by relying on equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*).
Here, the mention of the "mind of equanimity" refers to the causal mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This causal mind is capable of giving rise to the [formless attainments].

Their outflows of ignorance and wisdom are exhausted; having severed all defilements and delusions to reach perfect clarity, they transcend the three realms and do not abide in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, but enter the Bodhisattva vehicle.
These are called Great Arhats who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment].

△ Regarding the entry into the realm of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are four heavens. All of them advance by relying on the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). First, one becomes weary of form (*rūpa*) and relies on emptiness. Second, one becomes weary of emptiness and relies on consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Third, form, emptiness, and consciousness are all extinguished, yet one relies on the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). Fourth, by relying on the nature of consciousness, one reaches the ultimate extinction.

One investigates [the nature of cessation] but does not attain true extinction. These are all the superior fruits of conditioned goodness; they do not transcend saṃsāra, nor do they constitute the Path of the Sages.
If, within a mind of equanimity, one achieves the relinquishing of aversion—[proceeding] in this manner—one is called a member of the class known as the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana).

These individuals rely on equanimity and do not cultivate wisdom; they grow weary of their own physical form and limitations, and by resolutely practicing the contemplation of emptiness, they extinguish the body and return to non-existence.
Thus, they are those who, weary of form, rely upon emptiness; this is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi).
When all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; this state is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Since all obstructions have dissolved and ceased to exist, one does not rely on form (*rūpa*). Since even the non-existence of obstruction has ceased, one does not rely on space (*ākāśa*).
Only the *ālayavijñāna* and *manas* remain; this is the one who, weary of emptiness, relies upon consciousness. This is termed the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Because it is in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the resultant consciousnesses—the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* and the seventh *manas-vijñāna*—remain.
Since the body-faculty has already dissolved, the six consciousnesses no longer exist; thus, only these two remain.

Among the three objects of the *manas*—form (*rūpa*), space (*ākāśa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—in this stage, one becomes weary of form and space and relies upon consciousness. Consequently, the coarse objects of form and space are no longer present. Therefore...
Only the subtle half remains;
since both space and form have vanished and the consciousness-mind is entirely extinguished—reaching this state, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

In the preceding stage, one was able to eliminate space and form, yet the consciousness-mind had not been extinguished; here, however, it is completely extinguished, and thus the ten directions are tranquil.
However, it is utterly remote and has nowhere to go. Although this state lacks the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*), the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) has not yet been extinguished.

Practitioners today do not penetrate the nature deeply and often stagnate at this point; though they may thoroughly comprehend the emptiness of form and extinguish their mental deliberations until reaching a state of nothingness, they ultimately remain within the nature of consciousness.
Deeply hidden and subtly persistent, they cannot free themselves from the cavernous pit of birth and death.
The reality truly resides herein.
The nature of consciousness is unmoving; through the exhaustive investigation of its cessation (up to the point where) delusion and leakage leave no trace, one enters the cycle of rebirth.
As for "the nature of consciousness," it is the profound, fundamental source of the conscious mind. "Unmoving" means it is quiescent and has no destination. Being thus able to remain unmoving—

It moves; one again investigates and refines it until it ceases. Yet, because this cessation relies upon consciousness, it is ultimately not true cessation. This is merely forcing a manifestation of the nature of exhaustion within that which is inexhaustible.

Thus, it seems to exist yet does not exist; it seems to be exhausted yet is not exhausted. Because it seems to exist yet does not exist, it is not the Realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Because it seems to be exhausted yet is not exhausted, it is also not the Realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. This state, moreover, is profoundly subtle and continuous.
Cotton is the subtlest of appearances. Because the cotton is so fine that it cannot be separated out, it is said that the principle of emptiness is not yet fully exhausted.

Śrāvakas rely on this and take it to be the ultimate, ultimately achieving only the fruit of dullness. Non-Buddhists rely on this and have no place of refuge, ultimately remaining deluded within the realm of outflows.
When one cultivates the supramundane mind, this is its final limit; coarse karma has already ceased, and the nature of consciousness-only remains.
Stagnant! If one struggles with earnest resolve to escape this, one will transcend the three realms. However, this merely demonstrates the gradual ascent of the ordinary and shallow;
if one deeply realizes the essence of wisdom through suffering, one may also suddenly leap beyond to true realization.
"Ānanda, these various devas and celestial beings [from] each of the heavens... up to the path of practice for those dedicated to the noble ranks.
This refers collectively to the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Ānanda, from the extinction of body and mind in these four heavens of emptiness (up to the formless realms), *pudgalas* each follow their own kind.

The three realms arise through delusion, giving rise to the seven destinies. Through deluded grasping and attachment, there are *pudgalas*—here translated as "those who repeatedly take on existence"—which is the profound root of deluded grasping.
△ Regarding the Realm of Asuras:
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms... [up to] ...how could they further follow the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?
These take the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—as their root. If one is devoid of such karma, it is called the realm of devas; it is said that one will certainly ascend there.

Indeed, it is because one possesses such karma that one is called a "ghost" (*preta*). Lunyan said: "One will inevitably fall. Of the seven destinies (*gati*), two are cited here to comprehensively encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

One falls by virtue of existence (*bhava*) and ascends by virtue of non-existence (*abhāva*); therefore it is said: "Existence and non-existence mutually overturn one another, giving rise to the nature of saṃsāra.
If one attains right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), then the wondrous nature is eternally quiescent, and there is no further saṃsāra. Both existence and non-existence are non-existent.
"Words are the cessation of the karma of mutual inclination; non-existence is also extinction. Words are the forgetting of discriminative emotions.

When karma is severed and emotions forgotten, then the three kinds of delusive roots—the names and their traces—both vanish together. Therefore, if one wishes to sever the wheel of delusion, one must cultivate right concentration."
Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed; each has its own private [delusions]... (until) if another speaks thus, it is the speaking of Māra.
△ Chapter Twenty-nine: Detailed Discernment of the Realm of Māra.
"Māra" refers to the five māras. "Realm" refers to the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*). However, one must first be affected by the perversity of that realm before Māra can take advantage.
Therefore, it is necessary to examine and distinguish them in detail. There are five openings of the demonic realms (*māra-viṣaya*):

namely, the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the demon of birth-and-death (*mṛtyu-māra*), the celestial demon (*deva-māra*), and the ghostly demon (*bhūta-māra*). When combined, these consist only of the demon of the aggregates and the celestial demon.
The Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) refers to the afflictions of birth and death that arise based upon the five aggregates.
The celestial Māra (*deva-māra*) refers to those who delight in practicing perverted meditative concentrations and thereby harm the true path.

At that moment, the Tathāgata was about to conclude his discourse on the Dharma seat (up to the point where it says): "All these are established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization.
This was to transform those who are deluded; that is to say, to respond to their delusions by transforming them accordingly.
You should know that empty space arises within your own mind—how much more so, then, can the various worlds exist within empty space?
Empty space arises within the Great Enlightenment like a single bubble emerging from the ocean, or like a fragment of cloud;
this illustrates how the world is illusory and ephemeral, easily dissolved and extinguished.

If even one among you were to give rise to the true and return to the source—up until the point where all lands would not shatter—the essence of the true source is fundamentally vast and empty from the beginning. Space and lands are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization.
Once the true is realized and delusion ceases, there is no longer any such establishment; therefore, they naturally vanish away.

From "All Māras and various ghosts and spirits" to "How would they dare remain to disturb his meditative concentration," it is because all subsequent [beings] say that upon awakening there is no fault; this is precisely what is meant.
If one does not attain clear awakening and is deluded by the aggregates (skandhas), [one will] wallow in ruin and decay with no one to pity or rescue them.
△ Breaking through the Five Aggregates: Manifest Objects △ 1.
The Aggregate of Form (rūpa-skandha)
Ānanda, you should know that from "you sit at the site of enlightenment" up to this point, it is called the realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

"Aggregate" (*skandha*) takes the sense of covering and obscuring. Because it restricts the true nature, it is called a "realm" (*kṣetra*). Wuxing points out that this belongs to the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
This is indeed the place where power is gained in *dhyāna*, and the time when the dust of afflictions (*kleśa*) temporarily ceases; it is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Nevertheless, because the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has not yet been shattered, it is like being in darkness despite having clear vision;
even if one's eyes were bright and the ten directions were opened wide, [it would remain so] until one realizes that solidified false discrimination is its very foundation.

The characteristic of the exhaustion of the five aggregates is not the annihilation of the body into nothingness; rather, it is simply that the power of contemplation penetrates and illuminates them so that they no longer constitute delusive obstructions.

At the very first moment, when the view of emptiness and the [perceived] objects are not yet distinguished, this is called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*); it is the essence of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Therefore, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, one is able to transcend it. As for this aggregate of form:
it initially arises from the mutual conjunction of the three delusions between parents and oneself; hence it is said that "solidified deluded thought" constitutes its root.

△ The objective realms of the aggregate of form and the objective realms of the other five aggregates are all established and then subverted within your own mind; they exist solely within the interval between delusion and awakening.
Therefore, I shall now provide a detailed exposition so that you do not cling to false views. There are ten such points.
"Ānanda, you should investigate this wondrous clarity with precision herein... (up to)... if you take this to be a realization of holiness, you will immediately succumb to various demons.
This section is purely a demonic realm; it is different from the previous nine."
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a state of mutual conflict within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Thus, these things manifest. Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not measure themselves and claim to have attained the stage of a sage.
Because of such great falsehoods, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You should maintain and protect them, ensuring that the celestial Māras find no opportunity to exploit them.

△ Second, the Aggregate of Feeling (vedanā-skandha), Ānanda: That son of good family, when the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted, perceives the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a mirror.

Although he has attained something, he is not yet able to employ it; he is like a demon whose hands and feet are perfectly intact, yet who is not confused regarding what he sees and hears, his mind [remaining unawakened].
Contact with heterodox influences cannot move him; this is what is called the domain of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).

"Sensation" (*vedanā*) takes the meaning of receiving and experiencing external objects. Having already destroyed the *rūpa-skandha* (the aggregate of form), the internal and external are empty and harmonious; thus, he is able to perceive the minds of all Buddhas.

To perceive the minds of all Buddhas is precisely one’s own own wondrously enlightened and luminous mind. It is like a mirror manifesting images. This is what is meant by: [The original Chinese text continues: "As a mirror manifests images..."
Pure, empty, and pervasive, it is entirely devoid of form or obstruction. Although it possesses a wondrous essence, it is as yet unable to function, like a person in a demonic trance;
this is because it is shrouded by sensation (*vedanā*).

When the demonic afflictions have ceased, his mind detaches from the body; looking back at his own face, he comes and goes with complete freedom, no longer subject to obstruction or hindrance—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Observing its source, he sees it is but empty, luminous, and delusory.
This is considered its fundamental basis.

When the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) subsides and ceases, one is then able to detach from the body and reflect inwardly, moving and abiding without obstruction. However, when deluded views and perceptions arise, they disturb the tranquil nature;
this is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), which is the very substance of the aggregate of sensation. Therefore, when the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, it is eliminated.
Thus, due to illusory conditions of compliance and resistance, one gives rise to false perceptions of loss and gain. Consequently, the aggregate of sensation has no substance;
it is merely an empty manifestation of clarity. Therefore it is said: "Empty clarity and deluded thought constitute its root."
△ The Manifestation of the Aggregate of Sensation (vedanā-skandha).
There are ten categories, Ānanda. When that virtuous man attains great radiance within this state, his mind becomes luminously clear;

yet if he suppresses it to excess, he may suddenly give rise to boundless compassion amidst it. If he awakens to this, there is no fault, but it is not a mark of saintly realization. One must be clearly aware of this.

It will not cause delusion; after a long time, it will naturally subside and vanish. If you mistake this for a realization of holiness (*ārya*), then the demon of pity (*karuṇā-māra*) will enter your heart and innermost being.
You will lose your correct meditative absorption (*samyak-samādhi*) and shall surely fall into ruin.

Within this, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is also fixed in concentration. Since the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been destroyed, there is no longer any obscurity; thus, one attains great radiance.

Ānanda, furthermore, within that concentration, one sees the aggregate of form vanish and the aggregate of sensation become clear and bright, with superior signs manifesting before one, evoking a profound stirring.
This is excessive. Suddenly, amidst this state, one gives rise to boundless courage; the mind becomes fierce and sharp, and one’s resolve equals that of all Buddhas.

If one awakens to this as it truly is, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization. If one takes it to be a sign of sainthood, then a mad demon will enter one's heart and viscera, causing incomparable arrogance and a loss of right concentration, leading inevitably to a fall.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, he perceives the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becoming clear.

Having nothing new realized before him and having lost his former dwelling place, his power of wisdom declines and he falls into a state of ruin. Seeing nothing at all before him, a great parching thirst suddenly arises within his mind.
At all times, one sinks into recollection without dispersal, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor. This is called "cultivating the mind without wisdom and thereby losing oneself.
If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy ones. Otherwise, it becomes the demon of recollection.
One grasps the mind morning and evening, suspending it in a single place, yet loses right concentration (*samādhi*) and shall consequently fall into ruin.

Because the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is not yet exhausted, there is no new realization to advance toward; because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already dissolved, there is regression and loss.

Thus, dwelling in a state of neither progress nor regression, one lacks a foundation and is called the "ground of mid-level collapse. Due to this lack of foundation and lack of vision, one becomes parched and despondent, sinking into discursive thought and thereby inviting the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*).
The mind of recollection is falsely bound, like a bird caught in a snare.

Furthermore, good son, when you see that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, and when the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*) surpasses meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet you lose its sharp intensity;

with various superior qualities harbored within your breast, you take a little as sufficient. This is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind, thereby drowning in intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*).
If you awaken to this state, there is no fault; but if you take it to be a holy realization (*ārya-adhimukti*), you will fall into inferiority and become easily satisfied by the demon of contentment.

When people, in their innermost hearts and minds, claim to have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), they lose right concentration (samyak-samādhi) and shall inevitably fall into ruin.

Previously, their power of meditative concentration was strong while their wisdom was slight; now, however, the power of their wisdom exceeds their concentration. In both cases, there is a mutual deficiency.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, because what was newly realized has not yet been attained, the mind has already perished;

as one surveys these two limits, hardship and peril arise spontaneously, and an inexhaustible sorrow suddenly wells up within the mind, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison—the heart no longer desires to live.
They constantly seek out others to harm their lives, hoping for an early liberation; yet if they awaken [to the truth], there will be no fault.
If, however, they mistake this for the realization of sainthood (*ārya*), then a demon of "constant anxiety" (*śoka-māra*) will enter their heart and viscera.
They may then cut off their own flesh or flee into mountain forests, losing their right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) and falling into ruin.
Because one loses one's composure in advancing or retreating, the mind gives rise to perilous difficulties, thereby forming perverse anxieties.
Furthermore, while in that state of meditative concentration within purity, one may lose right reception (*samādhi*) and fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, one may perceive the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becoming clear and bright. Believing oneself to have reached fulfillment, one suddenly and groundlessly gives rise to great conceit (māna).

This is called "seeing oneself as superior. Lacking wisdom to save oneself, there is no fault if one awakens to this; however, if one takes it to be the realization of a sage (ārya), [one falls into error].
Then there is the demon of great conceit, which enters their hearts and innermost being. They fail to pay homage to stupas and temples, destroy sutras and images, and mislead sentient beings;
they enter the Avīci Hell, lose right concentration, and shall surely fall into ruin.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, one may perfectly realize the subtle principle and attain great compliance, suddenly giving rise to immeasurable pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Having already claimed to have become a sage and attained great mastery, if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, then a portion of the "delusive demon of lightness and purity" will enter their heart-mind.
They will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress; such a person is called a monk who has done much but heard little, and they are deluded by doubt.
Sentient beings enter the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration; they shall inevitably fall into ruin.
Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, amidst the clarity of awakening, they attain a nature of empty luminosity, yet therein they suddenly turn toward eternal extinction.
They deny cause and effect and enter exclusively into emptiness; as the mind of emptiness manifests before them, they even give rise to the view that there is perpetual annihilation.

If they awaken to this, there is no fault; but if they take it as a realization of sainthood, then the demon of emptiness will enter their hearts and entrails, leading them to slander those who uphold the precepts.
This is called the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). For a Bodhisattva who has realized emptiness, what is there to be upheld or transgressed?

To drink alcohol, eat meat, engage extensively in sexual misconduct, violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, mistakenly commit offenses against others, and lose right concentration—such acts lead inevitably to downfall.
Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, one relishes its empty clarity, which penetrates deep into the marrow of the heart. Suddenly, immeasurable craving arises;

when this craving reaches its peak, it becomes madness and manifests as greed. Lacking the wisdom to sustain oneself, one mistakenly enters into various desires. If one awakens to this, there is no fault;
however, if one takes it to be a realization of the sacred, then the demon of desire will enter one's heart and viscera, constantly preaching that desire is the path to Bodhi and ensnaring them.
The number of such ordinary fools will fill ten million; their demonic minds will grow weary and they will depart from their bodies.
Deprived of their majestic virtue, they will fall into royal calamity, mislead sentient beings, and enter the Avīci Hell. Having lost right concentration, they shall surely sink into ruin.
Exhortatory Text. As with the preceding section on the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). △ Third, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha):
Ānanda, when that virtuous man practices samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exhausted, although his outflows (āsrava) are not yet extinguished, his mind is detached.

Its form is like a bird emerging from a cage; having already achieved accomplishment, it ascends from its ordinary body through the sixty sacred stages of a bodhisattva to attain the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), proceeding everywhere without obstruction. This is what is called the realm of the conceptualized substance.

"Perception" refers to the floating characteristics of mental deliberation and the delusive habits of conscious cognition; these can obscure the wondrous luminosity and obstruct the Path of the Sages.

When that aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, the mind becomes detached from the body, and one gains freedom in going and staying, having already accomplished the cause for the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*).
Nevertheless, one still remains obscured by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). It is, for example, like a person who, while asleep, speaks in their sleep; although [they speak],...
There is nothing else known; it merely forms a sequence of phonetic tones. This is the characteristic of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions eliminated, one reaches the point where pervasive delusive conceptualization (*yì-róng wǎngxiǎng*) serves as its foundation.

When there is no movement, the perception of arising and ceasing vanishes. When awakening is pure, thoughts of beginning and end are extinguished. Thus, within the single cycle of birth and death, one illuminates from beginning to end.

Recollection, consciousness, recitation, and study give rise to the dust of knowledge and views; this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), which is the very substance of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Therefore, when perception is exhausted, one transcends it. Perception is capable of melting and transforming, causing the mind to follow objects and causing objects to...
It follows the mind. Just as one might imagine a sour plum, it can penetrate through material obstructions; therefore, it is called "pervasive delusive thought.
The Manifestation of the Realm of the Thought Aggregate (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
Its categories number ten. The first concerns celestial demons (*deva-māra*) possessing humans; next follow ghostly demons (*bhūta-māra*) possessing both humans and non-humans.
When that son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes void and subtle, he may expose the affairs of others and not avoid public censure;

such a person of false concentration can possess the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā). His past karma and former deeds result in the retribution of an animal in a future life—these two constitute the supernormal power of knowing past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna).

He knows the origins [of things], which is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (paracitta-jñāna); his exposing [others' faults] constitutes the supernormal power of the divine eye and ear (divyacakṣur-śrotra).
They are fond of speaking of future calamities and blessings (up to: they suddenly hope for transformation and change, yet maintain that subtle marks are permanent).

Only when the three delusions are exhausted does one abandon birth-and-death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*) and attain birth-and-death through transformation (*nirmāṇa-janma-maraṇa*). Thus it is seen in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
At that time, the celestial Māras waited for an opportunity... (until) maintaining and protecting them so that they accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
