Volume Ten. Recorded by the Buddhist disciple and lay practitioner Yun Kong (Yùnkōng), Lù Xīxīng, who studied under the masters of Huǎihăi.
Wang Fazuo, Collator. △ Four:
The Aggregate of Formations.
Ānanda, when that virtuous man cultivates *samādhi* (up to) "this is then called the realm of the aggregate of formations."
The five aggregates are coarse in the beginning and subtle in the end; therefore, when perception (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted, there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadowy phenomena.

Although one contemplates the myriad phenomena, there is no conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Thus, it is like the clarity of a mirror: without adhesion and without traces, it receives reflections in emptiness, with no lingering habitual tendencies.
This singular, pure, and true luminosity reaches its ultimate limit. Consequently, the hidden *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is thereby laid bare.
It is "exposure" (lu). Because it serves as the fundamental root of the marks of arising and ceasing within the myriad transformations of action, its manifestations are fully disclosed.

Thus, there is nothing among the origins of those twelve classes of beings that is not seen exhaustively. Nevertheless, although one has not yet been able to see their cultivation of causes and their pursuit of fruits, [the essence is revealed].
By means of the sequence of the Truths, one is already able to see the totality of sentient beings. These arise solely through the activity of mental formations (*saṃskāra*).

This aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) serves as the common basis for birth. If this [basis] is clear yet agitated, its primordial nature is radiant; yet, it takes subtle and hidden deluded thoughts as its root.

Birth and extinction ceaselessly alternate, and the movement of karma is constantly shifting; this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), which is the very substance of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Therefore, one who exhausts the aggregate of formations is able to transcend it.
Ānanda, you should know that this is the attainment of right awareness (*samyag-jñāna*). [From here until: This person falls into the two theories of causelessness.
When dreams and fantasies vanish, one remains constant whether awake or asleep; therefore, it is called "right awareness śamatha" and also "concentrated clarity and right mind.
These are all signs of the exhaustion of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). External objects are all summoned by the mind; therefore, when conceptualization is exhausted, concentrated clarity arises.
Then the celestial Māras will not approach. From this point on, it is solely a matter of losing the path while practicing dhyāna, resulting in frantic interpretations and false reckonings;

this is precisely the skandha-māra. The various classes of beings are fundamentally identical to the basis of co-arising (*sahaja-āśraya*). Within these fundamental classes, those in whom the primordial element (*dhātu*) is revealed—
Within the common ground of arising, one perceives the primordial source of one's own activity. This profound, pure, and moving source is precisely the source of activity.

Having perceived this, one concludes that all arising and ceasing is perfectly complete within it; thus, one fails to further investigate the beginning and end of the causes of consciousness and instead establishes two theories of causelessness.
△ Second, the Theory of Causelessness (Ahetuvāda). This category has two parts.
From here downward, these ten types are all delusory insights arising from *dhyāna*. They all pertain to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Because the mind is applied in a conflicting manner, these realizations manifest.
First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause [for existence] (extending to: they fall into the paths of externalists and delude the nature of bodhi).
Once the mechanism of birth is destroyed, the faculties depart from their respective cavities, and the eyes become pure; thus, one is able to see sentient beings through and through.

The stream of karma winds and turns; following the rotation of karma, one cannot emerge from it on one's own. Because they have not yet escaped the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), their power of meditative concentration is limited;

thus, beyond eighty thousand kalpas, they remain in darkness with nothing to see. Because there is nothing to see, they reckon that there is fundamentally no cause. The "mechanism of birth" is completely shattered;
"mechanism" is a metaphor for agitation, which is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It does not constitute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Because it is covered, it is said to be "completely destroyed.
Second, this person sees that the end has no cause (up to the point mentioned); this is called the first type of non-Buddhist who establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
They falsely cling to the arising of roots and fail to comprehend the principle of transformation. They hold that man remains man until the end, and even black remains black without further change.
Consequently, they take this as an analogy for the self: seeing no path at the beginning, there is likewise no realization at the end; hence it is said that the end has no cause.
△ Second, the Theory of Pervasive Permanence: Its categories are four.
Ānanda, among these sons of good family within the *samādhi*... (until)... they have never been lost or scattered, and thus they reckon it to be permanent.

Due to the false conceptualization of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the fundamental source of arising and ceasing, one consequently gives rise to false conceptualizations regarding the mind, objects, the four great elements, the eight consciousnesses, formations, and so forth.
One may either negate arising and ceasing while conceptualizing permanence, or maintain arising and ceasing while conceptualizing permanence.
Some conceive of permanence through the recognition of a deity; others give rise to false views and conceive of permanence. Now, regarding this ultimate state of mind:

its nature is fundamentally without cause and without arising or ceasing. Therefore, by means of the principle of arising and ceasing among the sentient beings of the ten directions, all things are seen as circulating;

fundamentally, there is no dispersal or loss. This is to negate arising and ceasing while conceiving of permanence. For one whose aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, it relies upon...

Because they cultivate contemplation on the two dharmas of mind and mental objects, their spiritual power enables them to know events of twenty thousand kalpas; the subsequent cases of forty thousand and eighty thousand kalpas follow this same principle.
Second, these people exhaustively investigate the origin of the four great elements [until they realize] that it has never been dispersed or lost, and they reckon it to be permanent.
Sentient beings arise and perish in dependence upon earth, water, fire, and wind; yet the fundamental nature of these four elements is eternally abiding.
Thus, all phenomena subject to arising and perishing possess an essence that is eternal. This is the case of one who clings to arising and perishing while calculating them to be eternal.
Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties (up to) exhausting them without losing their fundamental nature, reckoning them as permanent.
The six sense faculties and the manas constitute the eight consciousnesses. Within mind, intellect, and consciousness, the original source is precisely the *vijñāna-ātman* (the consciousness-spirit).
The ultimate origin of the eight consciousnesses can only be exhausted by a Buddha or a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). If one can truly exhaust them, [one attains liberation].
Thus one enters the realm of knowledge, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness. Now, within this very mind, intellect, and consciousness, one attains their original source;
that is to say, their fundamental nature is eternally constant. Sentient beings rely upon it, dwelling in cyclic existence without ever losing it.
This is a deluded reckoning based on the consciousness of cognition (*vijñāna*).
Fourth, when this person has exhausted the source of ideation (*saṃjñā*), they take what is measured by the mind as being permanent.

"The source of ideation" refers to the aggregate of ideation (*saṃjñā-skandha*); "the physiological processes" refer to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). They falsely claim that the flux of arising and ceasing all belongs to ideation.
The mind has now been eternally extinguished; thus, it neither arises nor ceases. It is by natural principle that this belongs to the formations (*saṃskāra*).
Not knowing that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the very source of arising and ceasing, one gives rise to false views and engages in deluded reckoning.
Because of this calculation of permanence, one loses right universal knowledge (samyak-saṃbodhi); this is called the second heterodox school that establishes the doctrine of perfect permanence.
△ Fourth, the four inverted views: their categories are four.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*... [up to] ...that which undergoes arising and ceasing is the true nature of impermanence.
This wondrous clarity and perfect stillness is free from "I" and "mine. Yet, the heterodox outsiders falsely establish a "spiritual self" (*ātman*) therein;

from this they calculate a self that is singular, concentrated, and immovable, and thus take it to be permanent. Meanwhile, all sentient beings, regarding birth and death, calculate others to be impermanent.
Second, this person does not contemplate the mind [up to the point where] that which is indestructible throughout the kalpas is called "ultimate permanence.
This refers to the stages from the third dhyāna downward; because they are ultimately destroyed by the three calamities, they are termed "of an impermanent nature.
From the fourth dhyāna upward, the calamities cannot destroy them; thus, they are termed "ultimate permanence."
Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind [up to] that which flows forth from it, designating it as having an impermanent nature.
In the former case, they made a calculation of non-existence regarding a single phenomenon; in this case, they make two calculations regarding a single nature. Both are false conceptualizations.
Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted—up to its present total cessation—and thus names it "impermanence.

Yet, they regard it as being of one essence with the illusory aggregates, sharing the single characteristic of flux. Nevertheless, they cling to "this" and reject "that," clinging to the present while rejecting the past;
they take that which flows on to be permanent and that which undergoes transition to be extinction.
Based on this deliberation that one portion is impermanent [up to]... it is called the third heterodox doctrine of the "partially eternal" (ekadeśa-śāśvata-vāda).
△ Fourth, the Doctrine of Finitude (antavāda): Its categories are four;
furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi* [up to]... such a person falls into the four doctrines of finitude.
There are four stages, which are the stages of arising and ceasing.
The first is when the human mind calculates the origin of birth (up to) calculating the continuous mind and naming it "boundless."
The source of birth, the flow of activity, is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because of this shifting flow, one calculates across the three periods of time.

Since that which has passed has already perished and that which is yet to come has not yet appeared, it is called "having a limit. Because that which is presently manifest continues in succession, it is called "having no limit. Thus, one fails to know the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Fundamentally, it is neither finite nor infinite.
These two types of people, contemplating eighty thousand kalpas [and so forth], fail to attain a mind that is infinite and perceive only a finite nature.
I have previously stated that one merely perceives that person appearing within the scope of one's own cognition, yet is unable to know the universal nature of that person;
therefore, one reckons that nature as being finite.
Fourth, this person thoroughly investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)... [up to] what is called the fourth non-Buddhist who establishes the nature of finitude.
Fifth, the discourse of deceptive confusion. Its categories are four;
furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*... [up to] causing the person before them to lose the chapters and sentences.

This person contemplates the myriad transformations and perceives their lack of uniformity; consequently, divergent interpretations arise, and being unable to reach a definitive resolution, they distort and confuse their speech.
Second, this person carefully observes the mind [until] there is nothing further to be expressed beyond the elimination of non-existence.
Each and every [moment] is non-existent; this is the characteristic of momentary extinction.
Third, this person contemplates the mind with precision (up to: apart from this, there is nothing further to be spoken).
Each and every one has it; it is the characteristic of arising in every thought-moment.
Fourth is the person who holds views of both existence and non-existence (up to) the deathless, evasive, and pervasive conceptualization of false theories.
△ Six: Speculations Regarding Existence After Death.
**Primary Speculation:** Furthermore, among the various good sons within *samādhi* (up to the point where they) give rise to perverted thoughts regarding the signs of existence after death.

The "inexhaustible flow" refers to the continuity of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*). Because arising and ceasing are extinguished yet continue without interruption, one knows that there are characteristics following death.
Alternatively, some firmly cling to the body, saying, "Form is the self," and so on; thus they cycle through sixteen such characteristics.
The "prior form" refers to the color of the clouds before one's eyes; the continuity within the formations (*saṃskāra*) is also form.
Having made these four reckonings, the same applies to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*); thus, sixteen characteristics are established from this.
From this point, some may calculate that the two natures of ultimate affliction and ultimate bodhi proceed side by side, each without touching the other.

They further calculate regarding all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena that they ultimately proceed side by side; those who calculate that affliction and bodhi do not mutually suppress or extinguish one another all belong to the category of "having a future existence" (*punarbhava*).
Because of this reckoning that there is existence after death, [it leads to] the inverted discourse of the mind regarding the characteristics of existence after death.
△ Seven: Reckoning of Non-existence After Death.
**Primary Reckoning:** Furthermore, among the various sons of good family within *samādhi*... (until) ...thus circulating, there are eight aspects of non-characteristic.

The five aggregates (*skandha*) dissolve. This refers to the cessation of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*). Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the underlying physiological process;
that is to say, when feeling and perception cease, volitional formations also cease. This is discussed in terms of the four aggregates: the present cause vanishes, and the future fruit ceases.
When cause and effect are treated together, they constitute the eight characteristics (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*).
From this point, some calculate the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* (up to the point of) the inverted theory that after death there is no characteristic.
△ Eight: Calculating the Eight "Neither-Is-Nor-Is-Not" [Theories]. *Primary Calculation*: *Secondary Calculation*:
Furthermore, among the various sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to the point of) the inverted theory arising from the claim that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence.

The persistence of the formations (*saṃskāra*) is the presence of marks (*sanimitta*); the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) is the absence of marks (*animitta*). By analogy with these preceding and succeeding marks, that which persists ultimately does not exist;

though it exists, it is non-existent. That which ceases will eventually exist; though it is non-existent, it is not non-existent. Because the four aggregates (*skandha*) are thus dualistically reckoned, eight fallacies (*asat*) are established.
Within form, sensation, and perception, one perceives both existence and non-existence (up to: all say that after death there is either a sign or no sign).
The three aggregates cease. Although the signs exist fundamentally, they do not undergo transmigration; because the signs persist, one contemplates them as neither non-existent nor existent.
Following the attainment of any single condition, one may take up any one of the four aggregates within the [five] aggregates.

Furthermore, because they calculate that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and distortion, their minds give rise to a false awakening wherein both existence and non-existence are negated, and both the empty and the real are lost.

"All conditioned phenomena" refers to all dharmas that are in a state of flux. Because they perceive that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is unstable and shifting, they consequently develop a perverse realization, claiming that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent and cannot be definitively pointed out.

From this, they engage in speculative reasoning regarding the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" state after death, leading to the inverted doctrine that [the self] exists as neither-perception-nor-non-perception after death.
△ Ninth: Speculation on Annihilation. Regarding the primary and secondary speculations:
Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi*... [as previously described]... these persons fall into the seven doctrines of annihilation.

Observing that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) perishes moment by moment, they designate this as "subsequent non-existence. Based on this false conceptualization, they conclude that even if one enters the seven stations of humans and gods, all will ultimately be annihilated.
Some reckon on the extinction of the body, or on the extinction of desire (up to) its manifest extinction; once extinguished, it no longer exists.
The extinction of the body refers to the two realms of humans and devas within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The extinction of desire refers to the first dhyāna.

The extinction of suffering refers to the second dhyāna. Extreme bliss refers to the third dhyāna. Extreme equanimity refers to the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). These are called the seven limits (*sapta-koṭi*). That is to say:
The phenomena of the seven limits all manifest and then perish; they do not arise again and ultimately return to total extinction.
Based on this speculative calculation, one falls into the inverted view that there is annihilation after death—namely, the theory of annihilation after death.
△ Ten Calculations on Nirvana: Correct Calculations and Peripheral Calculations.
Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi* (up to) "thus circulating through five locations to their ultimate conclusion."

"Transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti) means transforming birth-and-death into nirvāṇa. One may awaken to the principle of perfect luminosity within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereby the desire realm itself becomes the locus of transformation;

or one may take the first dhyāna as the locus of transformation because it is free from desire, the second dhyāna because it is free from suffering, and the third dhyāna because of its supreme joy and equanimity.
These are called the five nirvāṇas. It is not realized that all of these still belong to the realm of existence (*bhava*).
It is with outflows; it is not an unconditioned fruit; it is not the ultimate state.
Based on this conceptualization, one regards the five [aggregates] as nirvāṇa in the present, [proceeding] until one acts as a Great Awakened King, providing a pure guiding point.

Wuxing said: "This refers to the 'demon of the mind' (*citta-māra*). Later, in the section on the *vijñāna-skandha*, it is called the 'demon of views,' which is precisely the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).
5. Regarding the *vijñāna-skandha*:
"Ānanda, that good man cultivates *samādhi*... [up to] ...this is then called the domain of the *vijñāna-skandha*."

This is a general exposition on the cessation of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) and the manifestation of consciousness. *Saṃskāra* is the essential nature of the world’s flux and movement;
it is the pivotal cord that agitates the mechanism of life, and the deep-seated pulse through which the *pudgala* (individual) reaps the fruits of karma.

It is capable of obscuring the celestial realm of the true nature (*dharmatā*), causing the six sense faculties to gallop wildly, and disturbing the inner stillness. It serves as the ultimate pivot for the floating sense organs and their objects. Therefore, when the *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, birth...

The mechanism’s taut cord and knot suddenly snap asunder; the resonance between stimulus and response is severed, yet the celestial nature of one's inherent being is about to awaken with great clarity.

The six sense faculties no longer scatter or run wild. Because they do not scatter or run wild, both the internal and external become profoundly lucid; because there is no longer a pivot-hole through which they might turn, [the mind remains unmoved].
The person has nowhere to enter; they turn from movement back to stillness, becoming deeper and yet deeper, hence it is called "inner and outer.

The *nirvāṇa*-nature, like the sky, is covered by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and is as obscured as the long night. When the first three aggregates are exhausted, it is like the first crowing of a rooster;

although this is a sign of dawn, one is still submerged in the remaining two aggregates, and the subtle colors have not yet been distinguished. This is the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), like the rooster’s subsequent crowing.
Only one aggregate remains; thus, through this great illumination, one attains awakening. The primary source of receiving life is the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Because the activity of formations (*saṃskāra*) ceases and consciousness manifests, one deeply penetrates it. Since it has no pivot-hole, it can be observed; since it has no flux, it can be grasped; since it has no triggering mechanism, it cannot be summoned.
Consequently, one realizes that the environment and its inhabitants throughout the ten directions are all transformations of consciousness. Thus, one has already attained it.
It is the same. The essence of the nature-heaven (*dharmatā*), though not yet fully clear and penetrating, has already begun to gradually manifest its subtle and secret characteristics;
this is the characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
If, within the collective summons already attained, one reaches the point where inverted false conceptions are taken as the root—
this "collective summons" refers to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), the life-source of the twelve classes of beings— if, within this state,
one uses the power of concentration and wisdom to dissolve the six gates, so that the sense faculties merge without division and the objective realms open without obstruction, then...

Seeing and hearing are perfected and mutually penetrating; the six sense faculties function interchangeably. Consequently, there is no further obstruction between the external world and the internal body-mind.
This is the sign of the exhaustion of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). The nature of wood is one true reality, yet it is separated by dust;

between the nature and its functions, the standards for sameness and difference are lost, which is termed the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kāṣāya*). This constitutes the substance of the *vijñāna-skandha*; therefore, when consciousness is exhausted, [the turbidity is cleared].
Thus, the consciousness that transcends [the senses] is but a shadowy manifestation of deluded awakening; it fundamentally lacks an intrinsic nature and arises from inversion.
Therefore, it is termed "phantom-like, void, inverted, and delusory thought."
△ Delusory Understanding of the Aggregate of Consciousness. Its categories number ten.
Ānanda, you should know that such good sons (up to) turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa and give rise to the seeds of external paths.

Consciousness flows from formative activities (*saṃskāra*); therefore, when consciousness is empty, it returns to its source. Since the aggregate of formative activities (*saṃskāraskandha*) is already empty, birth and death have been extinguished.

Yet, because one still relies upon the source of consciousness, quiescent extinction is not yet perfected; nevertheless, one can gradually shatter the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and dissolve the six sense-gates.
Therefore, the six faculties of cognition (*ṣad-vijñāna-indriya*) are already merged without separation; the natures of all categories of perception are universally harmonized and non-dual.

Thus, one is able to enter the Perfect Origin (*yuan-yuan*). This Perfect Origin is precisely the fusion of the faculties and their separations, penetrating the fundamental source of consciousness across all categories.
If one takes this to be the true ground of return and establishes it as the "True Cause," one falls into the attachment to causes and what is caused. For [this] is the True...

Causes are not objects; all that exists as an object is illusory. The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists identify the primordial, obscure state prior to the manifestation of the *ālayavijñāna* as the true cause to which one returns;
this is exactly the same [as the aforementioned error]. This is because their minds maintain the notion of something to be attained.
If there is a fruit to which one returns, then both cause and fruit fall into the realm of the delusory. Thus, one violates perfect penetration and turns one's back on Nirvana.
When people today encounter true nature, they immediately give rise to the conscious mind, calculating cause and effect to form views and understandings.
To have something attained and something to which to return is merely to attain the source of consciousness and return to the obscure principle (amūrta-tattva).

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man exhausts all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to the point of emptiness—[extending] up to generating great pride and becoming a universal lord (*vibhu*)—he takes the fundamental consciousness (*vijñāna*) as his own self-nature.
He then claims that all sentient beings flow forth from this, thereby clinging to the notion "I can produce them," even though in reality he cannot.
Therefore, it is called "clinging to the capable as incapable. Maheśvara is [the embodiment of] form.
The Lord of the Summit (Māra) is also one who falsely conceives, "I am able to manifest the categories of both sentient beings and non-sentient beings.
That which is capable of being the mind, the capacity, and the fruit of an action depends upon my ability to act as its basis and to accomplish that task.
Great pride (*mahāmāna*) is precisely *heḍara*.
Furthermore, good sons, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to) turning their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa, they produce the seeds of inverted perfection.
Because they take the fundamental source of consciousness as their refuge, they doubt that it can give rise to themselves and all dharmas;
they consequently reckon the place from which these arise and flow forth to be the true, eternal, and non-arising essence. This, however, exists within the realm of arising and ceasing.

They falsely conceptualize [the self] as eternally abiding. Having already been deluded regarding the nature of true non-arising, they further confuse the perception of phenomena that arise and perish, taking the impermanent to be permanent;

thus it is called the "clinging to permanence and impermanence. Since they calculate that this [self] can produce the "I," they are identical to those who calculate that Īśvara can produce all things.
Because both rely on the source of consciousness to falsely conceptualize eternal abiding, it is called a "false cause."

Based on the mind, the fruit of false discrimination is established. The former [discrimination] conceives that the self produces the external world; this [discrimination] conceives that the external world produces the self.
Therefore, it is called "perverted roundness.
Furthermore, O son of good family, one who exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to: turning their back on the city of Nirvāṇa) gives rise to the seeds of perverted cognition.

That which is known is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness) that is observed. This means that consciousness possesses the capacity for cognition, and all phenomena arise through the transformations of this cognition.
Consequently, by conceptualizing the essence of cognition as being perfectly pervasive throughout all phenomena, various divergent interpretations were established;

namely, the claim that even insentient things are everywhere endowed with cognition, and because there is no discrimination, it is called "indiscriminate, pervasive cognition. Thus, this takes non-cognition to be cognition. Therefore—
This is called giving rise to the attachment of knowing and not-knowing. The two non-Buddhist teachers, Pāṭa and Sāṇi, cling to the notion that all things possess cognition;
that is, they cling to the view that everything has consciousness. This erroneous calculation takes perfect knowledge as the cause of the mind, yet the result will ultimately be empty and false.
To take what lacks consciousness as being conscious is inverted knowledge.
Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to) turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seeds of delusive transformations.

As for the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*): it involves the dissolution of the six gates so that the various faculties function interchangeably. At present, this has not yet been fully exhausted;

one has merely attained compliance with it. Because of this compliance and the mutual interchangeability, one then reckons that all dharmas are capable of universal transformation, and thus gives rise to [deluded views].
"Superior fruits": this refers to [the belief that] fire can manifest light, and so on, up to the claim that dust can bring about the formation of the physical world.

Consequently, they engage in perverse seeking and perverse contemplation, diligently honoring and serving these things with the conviction that they can produce superior fruits, when in reality they cannot.
Therefore, this is called "clinging to the non-arising of what arises. This refers to those such as the three Kāśyapas and other groups of non-Buddhists; they are deluded regarding the true mind.
To seek hope from external objects is for both cause and effect to be false; such a perverted transformation of principle is called the seed of distorted transformation.

Furthermore, O son of good family, to exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (until one reaches the point of) turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa and giving rise to the seed of nihilism.
Observing that principles are not real, they mistakenly fall into nihilism; thus, within the perfectly luminous nature, they calculate everything to be empty and void.

Consequently, they extinguish all manifestations and return to eternal extinction, yet remain unaware that this is erroneous. This is called the attachment to "non-attainment" (or the attachment to returning to nothingness).
*Śūnyatā* is translated here as "emptiness" (*kōng*). To speak of "non-conceptual emptiness" (*múxiǎng shùnyuò*) refers to the non-Buddhist practitioners who cling to emptiness.

Because they cling to a nihilistic emptiness, they take the mind that seeks the cause of perfect, void, and unconditioned existence and instead produce the fruit of nihilistic annihilation, wherein the basis for existence is forever extinguished.
This is precisely the nirvana of the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness—up to turning one’s back on the city of Nirvana and giving rise to the seeds of delusion—the consciousness-aggregate (vijñānaskandha) becomes brilliant and pure, abiding in a state of profound stillness without fluctuation; this is called "permanence. Now, seeing this permanence, one clings to form.
The body is likewise this same refined perfection. The body is fundamentally impermanent and truly not to be craved as something enduring.
Yet now you cling to it with firm attachment; thus it is said that craving is not merely craving, but an attachment.

Asita—here translated as "Longevity Immortal"—though he extended his life-span, ultimately returned to destruction. Now, to seek to solidify this deluded body in hopes of long-term abiding is but empty toil.
The ear falsely prolongs the ear.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to emptiness—[continuing] until—you turn your back on the city of Nirvāṇa and are born into the lineage of celestial Māras.

Taking the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as the root of life, it interpenetrates the three periods of time. [They think: "If this aggregate of consciousness were to end, my life would end."

They too will eventually be exhausted. Who then can realize the true and eternal? Consequently, while in meditative concentration, they transform various objects of desire in order to retain the dust of afflictions and prevent them from being extinguished.
Relying on such perverse thoughts, they seek to realize the true and eternal, yet remain unaware that this is not so; this is called "clinging to the non-true as true.
Takṣaka (吒枳迦羅) is able to transform objects of desire for his own amusement; he is the Lord of Desire at the Peak of Desire (*Kāmadhātu*).
This is the category [of retribution]. Due to such perverse thoughts, one invokes the birth of celestial Māras; indulging solely in worldly desires is called the "blazing fruit of the world.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when one exhausts all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness (up to: turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa), one gives rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
The "Instructor of Life" profoundly investigates the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and deeply clarifies the causes and conditions by which sentient beings receive their life-span.
Since birth and death arise from consciousness, while refinement and coarseness arise from karma, he relies upon the Four Noble Truths for analytical discernment.

He regards suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as coarse and false, and cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as refined and true. Thereupon, he focuses exclusively on cultivating the cause of the Path to seek the realization of the fruit of cessation. By means of this small...
This constitutes their "sufficiency"; thus they abide in cessation and immediately rest. These are the ranks of the śrāvakas who possess overweening pride.

Herein, the "perfectly refined" (yuanjing) should be taken as the causal mind, which achieves the minor fruit of entering quiescence. This "perfectly refined" [state] is precisely the decisive resolution of coarse karma.
They seek only the subtle response and realize the partial truth; they remain entangled in emptiness and proceed toward quiescence alone. Thus, they turn their backs on the path of purity.
"Purity" refers to the virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; among these four virtues, only one is briefly mentioned here.

Furthermore, when the good man exhausts the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (up to the point where) the arising of awareness becomes perfectly luminous and does not transform into a fixed seed, the fused and pure luminosity of awareness is precisely the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
Although it is free from the habits of delusion and is perfectly integrated, pure, and clear, it has not yet transcended consciousness;
therefore, it is called "luminous awareness" (*jue-ming*). If one were to take this as profound and subtle, establishing it as a realized fruit, then it would constitute a fixed nature.

They are merely pratyekabuddhas and solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*). This is precisely the *yong-hui* (the submerged) as the causal mind, which achieves the stagnant fruit of profound clarity (*zhan-ming*).

"Profound clarity" refers to the perfectly interfused awakening-clarity (*yuan-rong jue-ming*). What is awakened to stops at perfect brightness; the essence of consciousness becomes fixed in its nature and does not turn back.
Therefore, it is called "the perfection of awakening-clarity that does not transform into the perfect seed. The above has set forth the fifty demonic states.

All these are the refined essence of consciousness; they involve erroneous interpretations and heterodox awakenings, failing to attain right view. Whenever one directs the mind or stirs a thought, one falls into this state.
Even those who have realized the stage of a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer) still remain deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.
Therefore, the Awakened Sovereign spoke with bitter earnestness and bestowed his compassion, analyzing the matter with a piercing mind, desiring that people neither be deluded nor lose their way.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* (up to) their initial accomplishment ensure that one does not encounter byways.
The former obstructs the demons of the mind; these obstruct the demons of views.
Thus, this Dharma-door, from its origins in past lives until its ultimate cultivation and final instructions, [is complete].
△ The thirtieth and final request for instruction:

Having been slightly abridged, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying, "As the Buddha has taught... (up to)... the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise identical to delusive thought."
To clarify that delusion is causeless is to show that it cannot be subjected to speculative calculation. If one knows where delusion arises, one may speak of its causes and conditions;
if one does not know where it arises, how can there be causes and conditions? Furthermore, to infer that it is "spontaneous" (svabhāva) is surely nothing other than a false conceptualization.
△ The False Root of the Five Aggregates △ 1. The Root of Form: Firmness.
Your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents; (up to: it is called the first false thought of firmness.
Perception is a false and illusory image; the deep-seated channels of craving for desire are the residual body that flows forth from one's own perception of self-love.

Therefore, it is said that the body arises from the parents due to perception, and the five aggregates arise from the mind which rides upon perception. Because one seeks in darkness through craving, it is said that the mind transmits life within perception.
As stated in the *Kōmyō* (Acid Plum) and other treatises, this serves as proof that the body arises from false attachments; thus, it accords with the principle of falsity. If...
If it were not for false conceptualization, then delusion could not produce a response. The body arises because of thought; the mind arises because of thought;
life is transmitted because of thought. As various thoughts intersect and solidify, they form the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); therefore, it is called "solidified false conceptualization."
△ Second, experiencing the fundamental void-luminosity is precisely what is here described as the "mind contemplating loftiness" (up to) "is called the second delusion of void-luminosity.

While it is a mere empty contemplation of loftiness, there is a genuine sensation of bitterness and astringency. Both the adverse and the favorable are illusory, yet they manifest as loss and gain. Thus one rushes about.
The aggregate of sensation has no substance; it is empty yet possesses clarity. Therefore, it is called the delusive thought of "empty clarity.
△ Third, the root of perception is interpenetrating:
from "because of your thoughts and reflections, they cause your physical body" (up to) "is named the third delusive thought of interpenetration."

Thoughts and deliberations are empty phenomena; the physical body is substantial reality. Though the empty and the substantial are of different natures, that they can influence one another is due to their being integrated through *saṃjñā* (perception/conception).

The mind gives rise to empty images, while the form grasps substantial objects. Though the functions of mind and form differ, that they can correspond with one another is due to their being connected through *saṃjñā*.
This extends even to the disturbances and transformations of waking and sleeping, whereby the mind is made to follow its objects.
Objects follow the mind; all are the fusion of delusive thoughts. △ Fourth:
The essence of activity is profound and hidden;
the principle of transformation does not abide, but shifts and moves subtly and incessantly... (until) it is called the fourth delusive thought, "the profound and hidden."
△ The five consciousnesses are fundamentally formless;
furthermore, as for that place where your clarity and brilliance are profound and unmoving... up to "the fifth, inverted, subtle, and refined conception.
If this were a refined truth, it could not admit the practice of delusion. This refutes its permanence. "Clarity" refers to clarity and brilliance; "truth" refers to...
It is constant. For what reason? To demonstrate below the characteristics of deluded habituation: when one formerly beheld a marvelous object, its seed was deposited within consciousness.
If it were not perfumed [by that experience], then upon beholding that same strange thing again, there would necessarily be no recollection.

Since there is no loss of memory, we know that in the interim, ignorance constantly perfumes [the mind] from moment to moment. This perfuming is itself delusion; how could there be any refined or true nature therein? It is as if non-existent.
It is called "non-existence" (*wang*). That which appears as if existing is called "semblance" (*xiang*).
△ Regarding the limits of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*):

Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādāna-skandha*) arise from the five false imaginings... [up to] ...the profound penetration merging with the profound, returning to the limit of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the statement that the five aggregates (skandhas) arise from causes and realms (dhātus): fundamentally, there are no realms; they arise due to the cause of deluded conceptualization.
△ As for the sequence of the cessation of the aggregates:
these five aggregates originally arise in a layered succession... (up to)... what is it that you do not understand? Please inquire about this once more.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likened to the *karpāsa* cloth; form (*rūpa*) is likened to the final knot. Since the knots exist based on the cloth, their arising has consciousness as its cause.
Since their untying follows a sequence, their cessation proceeds from the removal of form. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise from the subtle to the coarse:
through delusion one perceives consciousness, and so on, up to the perception of form through sensation (*vedanā*). Their cessation, however, proceeds from the coarse to [the subtle].
"Subtle. It is necessary to break down form before sensation manifests, and so on, until one breaks down formations before consciousness manifests. "In principle, there is sudden enlightenment;
with enlightenment, [delusions] are eliminated all at once," means that just as the cloth originally did not exist, the knots likewise do not exist.

"In practice, it is not suddenly removed, but is exhausted through successive stages," means that those of middling capacity must necessarily rely on gradual cultivation. If one were to forget cultivation because of enlightenment, then...

There are those who possess understanding but lack practice; they cling to principle while being deluded regarding phenomena. Having fallen into partiality and deviation, they ultimately do not engage in right cultivation.
True samādhi—you should take this root of delusive thought [and proceed] until you know that there is nirvāṇa and no longer cling to the three realms.
May you, by means of this principle, awaken yourself and awaken others, forever severing the source of delusion and together returning to the ultimate fruit.
Ānanda, if there were another person who filled the ten directions... [up to] ...that which cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
The ten pārājikas are the ten grave offenses.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra... [up to] they all rejoice greatly, pay homage, and depart.
